Long-term concrete behavior references a function through a LongTerm, Concrete dataline, while tendon relaxation may directly reference a prestressing DB item through a LongTerm, Tendon dataline. vonMises Uses DB elastic properties and allows the Fy field-token in the value hardening yield position. UGeneric Uses concrete DB items indirectly through concrete envelope functions, and references a ConcreteTime function through a LongTerm, Concrete dataline for long-term concrete behavior. USteel Creates a Menegotto-Pinto-family input from a rebar or prestressing DB item plus a recipe token. Tendon relaxation may directly reference a prestressing DB item through a LongTerm, Tendon dataline. Tresca Replaces only the elastic-property first dataline; Fy may be used in the yield position. MohrCoulomb Replaces only the elastic-property first dataline. DruckerPrager Replaces only the elastic-property first dataline. ConcreteDamage Replaces only the elastic-property first dataline.

DB reference input uses the default density listed above. If a different density is needed, use material-db-item[, density][, ToDirectForm] and override only density. E, nu, alpha, and recipe values still come from the DB; the override density is a direct numeric value in the current global UnitSystem.

UGeneric does not accept concrete DB items directly in the material dataline. Use concrete DB items first in ParabolaCEnv, HognestadCEnv, EC2CEnv, MPPCEnv, or MaekawaTEnv, then reference the generated function name as EnvFunc. Concrete long-term behavior references a separate ConcreteTime function through a LongTerm, Concrete dataline. These concrete function DB inputs also require a prior global UnitSystem where the selected function type requires it. The current built-in concrete DB item forms are KDS-2026-C<fck>, ACI318-2025-C<fck>, and EC2-2004-C<fck> for envelope functions, and KDS-2026-C<fck>, EC2-2004-C<fck>, and ACI209-1992-C<fc> for ConcreteTime; the allowed standards depend on the selected function type as described in the *Function manual.

Define isotropic elasticity material

 E, nu, alpha, density

Choose only one of the three LongTerm dataline forms shown above.

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• E: elastic modulus (required)
  • nu: Poisson’s ratio (optional, default 0.)
  • alpha: thermal expansion coefficient (optional, default 0.)
  • density: Density for the direct numeric dataline (optional, default 0.). In a DB dataline, omitted density means the DB density, not 0.
  • material-db-item: material DB item name. It replaces E, nu, alpha, and density with DB elastic properties. If density follows the DB item, that value overrides only density; otherwise, the DB density is used.
  • ToDirectForm: Optional final DB dataline token. It expands the DB input to direct numeric values when saved or reprinted.

docs.title: LongTerm, Concrete dataline
docs.text:
• timeFunction: Name of a *Function, Type=ConcreteTime function. Standard ConcreteTime functions evaluate concrete age variables in day units.
  • nchain: Number of Kelvin chains (optional, default 4).
  • lambda1: First retardation time \(\lambda_1\) (optional). Enter this value in days. If omitted, the referenced ConcreteTime function supplies its internal default. Specify lambda1 here to override that Function-side default for this material.
  • nsample: Number of creep compliance fitting samples (optional, default 10*nchain). It must be larger than nchain.

The time variable \(t\) for long-term material models comes from ELTIME, the element elapsed physical time after activation. ELTIME starts at 0 when the element is activated and advances by physical-time step increments. To represent concrete age before loading, use an unloaded Static, Quasi step instead of an initial-age field in LongTerm, Concrete.

Do not combine LongTerm, Concrete and LongTerm, Tendon in the same IsoElasticity material.

docs.title: LongTerm, Tendon dataline
docs.text:
• standard: KDS-2025 or EC2-2004.
  • class: Relaxation class, one of Class1, Class2, or Class3.
  • fp: Characteristic tensile strength used in the stress ratio. Use \(f_{pu}\) for KDS-2025 and \(f_{pk}\) for EC2-2004. Direct numeric input uses the stress unit of the current global UnitSystem; in an N-mm unit system this is MPa(\(N/mm^2\)).
  • material-db-item: Prestressing material DB item name. The DB item supplies the standard, relaxation class, and characteristic tensile strength, converted from the DB source unit to the stress unit of the current global UnitSystem.
  • rho1000: Optional 1000-hour relaxation loss in percent. If omitted, the DB item value or class default is used; class defaults are 8 for Class1, 2.5 for Class2, and 4 for Class3.

docs.title: Theory and behavior
docs.text:
IsoElasticity + LongTerm, Concrete is interpreted as isotropic linear aging viscoelasticity. The E in the first dataline is used as the reference-age elastic modulus, and the elastic-modulus age factor \(a_E(t)\) from ConcreteTime defines the modulus at the current element elapsed time \(t\).

\[ E(t)=a_E(t)E_{28},\qquad G(t)= rac{E(t)}{2(1+ u)} \]

Stress is computed from the current-age elastic matrix \(\mathbf{D}_{ u}(E(t))\) and the elastic strain obtained after subtracting long-term nonmechanical strains.

\[ \sigma(t) = \mathbf{D}_{ u}(E(t)) \left[ \varepsilon(t) -\varepsilon^{cr}(t) -\varepsilon^{sh}(t) -\varepsilon^{ag}(t) -\varepsilon^{th}(t) ight] \]

Here, \( u\) is the IsoElasticity Poisson's ratio; there is no separate creep Poisson ratio input. \( ar{\mathbf{S}}_{ u}\) is the normalized isotropic compliance obtained by setting \(E=1\).

\[ \varepsilon^{cr}(t) = \int_0^{t} C(t, au)\, ar{\mathbf{S}}_{ u}\,d\sigma_c( au) \]

For LongTerm, Concrete, creep is driven by the compressive principal-stress path. The stress vector is first converted to a symmetric stress tensor, then split in principal space:

\[ oldsymbol{\sigma}^c = \sum_i \min(\sigma_i,0)\,\mathbf{n}_i\otimes\mathbf{n}_i \]

The creep-driving increment is \(\Delta oldsymbol{\sigma}^c_n= oldsymbol{\sigma}^c_{n+1}- oldsymbol{\sigma}^c_n\), converted back to the material stress-vector order before applying the normalized compliance. This split applies compression along each principal direction and handles tension-compression crossing at zero stress. If principal directions are rotated from the element axes, the reconstructed compressive tensor can contain shear components.

This definition has the following implications. Because tensile stress history does not contribute directly to creep history, time-dependent deformation along non-compressive paths — such as the tensile region after prestressing or near-cracking tensile loading — is not represented, and how conservative the result is depends on the stress state. In multiaxial form the compressive stress tensor is passed through the isotropic normalized compliance \( ar{\mathbf{S}}_{ u}\), so a tensile principal direction orthogonal to a compressive one still receives a lateral creep strain scaled by \(- u\). When a step crosses from compression to tension, \(\Delta oldsymbol{\sigma}^c_n\) enters as an unloading increment that removes the existing compressive stress and partially recovers the chain history, and during a subsequent tensile interval the chain state still decays by \(\exp(-\Delta t_n/\lambda_\alpha)\).

The ConcreteTime function supplies \(C(t, au)\) as creep compliance, and \( au\) is the loading age of each compressive stress-path increment. In incremental analysis, this history integral is approximated by a Kelvin chain. With nchain equal to \(m\), the retardation times are:

\[ \lambda_\alpha=\lambda_1\,10^{\alpha-1},\qquad \alpha=1,\dots,m \]

For each loading age \( au\), the coefficients \(c_\alpha( au)\) are fitted to the target ConcreteTime creep compliance by least squares over logarithmically spaced sample times \(s_j\). The sample range is from \(\lambda_1/3\) to \(2\lambda_m\), and the number of samples is nsample.

\[ C( au+s, au) \approx \sum_{\alpha=1}^{m} c_\alpha( au) \left(1-\exp\left[- rac{s}{\lambda_\alpha} ight] ight) \] \[ \min_{c_\alpha} \sum_j \left[ C( au+s_j, au) - \sum_{\alpha=1}^{m} c_\alpha( au) \left(1-\exp\left[- rac{s_j}{\lambda_\alpha} ight] ight) ight]^2 \]

The implementation stores internal variables \(\mathbf{q}^{\alpha}_n\) instead of reintegrating the full stress history. For a time increment \(\Delta t_n=t_{n+1}-t_n\), the existing chain history produces the creep-strain increment, and the new compressive stress-path increment is stored as the next chain history.

\[ \Delta\varepsilon^{cr}_n = \sum_{\alpha=1}^{m} \left(1-\exp\left[- rac{\Delta t_n}{\lambda_\alpha} ight] ight) \mathbf{q}^{\alpha}_{n} \] \[ \mathbf{q}^{\alpha}_{n+1} = \mathbf{q}^{\alpha}_{n}\exp\left[- rac{\Delta t_n}{\lambda_\alpha} ight] + c_\alpha(t_{n+1}) ar{\mathbf{S}}_{ u}\Delta\sigma^c_n rac{\lambda_\alpha}{\Delta t_n} \left(1-\exp\left[- rac{\Delta t_n}{\lambda_\alpha} ight] ight) \]

For \(\Delta t_n=0\), the final time-integration factor is treated as 1. Shrinkage is a stress-independent time strain supplied by ConcreteTime. Shrinkage and thermal strains are applied only in isotropic normal directions.

\[ \varepsilon^{sh}(t) = \varepsilon^{sh}(t)\mathbf{m},\qquad \varepsilon^{th} = \alpha\,\Delta T\,\mathbf{m} \]

\(\mathbf{m}\) is \([1]\) for uniaxial states, [1,1,0,1] for plane-family states, and [1,1,1,0,0,0] for 3D and shell-family states. EAG is the aging correction strain stored so that changing \(E(t)\) with age does not create an artificial stress jump. At the new time \(t_{n+1}\), the elastic strain matching the previous stress \(\sigma_n\) is recomputed, and the difference is stored in EAG.

\[ \varepsilon^{ag}_{n+1} = \varepsilon^{e}_{n} + \varepsilon^{ag}_{n} - rac{1}{E(t_{n+1})} ar{\mathbf{S}}_{ u}\sigma_{n} \]

In output, ELTIME is the element elapsed physical time after activation, and this value is used as the time variable \(t\) for long-term material behavior. ECR, ESH, and EAG are the creep, shrinkage, and aging-correction strains. ETH is thermal strain, and ENM is reported as:

\[ \varepsilon^{\mathrm{NM}} = \varepsilon^{\mathrm{CR}} +\varepsilon^{\mathrm{SH}} +\varepsilon^{\mathrm{AG}} +\varepsilon^{\mathrm{TH}} \]

Plane-family output components use [11, 22, 12, 33]; 3D and shell-family outputs use [11, 22, 33, 12, 23, 31].

IsoElasticity + LongTerm, Tendon is supported only in uniaxial stress conditions. Relaxation is evaluated only when the current tendon stress is tensile. The time increment is taken from the TUnit of the active Static, Quasi step and converted to hours for the standard formula. Re-tensioning or stress changes are modeled by the existing *State commands; the material input itself does not carry a jacking schedule.

The relaxation loss is accumulated monotonically and converted to a nonmechanical strain increment with the initial elastic modulus \(E_0\). This strain contributes to ENM and E, while no separate relaxation field is reported. See the USteel LongTerm, Tendon theory description for the standard equation and incremental update rule.

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• E1, E2, E3: Elastic moduli(required)
  • G12, G23, G31: Shear moduli (required)
  • nu12, nu23, nu31: Poisson's ratios(required)
  • a1,a2,a3: thermal expansion coefficient (optional, default 0)
  • density: density(optional, default 0.)
  • angle: angle in laminar condition for *Section, Type=CompositeShell (optional, default 0.)
  • cs: material coordinate system(optional). If not given, global coordinate system is used for material coordinates

Angle is the angle used to define the local coordinate system in the laminar stress condition when defining *Section, Type=CompositeShell. CS is used for all other stress conditions.

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• E: elastic modulus (required)
  • nu: Poisson’s ratio (optional, default 0.)
  • alpha: themal expansion coefficient (optional, default 0.)
  • density: Density for the direct numeric dataline (optional, default 0.). In a DB dataline, omitted density means the DB density, not 0.
  • material-db-item: material DB item name. It replaces E, nu, alpha, and density with DB elastic properties. If density follows the DB item, that value overrides only density; otherwise, the DB density is used.
  • ToDirectForm: Optional final DB dataline token. It expands the DB input to direct numeric values when saved or reprinted.

docs.title: Second data line for value (when the first entry is not a function name)
docs.text:
• yield: Initial yield value (required). If the first dataline used material-db-item, Fy may be used here to reference the DB yield strength.
  • H: slope after initial yield (optional, default 0)
  • theta: Mixed hardening parameter (optional, default 0)
  • Kinf: Saturation hardening parameter (optional, default 0)
  • K0: Saturation hardening parameter (optional, default 0)
  • delta: Saturation hardening parameter (optional, default 0)

docs.title: Second data line for function (when the first entry is a function name)
docs.text:
• isoHardFunc: Isotropic hardening function. (required)
  • kinHardFunc or H: Kinematic hardening function or modulus(optional, default 0)

When specified as value

When specified as value, the following equation is applied.

  • Linear mixed hardening model
\[ \begin{aligned} &K(\kappa) = \sigma_Y + \theta \bar{H} \kappa \\ &H'(\kappa) = (1-\theta) \bar{H}, ~ {\rm where,~} 0 \le \theta \le 1 \\ \end{aligned} \]
  • Saturation isotropic hardening and linear kinematic hardening model
\[ \begin{aligned} &K(\kappa) = \sigma_Y + \theta \bar{H} \kappa + ( \bar{K}_\infty- \bar{K}_0 )(1-exp(-\delta \kappa)) \\ &H'(\kappa) = (1-\theta) \bar{H}, ~ {\rm where,~} 0 \le \theta \le 1 \\ \end{aligned} \]

\(\bar{H}\) is a constant, and when \(\theta = 0\), only kinematic hardening is applied, while when \(\theta = 1\), only isotropic hardening is applied. The condition \(0 \le \theta \le 1\) must be satisfied. In the linear mixed hardening model, \(dK/d \kappa = (1-\theta)\bar{H}\) represents the isotropic hardening modulus, and \((1-\theta) \bar{H}\) is the kinematic hardening modulus.

If the conditions \(\bar{K}_\infty = \bar{K}_0\) or \(\delta = 0\) are satisfied, it corresponds to linear mixed hardening. In linear mixed hardening, \(\bar{H}\) can take negative values; however, in the saturation isotropic hardening and linear kinematic hardening model, the conditions \(\bar{H} \ge 0\), \(\bar{K}_\infty \ge \bar{K}_0 \gt 0\), and \(\delta \ge 0\) must be satisfied.

Fig. 7.2-1. Linear hardening

When specified as function

If uniaxial tensile test results for the material are available, proper calibration can be performed using them. In this case, the appropriate use of Type=Function can be applied. One important point to note is that when both isotropic hardening and kinematic hardening are present, the second elastic modulus must be configured to satisfy the equation as shown in Figure 7.2-2.

Fig. 7.2-2. Nonlinear hardening

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
# Linear isotropic hardening case
*Material, Type=vonMises, Name=steel1
 2000000.          # E, nu, alpha, density
 3000., 300.,1.    # yield, H, theta, Kinf, K0, delta

# Linear kinematic hardening case
*Material, Type=vonMises, Name=steel2
 2000000.        # E, nu, alpha, density
 3000., 300.,    # yield, H, theta, Kinf, K0, delta

# Nonlinear isotropic hardening case
*Function, Type=MultiLinear, Name=isoFunc
 0. 200.
 0.01 210.

*Material, Type=vonMises, Name=steel3
 200000.    # E, nu, alpha, density
 isoFunc    # isoHardFunc, kinHardFunc|H

# Nonlinear isotropic hardening, linear kinematic hardening case
*Material, Type=vonMises, Name=steel4
 200000.    # E, nu, alpha, density
 isoFunc, 20.      # isoHardFunc, kinHardFunc|H

# Nonlinear isotropic/kinematic hardening case
*Material, Type=vonMises, Name=steel5
 200000.    # E, nu, alpha, density
 isoFunc, kinFunc     # isoHardFunc, kinHardFunc|H

# Perfectly plastic steel from material DB
*Material, Type=vonMises, Name=SS275
 KDS-2026-SS275-t16
 Fy, 0, 1

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• E: elastic modulus (required)
  • nu: Poisson’s ratio (optional, default 0.)
  • alpha: themal expansion coefficient (optional, default 0.)
  • density: Density for the direct numeric dataline (optional, default 0.). In a DB dataline, omitted density means the DB density, not 0.
  • material-db-item: material DB item name. It replaces E, nu, alpha, and density with DB elastic properties. If density follows the DB item, that value overrides only density; otherwise, the DB density is used.
  • ToDirectForm: Optional final DB dataline token. It expands the DB input to direct numeric values when saved or reprinted.

docs.title: Second data line
docs.text:
• yield,dyield: initial yield value(required), and the derivative after initial yielding(optional, default 0.). If the first dataline used material-db-item, Fy may be used in the yield position.
  • yieldFunc: yield function(required)

docs.title: Optional last data line
docs.text:
• StrainHardening|IsotropicHardening: hardening type(optional, default “StrainHardening”)

The Tresca material model has the following yield function and flow potential:

\[ F({\sigma}, \kappa) = | \sigma_1 - \sigma_3 | - \sigma_Y (\kappa) \]

The hardening rule can apply strain hardening, work hardening, or the isotropic associative hardening rule. In the Tresca model, work hardening and associative isotropic hardening are identical.

Fig. 7.2-3. Tresca yield criteria

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• E: elastic modulus (required)
  • nu: Poisson’s ratio (optional, default 0.)
  • alpha: themal expansion coefficient (optional, default 0.)
  • density: Density for the direct numeric dataline (optional, default 0.). In a DB dataline, omitted density means the DB density, not 0.
  • material-db-item: material DB item name. It replaces E, nu, alpha, and density with DB elastic properties. If density follows the DB item, that value overrides only density; otherwise, the DB density is used.
  • ToDirectForm: Optional final DB dataline token. It expands the DB input to direct numeric values when saved or reprinted.

docs.title: Second data line
docs.text:
• coh,dcoh: initial value (required) and derivative of cohesion (optional, default 0.)
  • cohFunc: function name of cohesion function (required)

docs.title: Third data line (frictional quantities)
docs.text:
• fric,dfric: initial value(required) and derivative of friction angle. (optional, default 0.)
  • fricFunc: function name of friction angle function (required)

docs.title: Fourth data line (dilatant quantities)
docs.text:
• dila,ddila: initial value and derivative of dilatant angle (default 0., 0.)
  • dilaFunc: function name of dilatant function (optional)

docs.title: Optional last data line
docs.text:
• StrainHardening|IsotropicHardening: hardening type(optional, default “StrainHardening”)

The units for the frictional angle and dilatant angle are in degrees, not radians. If the value of the dilatant angle is equal to the frictional angle, the associative flow rule is applied. Otherwise, the non-associative flow rule is applied. The initial cohesion (cohesion0) must be specified as a non-zero value. When using the associative isotropic hardening (i.e., IsotropicHardening) as the hardening rule, constant frictional and dilatant angles must be used.

The Mohr-Coulomb material model uses the following yield function and plastic potential.

\[ F( \sigma, \kappa) = (\sigma_1 - \sigma_3) +(\sigma_1+\sigma_3) \sin \phi - 2 c(\kappa) \cos(\phi(\kappa)) \] \[ G( \sigma, \kappa) = (\sigma_1 - \sigma_3) +(\sigma_1+\sigma_3) \sin \psi - 2 c(\kappa) \cos(\psi(\kappa)) \]

Fig. 7.2-4. Mohr-Coulomb yield criteria

The hardening rules include strain hardening and isotropic hardening. The Mohr-Coulomb model does not include work hardening.

Define Isotropic elasticity material

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• E: elastic modulus (required)
  • nu: Poisson’s ratio (optional, default 0.)
  • alpha: themal expansion coefficient (optional, default 0.)
  • density: Density for the direct numeric dataline (optional, default 0.). In a DB dataline, omitted density means the DB density, not 0.
  • material-db-item: material DB item name. It replaces E, nu, alpha, and density with DB elastic properties. If density follows the DB item, that value overrides only density; otherwise, the DB density is used.
  • ToDirectForm: Optional final DB dataline token. It expands the DB input to direct numeric values when saved or reprinted.

docs.title: Second data line
docs.text: • beta: beta (required)

docs.title: 3<sup>rd</sup> data line
docs.text:
• coh, dcoh: initial value(required) and derivative of cohesion (optional, default 0.,0.)
  • cohFunc: function name of cohesion(required)

docs.title: 4<sup>th</sup> data line (frictional quantity)
docs.text:
• af, daf: initial value and derivative of alpha. ( default 0., 0.)
  • afFunc: function name of alpha (required)

docs.title: 5<sup>th</sup>  data line (dilatent quantity)
docs.text:
• ap, dap: initial value(required) and derivative of alphaP (dilatency) (optional, default 0.)
  • apFunc: function name of alphaP (required)

docs.title: Optional last data line
docs.text:
• StrainHardening|IsotropicHardening: hardening type(optional, default “StrainHardening”)

The units for the frictional angle and dilatant angle are in degrees, not radians. If the value of the dilatant angle is equal to the frictional angle, the associative flow rule is applied. Otherwise, the non-associative flow rule is applied. The initial cohesion (cohesion0) must be specified as a non-zero value. When using the associative isotropic hardening (i.e., IsotropicHardening) as the hardening rule, constant frictional and dilatant angles must be used.

In the Drucker-Prager material model, the yield function and plastic potential are as follows.

\[ F( \sigma, \kappa) = || s || + \alpha (\kappa) I_1 - \beta c(\kappa) \]

▪ Flow potential : same to yield function

\[ G( \sigma, \kappa) = || s || + \alpha_p (\kappa) I_1 \]

There are two types of hardening laws: strain hardening and isotropic hardening. In the Drucker–Prager model, work hardening does not exist.

Fig. 7.2-5. Flow rule of Drucker-Prager model

docs.title: 7.1.7 *Material, Type=ConcreteDamage [Reserved]
docs.text:
Define concrete damage plasticity material model.

*Material, Type=ConcreteDamage, Name=name
 E, nu, alpha, density | material-db-item[, density][, ToDirectForm]
 fc, Dc, wc
 ft, Dt, wt
 a, Kc, ap, ecc

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• E: elastic modulus (required for direct numeric input)
  • nu: Poisson's ratio (optional, default 0.)
  • alpha: thermal expansion coefficient (optional, default 0.)
  • density: Density for the direct numeric dataline (optional, default 0.). In a DB dataline, omitted density means the DB density, not 0.
  • material-db-item: material DB item name. It replaces only E, nu, alpha, and density with DB elastic properties. If density follows the DB item, that value overrides only density; otherwise, the DB density is used.
  • ToDirectForm: Optional last token for DB input. When used, save/reprint expands the DB input into direct numeric values in the current global UnitSystem.

docs.title: First data line and optional second data line
docs.text:
• Compression|Tension: Indicates whether the current line defines compression-side or tension-side properties.
  • EnvFunc: Envelope function (required)
  • Plastic|Secant|IEFunc: Specify function for plastic unloading, secant unloading, or damage plastic unloading (optional, default Plastic)

docs.title: LongTerm, Concrete data line
docs.text:
• timeFunction: Name of a *Function, Type=ConcreteTime function. Standard ConcreteTime functions evaluate concrete age variables in day units.
  • nchain: Number of Kelvin chains \(m\) (optional, default 4).
  • lambda1: First retardation time \(\lambda_1\) (optional). Enter this value in days. If omitted, the referenced ConcreteTime function supplies its internal default. Specify lambda1 here to override that Function-side default for this material.
  • nsample: Number of sampling points used for Kelvin chain fitting (optional, default 10*nchain). When specified directly, nsample > nchain is required.

Material time starts at 0 and advances by step time increments. Pre-loading concrete age is represented by an unloaded Static, Quasi step.

docs.title: Optional Last data line if necessary
docs.text:
• alpha: themal expansion coefficient (optional, default 0.)
  • density: density (optional, default 0.). UGeneric does not take a material DB item dataline, so enter density here directly. Even when EnvFunc names a concrete function created from DB input, that DB density is not applied automatically to UGeneric.

The UGeneric model is a uniaxial material model that allows independent definition of tension and compression behavior. In particular, it can be used as a simplified plastic-damage model for concrete by neglecting energy dissipation during unloading and reloading in compression. Independent failure envelopes must be defined for both compression and tension sides, and during unloading/reloading, one can choose between a plastic model without damage (hereafter referred to as plastic), a plastic-damage model (hereafter referred to as damage plastic), or a plastic-elastic model (hereafter referred to as damage elastic). If applying the plastic-damage model, unloading and reloading are carried out along the segment connecting the point corresponding to the most recent strain (\(\epsilon_{cun}\) or \(\epsilon_{tun}\) at point \((\epsilon_{cun},\sigma_{cun})\) or \((\epsilon_{tun},\sigma_{tun})\)) and the plastic strain specified by the plastic strain function (corresponding to \(\epsilon_{cpl}\) or \(\epsilon_{tpl}\)). Therefore, it is necessary to specify the function in the form of \((\epsilon_{cpl},\sigma_{cun})\) or \((\epsilon_{tpl},\sigma_{tun})\).

Concrete DB items such as KDS-2026-C<fck>, ACI318-2025-C<fck>, and EC2-2004-C<fck> are not entered directly in a UGeneric material dataline. Create envelope functions first with *Function, Type=ParabolaCEnv, HognestadCEnv, EC2CEnv, MPPCEnv, or MaekawaTEnv, then use those function names in the EnvFunc position. These Function DB inputs require a global UnitSystem. ParabolaCEnv generates section-analysis parameters, so do not mix it with general compressive envelope material properties.

Compression and tension envelopes are independent. MaekawaTEnv does not take a compression envelope name in its dataline; direct input is Ec, ft[, c], and DB input is KDS-2026-C<fck>|ACI318-2025-C<fck>|EC2-2004-C<fck>[, c][, ToDirectForm].

Fig. 7.2-6. Failure envelope, unloading/reloading of UGeneric

Fig. 7.2-7. Secant unloading/unloading of UGeneric

Under cyclic loading conditions, elastic behavior continues until the yield value corresponding to the plastic strain is reached, after which yielding follows the failure envelope. When secant loading/unloading is specified, there is no corresponding inelastic strain.

Fig. 7.2-8. Cyclic loading of UGeneric

Fig. 7.2-9. Cyclic loading of UGeneric for tensile secant unloading

docs.title: LongTerm, Concrete option
docs.text:
LongTerm, Concrete combines the compression and tension envelope functions defined above with a separate ConcreteTime function for aging, creep, and shrinkage. The material dataline itself does not accept concrete DB items such as KDS-2026-C<fck>, ACI318-2025-C<fck>, EC2-2004-C<fck>, or ACI209-1992-C<fc> directly. Put DB items in the appropriate *Function datalines, then reference the resulting function names from UGeneric.

The equations below summarize the time-dependent components used by this option. See the *Function manual for ConcreteTime DB input formats and allowed standards.

docs.title: LongTerm, Concrete time-dependent behavior
docs.text:
The ConcreteTime function provides age factors, creep compliance, and shrinkage strain through the following series.

\[ \left[a_c(t),\;a_t(t),\;a_E(t),\;c_r(t-\tau),\;c_l(\tau),\;\varepsilon^{sh}(t)\right] \]

The aging effect scales the 28-day envelope to the material properties at time \(t\).

\[ f_c(t)=a_c(t)f_c(28),\qquad f_t(t)=a_t(t)f_t(28),\qquad E_c(t)=a_E(t)E_c(28) \]

The aging effect creates an aging strain stored as EAG. For uniaxial concrete time-dependent material, the non-mechanical strain is split as follows.

\[ \varepsilon^{\mathrm{NM}} = \varepsilon^{\mathrm{CR}} +\varepsilon^{\mathrm{SH}} +\varepsilon^{\mathrm{AG}} +\varepsilon^{\mathrm{TH}} \]

Creep compliance is evaluated as a separated function of elapsed time after loading \(t-\tau\) and loading age \(\tau\).

\[ C(t,\tau)=c_r(t-\tau)c_l(\tau) \]

UGeneric + LongTerm, Concrete approximates this creep compliance with a Kelvin chain. With nchain equal to \(m\), the retardation times are arranged as follows.

\[ \lambda_\alpha=\lambda_1 10^{\alpha-1},\qquad \alpha=1,\dots,m \]

The Kelvin moduli \(E_\alpha(\tau)\) are identified by least-squares fitting to the target creep compliance.

\[ C(t,\tau)\approx \sum_{\alpha=1}^{m} \frac{1}{E_\alpha(\tau)} \left(1-\exp\left(-\frac{t-\tau}{\lambda_\alpha}\right)\right) \]

For LongTerm, Concrete, creep uses only the compressive stress path. In uniaxial form this is \(\Delta\sigma^c_n=\min(\sigma_{n+1},0)-\min(\sigma_n,0)\). In multiaxial IsoElasticity, the same idea is applied in principal-stress space and then transformed back to the material axes.

This uniaxial compression-only formulation does not act on tensile stress history, so time-dependent deformation in prestressed-concrete tensile regions or near-cracking tensile loading is not represented, and how conservative the result is depends on the stress state. When a step crosses from compression to tension, \(\Delta\sigma^c_n\) enters as an unloading increment that removes the existing compressive stress and partially recovers the chain history, and during a subsequent tensile interval the chain state still decays by \(\exp(-\Delta t_n/\lambda_\alpha)\).

During incremental analysis, internal variables \(q^\alpha_n\) are stored instead of the full stress history.

\[ \Delta\varepsilon_n^c= \sum_{\alpha=1}^{m} \left(1-\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta t_n}{\lambda_\alpha}\right)\right) q_n^\alpha \] \[ q_{n+1}^{\alpha}= q_n^{\alpha}\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta t_n}{\lambda_\alpha}\right) +\frac{\Delta\sigma^c_n}{E_\alpha(t_{n+1})} \frac{\lambda_\alpha}{\Delta t_n} \left(1-\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta t_n}{\lambda_\alpha}\right)\right) \]

Shrinkage is supplied by ConcreteTime as the stress-independent signed value \(\varepsilon^{sh}(t)\); ordinary shrinkage is stored internally as a negative strain in Hyfeast.

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• E0: Initial tangent modulus (required)
  • yield: yield stress ( required )
  • E1: Second tangent modulus (optional, default 0.)
  • R0,a1,a2: curvature parameters (optional, default 20, 0, 0)
  • a3,a3: isotropic hardening parameters (optional, default 0, 1.)
  • eu: ultimate strain (optional, default 0). If eu = 0., then ultimate strain is not checked.
  • alpha: themal expansion coefficient (optional, default 0.)
  • density: density (optional, default 0.)

docs.title: DB recipe data line
docs.text:
• material-db-item: General/weldable rebar or prestressing material DB item name. Structural steel DB items are not USteel recipe items, and seismic rebar DB recipes are not defined in v1.0.0.
  • NoHardening: USteel curve with E1 = 0; this is not perfectly plastic because the Menegotto-Pinto transition parameters still apply.
  • Hardening: Hardening recipe for rebar.
  • Mattock-StressRelieved: Mattock recipe for stress-relieved 7-wire strand.
  • Mattock-LowRelaxation: Mattock recipe for low-relaxation 7-wire strand.
  • density: Optional override for the DB recipe density only. If omitted, the DB density is used.
  • ToDirectForm: Optional final DB recipe dataline token. It expands the DB recipe to direct numeric values when saved or reprinted.

docs.title: LongTerm, Tendon dataline
docs.text:
• standard: KDS-2025 or EC2-2004.
  • class: Relaxation class, one of Class1, Class2, or Class3.
  • fp: Characteristic tensile strength used in the stress ratio. Use \(f_{pu}\) for KDS-2025 and \(f_{pk}\) for EC2-2004. Direct numeric input uses the stress unit of the current global UnitSystem; in an N-mm unit system this is MPa(\(N/mm^2\)).
  • material-db-item: Prestressing material DB item name. Specify it again in this dataline even when it is the same item used by the DB recipe dataline. The DB item supplies the standard, relaxation class, and characteristic tensile strength, converted from the DB source unit to the stress unit of the current global UnitSystem.
  • rho1000: Optional 1000-hour relaxation loss in percent. If omitted, the DB item value or class default is used; class defaults are 8 for Class1, 2.5 for Class2, and 4 for Class3.

docs.title: Mechanical behavior
docs.text:
USteel uses Menegotto-Pinto model with some modifications of partial reloading problem. It can be used for modeling rebar or prestressing steel.

Fig. 7.2-10 Menegotto-Pinto Model

The recommended values of modeling rebar and 7-wire strand is given in the example.

Fig. 7.2-11 Stress-strain curve of a weldable rebar with 400 MPa yield strength

Fig. 7.2-12 Stress-strain curve of 7-wire strand with ultimate strength 1860 MPa

docs.title: Long-term behavior
docs.text:
LongTerm, Tendon applies only to uniaxial tendon relaxation. It advances during Static, Quasi time increments using the step TUnit, acts only in tension, and converts the monotonic stress loss to relaxation strain with the initial elastic modulus E0. Re-tensioning is handled through the existing *State input flow.

KDS and EC2 inputs use the following tendon prestress relaxation equation. Let \(\sigma_p^*\) be the reference stress obtained by adding the already accumulated relaxation loss to the current tensile stress, and let \(f_p\) be the characteristic tensile strength. The stress ratio is:

\[ \mu=\frac{\sigma_p^*}{f_p} \]

For KDS-2025, \(f_p=f_{pu}\). For EC2-2004, \(f_p=f_{pk}\). Time \(t\) is in hours, and rho1000 is the 1000-hour relaxation loss in percent.

\[ \Delta\sigma_{p,r}(t) = \sigma_p^*\,c_r\rho_{1000}\exp(a_r\mu) \left(\frac{t}{1000}\right)^q 10^{-5}, \qquad q=\max\left(0,0.75(1-\mu)\right) \]

The class coefficients are:

class \(c_r\) \(a_r\) default \(\rho_{1000}\) Class1 5.39 6.7 8 Class2 0.66 9.1 2.5 Class3 1.98 8.0 4

In incremental analysis, the accumulated relaxation loss \(L_n\) is converted to an equivalent time of the standard equation, then the current step time increment \(\Delta t\) is added to compute the target accumulated loss.

\[ L_{1000} = \sigma_p^*\,c_r\rho_{1000}\exp(a_r\mu)10^{-5} \] \[ t_{\mathrm{eq}} = 1000\left(\frac{L_n}{L_{1000}}\right)^{1/q} \quad (L_n>0,\;L_{1000}>0,\;q>0) \] \[ L_{n+1}^{\mathrm{target}} = L_{1000} \left(\frac{t_{\mathrm{eq}}+\Delta t}{1000}\right)^q \]

The added loss in the step is \(\max(0,L_{n+1}^{\mathrm{target}}-L_n)\) and is capped by the remaining tensile stress. This stress loss is divided by the initial elastic modulus \(E_0\), not the tangent modulus, to store the relaxation strain increment.

\[ \Delta\varepsilon_{p,r} = \frac{\Delta L}{E_0} \]

docs.title: 7.1.10 *Material, Type=GapHook
docs.text:
Specify uniaxial gap-hook material.

*Material, Type=GapHook, Name=name
  kg,g, kh,h

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• kg,g: tangent and gap in compression part (optional, default 0.,0.)
  • kh,h: tangent and hook tension part (optional,default 0.,0.)

Using the GapHook command, you can model tension-only or compression-only behavior. Both kg and kh cannot be zero at the same time.

Fig. 7.2-13.GapHook Model

docs.title: First data line
docs.text: • Eaa, Ebb, Enn, Eab, Ebn, Ena: Stiffness components in each local direction (aa, bb, nn, ab, bn, na). Each value may be a scalar (stiffness) or a material name representing a stress-displacement relationship. Eab, Ebn, and Ena are optional. If omitted, they default to zero.

docs.title: Optional two data lines if damage exists
docs.text:
• MaxStress|MaxSeparation|QuadStress|QuadRelativeDisplacement, da0, db0, dn0: MaxStress|MaxRelativedisplacement|QuadStress|QuadRelativeDisplacement indicate damage initiation criterion. da0, db0, and dn0 are directional relative displacements at damage initiation.
  • Linear: Linear softening curve for damage evolution
  • Exponential, alpha: Exponential softening curve and its parameter for damage evolution
  • df: Effective relative displacement at failure
  • kappa: Viscosity prameter. optional. defaut 0.

When only the first data line is defined, a purely elastic model is applied.

\[ \begin{bmatrix} t_a \\ t_b \\ t_n \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} E_{aa} & E_{ab} & E_{an} \\ E_{ab} & E_{bb} & E_{bn} \\ E_{an} & E_{bn} & E_{nn} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \delta_a \\ \delta_b \\ \delta_n \end{bmatrix} \]

Here, the subscripts \(a\), \(b\), and \(n\) refer to the local coordinate system, representing the two tangential directions and the normal direction, respectively.

\[ \begin{bmatrix} t_a \\ t_b \\ t_n \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 - D & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 - D & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 - D \cdot H(t_n) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} E_{aa} & E_{ab} & E_{an} \\ E_{ab} & E_{bb} & E_{bn} \\ E_{an} & E_{bn} & E_{nn} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \delta_a \\ \delta_b \\ \delta_n \end{bmatrix} \]

where, D is a damage evolution index, which is determined by internal state. D is zero before damage, one at failure. To considering combined stress state(mixed fracture mode), effective relative displacement is defined as follows:

\[ \delta = \sqrt{\delta_a^2 + \delta_b^2 + \langle \delta_n \rangle^2} \]

where \(<∗>\) is the Macaulay bracket, which returns the value if it is positive, and zero otherwise.

To define damage behavior, both the damage initiation and the damage evolution after initiation must be specified. Damage initiation can be defined based on one of four criteria as shown in the figure below. Once damage begins, the cohesive traction follows a softening behavior. This softening function can be either linear or exponential.

Fig. 7.2-14.Cohesive Material

docs.title: 7.1.12 *Material, Type=Acoustic
docs.text:
Define properties for acoustic solid element

*Material, Type=Acoustic, Name=name
  bulk, density

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• bulk: Bulk modulus (required). If zero bulk modulus is given, the acoustic medium is assumed to be incompressible (Laplace equation is used)
  • density: density (required)

docs.title: 7.1.13 *Material, Type=Seepage
docs.text:
Define properties for seepage solid element

*Material, Type=Seepage, Name=name
  k | kx, ky | kx, ky, kz[, CS][, TUnit=tUnit]
  gamma|auto, Ss
  VGM, thetaR, thetaS, air, n[, m, l] | User, SWCC, RelHCF

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• k | kx, ky | kx, ky, kz: Permeability [L/T] (required). For seepage quantities whose dimensions include time, the time basis must be consistent with the seepage step time.
  • CS: Coordinate system with type Orientation (optional)
  • TUnit=tUnit: Specifies the [T] unit used by the permeability values (optional). Supported tUnit values are s, min, hr, and day. If omitted, the permeability values are interpreted as already consistent with the TUnit of the relevant Seepage, Transient step. If the material TUnit differs from the step TUnit, only the permeability values are converted to the step time basis.

docs.title: Second data line
docs.text:
• gamma: Water weight density [F/L^3] (required). Use a numeric value or arithmetic expression. Use auto to set the standard water unit weight from the current global *Environment, Type=UnitSystem; auto uses \(g_0=9.80665\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\) and \(\gamma_w=1000g_0\), converted to the current force-length unit system. Direct expressions using g0, such as 1000*g0, also require a global *Environment, TYPE=UnitSystem. Numeric input is printed back as numeric input and is not inferred as auto.
  • Ss: Specific storage (required). It is usually a [1/L] quantity, so no separate time unit is specified.

docs.title: Third data line for SWCC/HCF using VGM (optional)
docs.text: • VGM, tR, tS, air, n, m, l: van Genuchten-Mualem (VGM) SWCC and HCF. If given m,l is optional. If not given, m=1-1/n, l = 0.5

docs.title: Third data line for SWCC/HCF using User (optional)
docs.text:
• User, SWCC, RelHCF: User-defined unsaturated SWCC/HCF models. SWCC represents the volumetric water content, and RelHCF represents the relative hydraulic conductivity (the ratio relative to saturated hydraulic conductivity). Both are defined as functions of suction.

If the third data line is omitted, the material is treated as saturation-only. In this case, even if negative pore water pressure (= suction) occurs during the analysis, the SWCC and the reduction in relative hydraulic conductivity are not applied, and the hydraulic conductivity remains at the saturated value, Ks. Therefore, for analyses in which an unsaturated zone may develop, the SWCC and HCF (e.g., VGM or User) must be specified.

docs.title: 8. Function
docs.text:
*Function defines a named function object. Defined functions are referenced by material-model envelopes, load time histories, and similar inputs. Names must be globally unique.

Function-related commands define relationships such as \(y=f(x)\) or \(y_1=f_1(x), y_2=f_2(x), ...\).

Some function types support DB sources. TimeSignal reads time-history DB records, and concrete-related function types create compressive, tensile, and time-dependent properties from concrete DB items.

  • *Function, Type=TimeSignal: time-history DB
  • *Function, Type=ParabolaCEnv|HognestadCEnv|EC2CEnv|MPPCEnv: concrete DB for compressive behavior
  • *Function, Type=MaekawaTEnv: concrete DB for tensile behavior
  • *Function, Type=ConcreteTime: concrete DB for time-dependent properties

See *Function, Type=TimeSignal for TimeSignal DB input. The following sections describe the common concrete DB rules.

docs.title: Concrete DB overview
docs.text:
Concrete DB items are not material names entered directly in a Material dataline. They are sources used in concrete *Function datalines to fill the parameters of the selected function model. The current built-in envelope DB item forms are KDS-2026-C<fck>, ACI318-2025-C<fck>, and EC2-2004-C<fck>; the built-in time-dependent DB item forms are KDS-2026-C<fck>, EC2-2004-C<fck>, and ACI209-1992-C<fc>. Each function type supports a specific subset of those DB standards, and a UGeneric material dataline references the generated function name instead of the DB item itself.

The first distinction is ParabolaCEnv. Its DB input is a separate section-analysis parabolic compression input. It does not use the DB-derived concrete material-property recipe introduced below: fcm, Ec, Eci, ft, and the per-model recipe mapping. The DB supplies section-analysis fck, n, eco, and ecu; the optional alpha token applies the design reduction to fck. ACI318-2025-C<fck> is not accepted by ParabolaCEnv.

By contrast, HognestadCEnv, EC2CEnv, MPPCEnv, and MaekawaTEnv use concrete mechanical properties derived from the DB item as inputs to Hyfeast's built-in recipes. ConcreteTime uses standard-dependent aging, creep, and shrinkage equations. The reference below is organized by standard so the mechanical properties and time-dependent properties are read together.

For concrete envelope functions, Type means the function model to create. The same Type is used for both direct numeric input and DB item input. For example, with Type=ParabolaCEnv, a dataline of fck, n, eco, ecu, alpha is direct numeric input, while KDS-2026-C30 or EC2-2004-C30 fills the section-analysis parameters of the same Parabola model from the DB. TimeSignal DB records also keep Type=TimeSignal; they are referenced by source lines in the form DB, recordName[, scaleFactor].

Function inputs that use the concrete material DB require a prior global *Environment, Type=UnitSystem. DB source values are converted by the parser to the current global UnitSystem. These inputs do not allow UnitSystem on the keyword line; specifying it is an input error. TimeSignal DB source lines follow the unit metadata carried by each record; see the Type=TimeSignal section for details.

For concrete envelope DB item datalines, append ToDirectForm as the last token when the saved/formatted input should show the resolved numeric parameters. With ToDirectForm, the saved/formatted direct numeric form is written in the current global UnitSystem. If that unit system is the same as the global UnitSystem, no local UnitSystem is attached to the keyword line. Without ToDirectForm, the DB item dataline is preserved and no local UnitSystem is attached to the keyword line. HognestadCEnv, EC2CEnv, and MPPCEnv also accept EciCurve before ToDirectForm; when omitted, HognestadCEnv and EC2CEnv are linearized from the origin to 0.4*fco or 0.4*fcm using Ec, while MPPCEnv derives the internal curve from the unconfined secant Ec and then linearizes to the current 0.4 strength point.

Fig. 8.2-0. Concrete envelope initial curve option

Function-type DB dataline syntax is documented in the later Type= subsections. This front reference is limited to standard-specific properties and unit systems.

docs.title: Common rules for concrete DB
docs.text:
Each standard subsection below uses the same order.

  • DB item forms and source units: the envelope DB item name, the ConcreteTime item name when available, and the units used by the standard equations.
  • Mechanical envelope properties: the 28-day properties and strain coefficients used by concrete envelope functions.
  • ConcreteTime properties: the aging, creep, and shrinkage series for the same standard. These subsections do not repeat mechanical properties already defined above; they only add coefficients required by the time-dependent equations.

ConcreteTime stores six function series in the following order:

\[ \left[a_c(t),\;a_t(t),\;a_E(t),\;c_r(t-\tau),\;c_l(\tau),\;\varepsilon^{sh}(t)\right] \]

For a user-defined function set, the intended material-level use is:

\[ f_c(t)=a_c(t)f_c(28) \] \[ f_t(t)=a_t(t)f_t(28) \] \[ E_c(t)=a_E(t)E_c(28) \] \[ C(t,\tau)=c_r(t-\tau)c_l(\tau) \] \[ \varepsilon^{sh}(t)=-e_{sh}(t) \]

Shrinkage distinguishes positive shrinkage magnitudes from the signed shrinkage/swelling strain stored by Hyfeast. For a user-defined shrinkage Function, \(e_{sh}(t)\) is a positive shrinkage magnitude. In the EC2 equations, \(\varepsilon_{cd}\) and \(\varepsilon_{ca}\) are positive magnitudes; in the ACI equations, \(\varepsilon_{sh,u}\) is a positive magnitude. The final series \(\varepsilon^{sh}(t)\) is the signed value stored by Hyfeast: contraction is stored as negative, and swelling is stored as positive. In the KDS equations, the computed \(\varepsilon^{sh}(t)\) itself is used as the signed stored value; it is negative shrinkage for \(RH<99\%\) and positive swelling for \(RH\ge99\%\).

Here, \(t\) is the concrete age, \(\tau\) is the loading age, and \(t-\tau\) is the creep duration. Standard and User ConcreteTime inputs evaluate these age variables in days, so a Static, Quasi step that uses them must specify TUnit=day. This does not imply changing the time field of the global UnitSystem to days. The function does not decide \(\tau\); the later concrete material implementation supplies it from the analysis state.

Here \(C(t,\tau)\) is creep compliance, not the dimensionless creep coefficient \(\phi(t,\tau)\). If \(c_r\) is dimensionless, \(c_l\) has inverse-stress units.

The KDS and EC2 built-in creep equations use the same separated form. The duration part is dimensionless, and the loading-age part includes the elastic-modulus denominator. The standard-specific subsections give only \(E_{ci,28}\), \(\phi_{RH}\), and \(\beta_H\).

\[ C(t,\tau)=c_r(\max(t-\tau,0))c_l(\tau) \] \[ \Delta t=\max(t-\tau,0) \] \[ c_r(\Delta t)= \begin{cases} 0 & (\Delta t=0) \\ \left(\dfrac{\Delta t}{\beta_H+\Delta t}\right)^{0.3} & (\Delta t>0) \end{cases} \] \[ c_l(\tau)=\dfrac{1}{E_{ci,28}}\phi_{RH}\dfrac{16.8}{\sqrt{f_{cm}}}\dfrac{1}{0.1+\tau^{0.2}} \]

ConcreteTime does not allow keyword-line UnitSystem. A User dataline references existing function names and does not require a global UnitSystem at input time. The six referenced Functions are evaluated with day-based \(x\) values supplied by ConcreteTime; therefore, a referenced Function must not define keyword-line UnitSystem=....

ConcreteTime standard datalines require a global *Environment, Type=UnitSystem, but the input units of the standard equations are fixed to the units specified by each standard. EC2/KDS strengths are entered in MPa, ACI strength is entered in psi, EC2/KDS h0 is entered in mm, ACI 209 V/S and slump are entered in inch, and time variables are entered in days. The parser does not convert these length inputs from the global length unit. Elastic moduli in the creep-compliance denominator are converted to the current global stress unit before storage.

docs.title: KDS-2026 concrete DB
docs.text:
DB item forms and source units. KDS envelope functions use KDS-2026-C<fck>; ConcreteTime uses the same KDS-2026-C<fck> item form. Strengths and elastic moduli are evaluated in MPa, length parameters in mm, and time variables in days.

Mechanical envelope properties (KDS-2026-C<fck>).

\[ f_{cm}=f_{ck}+\Delta f \] \[ \Delta f= \begin{cases} 4 & (f_{ck} \le 40) \\ 4 + 0.1(f_{ck}-40) & (40 < f_{ck} < 60) \\ 6 & (f_{ck} \ge 60) \end{cases} \] \[ E_c=8500\sqrt[3]{f_{cm}}\;[\mathrm{MPa}] \] \[ E_{ci}=E_c \] \[ f_t=f_{ctm}=0.30\,f_{cm}^{2/3} \]

This \(E_c\) expression applies the KDS normal-weight concrete assumption \(m_c=2300\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\); material density does not recompute it. Use direct numeric input when fck exceeds 90 MPa.

EC2CEnv nonlinear-analysis strain coefficients. For KDS DB input, strengths are in MPa and strains are dimensionless:

\[ \varepsilon_{co}=\min\left(0.7 f_{cm}^{0.31},\,2.8\right)/1000 \] \[ \varepsilon_{cu}= \begin{cases} 0.0033 & (f_{ck}\le 40) \\ \left(3.3-0.1(f_{ck}-40)/10\right)/1000 & (40<f_{ck}\le 90) \end{cases} \]

ConcreteTime properties (KDS-2026-C<fck>).

The KDS-2026-C<fck> time-dependent equations use the \(f_{cm}\) and \(E_c\) defined above as the 28-day values. \(h_0\) is evaluated in mm, and the time variables \(t\), \(\tau\), and \(t_s\) are evaluated in days. The creep-compliance denominator uses the following initial modulus:

\[ E_{ci,28}=1.18E_c \]

The age factors are:

\[ \beta_c(t)=\exp\left[\beta_{sc,a}\left(1-\sqrt{28/t}\right)\right] \quad (t>0) \] \[ a_c(t)=\beta_c(t) \] \[ a_t(t)=\beta_c(t)^{2/3} \] \[ a_E(t)=\sqrt{\beta_c(t)} \]

The aging coefficient \(\beta_{sc,a}\) is 0.35 for Moist and 0.15 for Steam with Type1, 0.40 and 0.40 with Type2, 0.25 and 0.12 with Type3, and 0.35 and 0.15 with Type5.

KDS creep uses the common KDS/EC2 separated form. Its humidity and size factors are:

\[ \phi_{RH}=1+\dfrac{1-RH/100}{0.1h_0^{1/3}} \] \[ \beta_H=\min\left(1.5\left[1+(0.012RH)^{18}\right]h_0+250,\;1500\right) \]

In the KDS expression, \(\varepsilon_s(f_{cm})\) and \(\beta_s\) are positive, with \(\beta_{RH}<0\) for \(RH<99\%\) and \(\beta_{RH}=0.25>0\) for \(RH\ge99\%\). Therefore \(\varepsilon^{sh}(t)\) is computed as negative shrinkage under ordinary drying conditions and positive swelling under near-saturated conditions, and the computed value is stored directly as the signed Hyfeast shrinkage/swelling strain without adding another leading minus sign.

\[ \varepsilon^{sh}(t)= \begin{cases} 0 & (t<t_s) \\ \varepsilon_{sho}\beta_s(t-t_s) & (t\ge t_s) \end{cases} \] \[ \varepsilon_{sho}=\varepsilon_s(f_{cm})\beta_{RH} \] \[ \varepsilon_s(f_{cm})=\left[160+10\beta_{sc,s}\left(9-f_{cm}/10\right)\right]10^{-6} \] \[ \beta_{RH}= \begin{cases} -1.55\left[1-\left(RH/100\right)^3\right] & (RH<99) \\ 0.25 & (RH\ge 99) \end{cases} \] \[ \beta_s(t-t_s)=\sqrt{\dfrac{t-t_s}{0.035h_0^2+(t-t_s)}} \]

The shrinkage coefficient \(\beta_{sc,s}\) is 4 for Type2, 5 for Type1 or Type5, and 8 for Type3.

docs.title: EC2-2004 concrete DB
docs.text:
DB item forms and source units. EC2 envelope functions use EC2-2004-C<fck>; ConcreteTime uses the same EC2-2004-C<fck> item form. Strengths and elastic moduli are evaluated in MPa, length parameters in mm, and time variables in days.

Mechanical envelope properties (EC2-2004-C<fck>).

\[ f_{cm}=f_{ck}+8 \] \[ E_c=E_{cm}=22000\left(f_{cm}/10\right)^{0.3} \] \[ E_{ci}=1.05\,E_c \] \[ f_t= \begin{cases} 0.30\,f_{ck}^{2/3} & (f_{ck} \le 50) \\ 2.12\ln(1+f_{cm}/10) & (50 < f_{ck} \le 90) \end{cases} \]

Here <fck> is the EC2 cylinder strength in MPa. Use direct numeric input when fck exceeds 90 MPa.

EC2CEnv nonlinear-analysis strain coefficients. For EC2 DB input, strengths are in MPa and strains are dimensionless:

\[ \varepsilon_{co}=\min\left(0.7 f_{cm}^{0.31},\,2.8\right)/1000 \] \[ \varepsilon_{cu}= \begin{cases} 0.0035 & (f_{ck}\le 50) \\ \left(2.8+27\left((98-f_{cm})/100\right)^4\right)/1000 & (50<f_{ck}\le 90) \end{cases} \]

ConcreteTime properties (EC2-2004-C<fck>).

The EC2-2004-C<fck> time-dependent equations use the \(f_{cm}\) and \(E_c=E_{cm}\) defined above as the 28-day values. \(h_0\) is evaluated in mm, and the time variables \(t\), \(\tau\), and \(t_s\) are evaluated in days. The creep-compliance denominator uses the following initial modulus:

\[ E_{ci,28}=1.05E_c \]

The age factors are:

\[ \beta_{cc}(t)=\exp\left[s\left(1-\sqrt{28/t}\right)\right] \quad (t>0) \] \[ a_c(t)=\beta_{cc}(t) \] \[ a_t(t)= \begin{cases} \beta_{cc}(t) & (t<28) \\ \beta_{cc}(t)^{2/3} & (t\ge 28) \end{cases} \] \[ a_E(t)=\beta_{cc}(t)^{0.3} \]

The cement-class coefficient \(s\) is 0.38 for S, 0.25 for N, and 0.20 for R.

EC2 creep uses the common KDS/EC2 separated form. Its humidity and size factors depend on the strength range.

For \(f_{cm}\le 35\):

\[ \phi_{RH}=1+\dfrac{1-RH/100}{0.1h_0^{1/3}} \] \[ \beta_H=\min\left(1.5\left[1+(0.012RH)^{18}\right]h_0+250,\;1500\right) \]

For \(f_{cm}>35\):

\[ \alpha_1=\left(35/f_{cm}\right)^{0.7} \] \[ \alpha_2=\left(35/f_{cm}\right)^{0.2} \] \[ \alpha_3=\left(35/f_{cm}\right)^{0.5} \] \[ \phi_{RH}=\left(1+\dfrac{(1-RH/100)\alpha_1}{0.1h_0^{1/3}}\right)\alpha_2 \] \[ \beta_H=\min\left(1.5\left[1+(0.012RH)^{18}\right]h_0+250\alpha_3,\;1500\alpha_3\right) \]

The following \(\varepsilon_{cd}\) and \(\varepsilon_{ca}\) are positive shrinkage magnitudes from the EC2 equations. The shrinkage strain stored by Hyfeast is negative for contraction:

\[ \varepsilon^{sh}(t)=-\left(\varepsilon_{cd}(t,t_s)+\varepsilon_{ca}(t)\right) \] \[ \varepsilon_{cd}(t,t_s)=\beta_{ds}(t,t_s)\varepsilon_{cd,\infty} \] \[ \beta_{ds}(t,t_s)= \begin{cases} 0 & (t<t_s) \\ \dfrac{t-t_s}{(t-t_s)+0.04h_0^{3/2}} & (t\ge t_s) \end{cases} \] \[ \varepsilon_{cd,\infty}=0.85k_h\left[(220+110\alpha_{ds1}) \exp\left(-\alpha_{ds2}\dfrac{f_{cm}}{10}\right)\right]10^{-6}\beta_{RH} \] \[ \beta_{RH}=1.55\left[1-\left(RH/100\right)^3\right] \] \[ \varepsilon_{ca}(t)=\beta_{as}(t)\varepsilon_{ca,\infty} \] \[ \beta_{as}(t)= \begin{cases} 0 & (t\le 0) \\ 1-\exp(-0.2\sqrt{t}) & (t>0) \end{cases} \] \[ \varepsilon_{ca,\infty}=2.5(f_{ck}-10)10^{-6} \]

The drying shrinkage coefficients are \(\alpha_{ds1}=3\) and \(\alpha_{ds2}=0.13\) for S, \(\alpha_{ds1}=4\) and \(\alpha_{ds2}=0.12\) for N, and \(\alpha_{ds1}=6\) and \(\alpha_{ds2}=0.11\) for R.

The size factor \(k_h\) is 1.00, 0.85, and 0.75 at \(h_0=100\), 200, and 300 mm, respectively, and 0.70 for \(h_0\ge500\) mm. Intermediate values are linearly interpolated.

docs.title: ACI concrete DB
docs.text:
DB item forms and source units. ACI envelope functions use ACI318-2025-C<fck>, where <fck> represents the specified compressive strength \(f'_c\) in psi. ConcreteTime uses ACI209-1992-C<fc>, also with \(f'_c\) in psi. ACI 209 length correction equations are evaluated in inch, time variables are evaluated in days, and detailed cementContent is evaluated in \(\mathrm{lb/yd^3}\).

Mechanical envelope properties (ACI318-2025-C<fck>).

\[ f_{cm}=f'_c \] \[ E_c=57000\sqrt{f'_c}\;[\mathrm{psi}],\quad w_c\approx145\,\mathrm{lb/ft^3} \] \[ E_{ci}=E_c \] \[ f_t=7.5\sqrt{f'_c}\;[\mathrm{psi}] \]

Here <fck> is the ACI specified compressive strength \(f'_c\) in psi. ACI DB items are used by HognestadCEnv, MPPCEnv, and MaekawaTEnv; they are not accepted by ParabolaCEnv or EC2CEnv.

ConcreteTime properties (ACI209-1992-C<fc>).

For ACI209-1992-C<fc>, \(f'_c\) is evaluated in psi, detailed cementContent is evaluated in \(\mathrm{lb/yd^3}\), and the time variables \(t\), \(\tau\), \(t_s\), and moistCuringDuration are evaluated in days. V/S and slump are entered in inch, the standard unit used by the ACI 209 length correction equations; the parser does not convert them from the global length unit. The 28-day modulus \(E_c(28)\) is the ACI mechanical-property \(E_c\) above. In the ACI 209 correction equations, V/S is the volume-to-surface ratio in inch. The implemented age factor is normalized by its 28-day value:

\[ g(t)=\dfrac{t}{a+bt} \] \[ a_c(t)=\dfrac{g(t)}{g(28)} \] \[ a_t(t)=\sqrt{a_c(t)} \] \[ a_E(t)=\sqrt{a_c(t)} \]

The ACI 209 coefficients are:

curingType cementType \(a\) \(b\) \(c\) \(d\) \(f\) Moist TypeI 4.0 0.85 1.25 0.118 35 Moist TypeIII 2.3 0.92 1.25 0.118 35 Steam TypeI 1.0 0.95 1.13 0.094 55 Steam TypeIII 0.7 0.98 1.13 0.094 55

The dimensionless ACI 209 creep coefficient is converted to creep compliance with the loading-age elastic modulus:

\[ C(t,\tau)=c_r(\Delta t)c_l(\tau) \] \[ \Delta t=\max(t-\tau,0) \] \[ c_r(\Delta t)= \begin{cases} 0 & (\Delta t=0) \\ \dfrac{\Delta t^{0.6}}{10+\Delta t^{0.6}} & (\Delta t>0) \end{cases} \] \[ E_c(\tau)=a_E(\tau)E_c(28) \] \[ c_l(\tau)=\dfrac{2.35c\tau^{-d}\gamma_{RH,c}\gamma_{VS,c}\gamma_{add,c}}{E_c(\tau)} \] \[ \gamma_{RH,c}=1.27-0.0067RH \] \[ \gamma_{VS,c}=\dfrac{2}{3}\left[1+1.13\exp\left(-0.54V/S\right)\right] \]

For the compact ACI form, \(\gamma_{add,c}=\) creepUltimateScale. For the detailed ACI form:

\[ \gamma_{add,c}=\gamma_{sl,c}\gamma_{\psi,c}\gamma_{\alpha,c} \] \[ \gamma_{sl,c}=0.82+0.067s_l \] \[ \gamma_{\psi,c}=0.88+0.0024\psi \] \[ \gamma_{\alpha,c}=\max(1.0,\;0.46+0.09\alpha) \]

Here, \(V/S\) and \(s_l\) are in inch, \(\psi\) is fine aggregate percentage, and \(\alpha\) is air content percentage.

In the ACI expression, \(\varepsilon_{sh,u}\) is a positive ultimate shrinkage magnitude. The shrinkage strain stored by Hyfeast is negative for contraction, so the equation carries the leading minus sign.

\[ \varepsilon^{sh}(t)= \begin{cases} 0 & (t<t_s) \\ -\dfrac{t-t_s}{f+(t-t_s)}\varepsilon_{sh,u} & (t\ge t_s) \end{cases} \] \[ \varepsilon_{sh,u}=780\times10^{-6}\gamma_{RH,s}\gamma_{VS,s}\gamma_{add,s} \] \[ \gamma_{RH,s}= \begin{cases} 1.4-0.01RH & (RH\le 80) \\ 3.0-0.03RH & (RH>80) \end{cases} \] \[ \gamma_{VS,s}=\max\left(0.2,\;1.2\exp(-0.12V/S)\right) \]

For the compact ACI form, \(\gamma_{add,s}=\) shrinkageUltimateScale. For the detailed ACI form:

\[ \gamma_{add,s}=\gamma_{mc}\gamma_{sl,s}\gamma_{\psi,s}\gamma_{cc,s}\gamma_{\alpha,s} \] \[ \gamma_{sl,s}=0.89+0.041s_l \] \[ \gamma_{\psi,s}= \begin{cases} 0.30+0.014\psi & (\psi\le 50) \\ 0.90+0.002\psi & (\psi>50) \end{cases} \] \[ \gamma_{cc,s}=0.75+0.00036c_c \] \[ \gamma_{\alpha,s}=0.95+0.008\alpha \]

Here, \(c_c\) is cement content in \(\mathrm{lb/yd^3}\). For Steam curing, \(\gamma_{mc}=1.0\). For Moist curing, \(\gamma_{mc}\) is 1.20, 1.10, 1.00, 0.93, 0.86, and 0.75 at moistCuringDuration values of 1, 3, 7, 14, 28, and 90 days, respectively; intermediate values are linearly interpolated.

docs.title: Keyword line
docs.text:
• TYPE=type: type of function
    • MultiLinear: Multi-linear function
    • TimeSignal: Time signal. Multi-linear function with fixed step size. Supports both file source lines and tools/db/timeSignal DB source lines
    • ResponseSpectrum: Response spectrum function generated from a TimeSignal, KDS17, or KDS41 source
    • String: function by mathematical expression
    • ParabolaCEnv: section-analysis parabola concrete compressive envelope
    • HognestadCEnv: Hognestad concrete compressive envelope
    • EC2CEnv: EC2-family concrete compressive envelope
    • MPPCEnv: Mander-Priestley-Park concrete compressive envelope
    • MPPCIE: Mander-Priestley-Park concrete compressive inelastic strain
    • MaekawaTEnv: Maekawa concrete tensile envelope
    • ConcreteTime: concrete time-dependent function set for aging, creep, and shrinkage
  • UnitSystem=unitSystem: Local UnitSystem used for a function defined by direct numeric datalines. It shall be specified in the four-field format force-length-time-temperature. This value is preserved as local metadata and is not an input-time error even when *Environment, Type=UnitSystem is not currently defined. If a global UnitSystem is available, it is interpreted through the local-to-global relationship when needed. If omitted, it is taken to be the same as the global UnitSystem. Type=MPPCIE, Type=ConcreteTime, Type=ResponseSpectrum, and concrete envelope DB item datalines do not support UnitSystem. For Type=TimeSignal, file source lines are interpreted in this unit system, while DB source lines are read in the record UnitSystem and converted into the function UnitSystem.
  • Name=name: function name

docs.title: 8.1.1 *Function, Type=MultiLinear
docs.text:
Multilinear function

*Function, Type=MultiLinear, Name=name
 x, y1, y2, ..., yn
 ...

docs.title: First data line and subsequent data lines
docs.text:
• x, y1, y2, ..., yn: Enter values in the form (x, y1, y2, ..., yn).

The MultiLinear function defines the functions y1(x), y2(x), ... in the form of (x, y1(x), y2(x), ..., yn(x)).

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• dtime: Time step or auto (required). auto is allowed only when at least one DB source line is provided, and it is resolved from the DB record dtime. When multiple DB records are listed, all DB record dtime values shall match after conversion to the reference UnitSystem.
  • ntime: Number of time data or auto (required). With auto, ntime is set to the length of the longest loaded time series. If the number of rows in the read data exceeds ntime, the extra rows are ignored. If it is less than ntime, the remaining values are padded with zeros.

docs.title: Second data line and subsequent data lines
docs.text:
• file: File to be read (required). A text file with values separated by commas, spaces, etc., or an npy file.
  • nseries: Number of time series in the file (optional, default 1). For npy files, the number of columns must be the same.
  • scale: Scale factor (optional, default 1).
  • skipRows: Number of rows to skip at the beginning of the file (optional, default 0). Ignored for npy files.
  • quantity: Signal quantity class for the file source line (optional). Allowed values are acc/acceleration, vel/velocity, disp/displacement, and other/others/dimensionless. When omitted, Signal Analysis uses the common DB record quantity if the TimeSignal also contains DB source lines; otherwise it treats the file source as acceleration.
  • DB: Literal keyword that references a tools/db/timeSignal DB record.
  • recordName: DB record name defined in tools/db/timeSignal (required).
  • scaleFactor: Optional user multiplier applied to all Y-series from that record after DB normalization (optional, default 1).

The TimeSignal function, suitable for representing time histories, can be understood as a multi-linear function with fixed interval x values. File source line data is read with values separated by whitespace (colon, space, tab, newline). Each file consists of nseries time series data. It reads ntime entries for each of the nseries data. If the file has fewer data entries, the missing values are filled with zeros. At time 0, the value is assumed to be 0, and the first value given in the data corresponds to the value at time dt. The final value corresponds to the value at time ntime*dt.

Fig. 8.2-1. TimeSignal function

A DB source line is written as DB, recordName[, scaleFactor]. The DB metadata defines the source file, quantity, local UnitSystem, dtime, ntime, nseries, sourceScaleFactor, and skipRows. When multiple DB records are listed in one TimeSignal, their quantities may differ, and dtime shall match after conversion to the reference UnitSystem. DB record UnitSystems may differ. The resulting series order follows the source-line order. The keyword-line UnitSystem is the interpretation basis for file source lines and the target function UnitSystem for DB source conversion. DB source lines are read in the record UnitSystem, then converted into the function UnitSystem according to each record quantity before storage. A pure DB TimeSignal with no keyword UnitSystem preserves the first DB record UnitSystem as function metadata. File source lines and DB source lines may be mixed in the same TimeSignal. The following rules apply to TimeSignal DB source-line UnitSystems.

- A `DB, recordName[, scaleFactor]` source line does not require a global `*Environment, Type=UnitSystem`.
- If the keyword line has `UnitSystem=U`, file source lines are interpreted in `U`. DB source lines are read in the record UnitSystem, then converted into `U` according to the record quantity before being stored in the function.
- If the keyword line has no `UnitSystem` and a global UnitSystem exists, file source lines are interpreted in the global UnitSystem. DB source lines are read in the record UnitSystem, then converted into the global/function UnitSystem before being stored.
- If the keyword line has no `UnitSystem` and all source lines are DB lines, the function metadata is stored with the first DB record UnitSystem, and the remaining DB source lines are converted into that UnitSystem.
- If the keyword line has no `UnitSystem`, no global UnitSystem exists, and file and DB source lines are mixed, the input is rejected because there is no reference UnitSystem.
- It is not an input error for the keyword `UnitSystem` and DB record UnitSystem to differ. Multiple DB record UnitSystems and quantities may also differ, but their dtime shall match after conversion.
- If source lines have different quantities, the TimeSignal definition is still valid. Signal Analysis and preview features may restrict operations that require a single physical quantity.

For example, the following input is valid without a global UnitSystem. The function metadata is stored with the UnitSystem of the elcentro_chopra record.

*Function, Type=TimeSignal, Name=EQ
 auto, auto
 DB, elcentro_chopra

In the following input, my_acc.txt is interpreted as a kN-mm-s-K file source, while the elcentro_chopra DB values are converted from the record UnitSystem into kN-mm-s-K before being stored in the same TimeSignal.

*Function, Type=TimeSignal, UnitSystem=kN-mm-s-K, Name=EQ
 auto, auto
 my_acc.txt
 DB, elcentro_chopra

TimeSignal DB records are loaded from the built-in factory catalog at tools/db/timeSignal/catalog.yml and, when present, the user catalog at tools/db/timeSignal/user/catalog.yml. In hfStudio, the TimeSignal DB dialog can register a text or .npy time-history file as a user DB record with Add Record...; the source copy is stored under tools/db/timeSignal/user/files/. The user DB lives inside the installation folder rather than a separate %APPDATA% location, so before updating the program or replacing the folder, back up or copy the whole tools/db/timeSignal/user/ folder if those user records should be kept. Separately, KDS17 and KDS41 in Type=ResponseSpectrum are built-in design-spectrum DB-style sources; they are formula sources and do not use an external DB file.

In the time data file, any content after # is ignored (comment).

docs.title: 8.1.3 *Function, Type=ResponseSpectrum
docs.text:
Response spectrum function generated as a single-series period function.

*Function, Type=ResponseSpectrum, Name=name
 TimeSignal, timeSignalName, seriesIndex, dampingRatio
 Linear|Log, Tmin, Tmax, nPeriod[, ToDirectForm]

*Function, Type=ResponseSpectrum, Name=name
 KDS17|KDS41, siteClass, effectiveGroundAcceleration[, dampingRatio]
[ Linear|Log, Tmin, Tmax, nPeriod]

docs.title: First dataline for TimeSignal
docs.text:
• TimeSignal: Generates the response spectrum from an existing *Function, Type=TimeSignal.
  • timeSignalName: Existing TimeSignal function name. The selected signal is interpreted as acceleration, and the generated values are stored as \(S_a/g\).
  • seriesIndex: TimeSignal series index, 1-based.
  • dampingRatio: For TimeSignal, the required damping ratio used in the single-degree-of-freedom response calculation.

docs.title: Second dataline for TimeSignal
docs.text:
• Linear|Log, Tmin, Tmax, nPeriod: Linear|Log selects the generated period-grid spacing; Tmin and Tmax define the generated period range in seconds; nPeriod is the number of generated period points.
  • ToDirectForm: Optional output flag that prints the generated curve as Type=MultiLinear. It does not change the analysis result.

docs.title: First dataline for KDS17|KDS41
docs.text:
• KDS17: Generates the standard design response spectrum for design ground motions in KDS 17 10 00. S1 uses the rock-site expression, while S2 to S5 use the soil-site amplification expression.
  • KDS41: Generates the building design response acceleration spectrum in KDS 41 17 00. S1 to S5 use the building-code \(F_a\), \(F_v\) tables and the \(2/3\) design-level factor.
  • siteClass: KDS site class. S1, S2, S3, S4, or S5. For KDS17, S1 is the rock site and S2 to S5 are soil sites.
  • effectiveGroundAcceleration: The coefficient \(S\) entered in g. For KDS17, this is the effective horizontal ground acceleration for the selected design ground-motion level. When it is determined by the administrative-zone method, use the seismic zone factor \(Z\) and the risk factor \(I\) for the selected mean return period, so \(S=Z\times I\). For KDS41, this is the effective ground acceleration of the 2400-year maximum considered earthquake.
  • dampingRatio: Optional only for KDS17 with siteClass=S1; default is 0.05. When specified, it must be at least 0.005. Enter it as a ratio, so 5% is 0.05. KDS41 and KDS17 with S2 to S5 use only the default 5% spectrum and do not accept this token.

docs.title: Second dataline for KDS17|KDS41 (optional)
docs.text:
• Linear|Log, Tmin, Tmax, nPeriod: Linear|Log selects the generated period-grid spacing; Tmin and Tmax define the generated period range in seconds; nPeriod is the number of generated period points. If this line is present, the generated curve is printed as Type=MultiLinear.

For TimeSignal sources, the period grid dataline is required because the response spectrum is generated on that period grid. For KDS sources, the period grid dataline is optional. If it is omitted, the function keeps the KDS closed-form expression and evaluates that expression during analysis. If it is present, the KDS expression is sampled on the given grid and stored as direct MultiLinear data; values outside the generated range use the nearest end value. Use *Spectrum's scaleFactor for direction-specific scaling such as a vertical-to-horizontal ratio. For KDS17 soil sites, however, do not treat any vertical-to-horizontal ratio as a fixed built-in rule; define a separate spectrum or scale according to the applicable standard and engineering judgment. Any dampingRatio in this function is separate from the dampingRatio of *Spectrum; the latter is used for CQC modal combination.

For KDS17 with S1, the rock-site standard design response spectrum is defined directly:

\[ T_0=0.06,\quad T_s=0.3,\quad T_L=3.0 \] \[ \frac{S_a}{g}= \begin{cases} (1+30T)S, & 0 \le T \le T_0 \\ 2.8S, & T_0 < T \le T_s \\ \frac{0.84S}{T}, & T_s < T \le T_L \\ \frac{2.52S}{T^2}, & T > T_L \end{cases} \]

When the optional dampingRatio is specified for KDS17 with S1, the damping correction below is multiplied into the rock-site spectrum. Here \(\xi\) is the ratio entered in the dataline.

\[ C_\xi^\ast=\left(\frac{6.42}{1.42+100\xi}\right)^{0.48},\quad C_\xi(T)= \begin{cases} 1+(C_\xi^\ast-1)\frac{T}{T_0}, & 0 < T < T_0 \\ C_\xi^\ast, & T \ge T_0 \end{cases} \]

For KDS17 with S2 to S5, use the soil-site spectrum below for 5% damping. It starts from \(F_aS\) at \(T=0\) and reaches \(2.5F_aS\) at \(T_0\). This function currently supports only \(\xi=0.05\) for KDS17 soil sites.

\[ \begin{aligned} T_s &= \frac{F_v}{2.5F_a}, & T_0 &= 0.2T_s, & T_L &= 3.0 \end{aligned} \] \[ \frac{S_a}{g}= \begin{cases} F_aS\left(1+1.5\frac{T}{T_0}\right), & 0 \le T \le T_0 \\ 2.5F_aS, & T_0 < T \le T_s \\ \frac{F_vS}{T}, & T_s < T \le T_L \\ \frac{F_vST_L}{T^2}, & T > T_L \end{cases} \]

For KDS41, use the design response acceleration spectrum below for 5% damping. Here \(S\) is the effective ground acceleration of the 2400-year maximum considered earthquake, and the \(2/3\) design-level factor is applied when forming \(S_{DS}\) and \(S_{D1}\). This function currently supports only \(\xi=0.05\) for KDS41.

\[ \begin{aligned} S_{DS} &= \frac{2}{3}(2.5F_aS), & S_{D1} &= \frac{2}{3}F_vS, & T_0 &= 0.2\frac{S_{D1}}{S_{DS}}, & T_s &= \frac{S_{D1}}{S_{DS}}, & T_L &= 5.0 \end{aligned} \] \[ \frac{S_a}{g}= \begin{cases} S_{DS}\left(0.6\frac{T}{T_0}+0.4\right), & 0 \le T \le T_0 \\ S_{DS}, & T_0 < T \le T_s \\ \frac{S_{D1}}{T}, & T_s < T \le T_L \\ \frac{S_{D1}T_L}{T^2}, & T > T_L \end{cases} \]

For KDS17 soil sites and for KDS41, \(F_a\) and \(F_v\) are read from the site-class table below. Values between \(S=0.1\), \(0.2\), and \(0.3\) are linearly interpolated; values outside this tabulated range use the nearest tabulated value. KDS17 soil sites use only rows S2 to S5; KDS41 uses rows S1 to S5.

Site \(F_a\) at \(S=0.1,0.2,0.3\) \(F_v\) at \(S=0.1,0.2,0.3\) S1 1.12, 1.12, 1.12 0.84, 0.84, 0.84 S2 1.40, 1.40, 1.30 1.50, 1.40, 1.30 S3 1.70, 1.50, 1.30 1.70, 1.60, 1.50 S4 1.60, 1.40, 1.20 2.20, 2.00, 1.80 S5 1.80, 1.30, 1.30 3.00, 2.70, 2.40

Fig. 8.2-1a. KDS17 rock-site, KDS17 soil-site, and KDS41 response spectrum schematics.

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• expression: Expression with x independent variable, such as "sin(x)+1". Note that white space is not allowed.
  • min,max: minimum and maximum range. Zero function value is assumed beyond the given range. If Range keyword is not given, no range check is performed

'*Function, Type=String' has the feature of parsing the expression. The internal parser supports typical mathematical functions, such as sin(x), cos(x), tan(x), acos(x), atan(x), cosh(x), sinh(x), tanh(x), fabs(x), exp(x), log(x), log10(x), sqrt(x), step(x), sgn(x), and pow(x,n).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
*Function, Type=String, Name=Half-sine
 sin(2*pi/1.2*x), 0., 0.6

docs.title: 8.1.5 *Function, Type=ParabolaCEnv
docs.text:
Define the stress-strain compressive envelope for cross-sectional design as specified by EC2 and KDS.

*Function, Type=ParabolaCEnv, UnitSystem=unitSystem, Name=name
  fck, n, eco, ecu[, alpha]

*Function, Type=ParabolaCEnv, Name=name
  KDS-2026-C<fck>|EC2-2004-C<fck>[, alpha][, ToDirectForm]

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• fck: design compressive strength, (required)
  • n: shape factor (required)
  • eco: peak strain (optional, 0.002)
  • ecu: ultimate strain (optional, always set to max(eco, ecu) )
  • alpha: reduction factor multiplied by fck (optional, default 1.0)
  • KDS-2026-C<fck> or EC2-2004-C<fck>: Concrete DB item accepted by ParabolaCEnv. It can be used instead of the numeric dataline when keyword UnitSystem is omitted and a global UnitSystem is defined. Both standards fill the direct numeric fck field; n, eco, and ecu follow the equations below; alpha is read from the dataline or defaults to 1.0. These values are section-analysis compression relation parameters and should not be mixed with general compressive envelope material properties.
  • ToDirectForm: Optional output option for DB item datalines. It must be the last token. When specified, saved/formatted output writes the resolved numeric dataline in the current global UnitSystem. If that unit system is the same as the global UnitSystem, no local UnitSystem is printed on the keyword line. If omitted, the DB item dataline is preserved.

The curve given as

\[ f_c= \begin{cases} \alpha f_{ck}\left[1-\left(1-\dfrac{\epsilon_c}{\epsilon_{co}}\right)^n\right] & (\epsilon_c\le\epsilon_{co}) \\ \alpha f_{ck} & (\epsilon_{co}<\epsilon_c\le\epsilon_{cu}) \end{cases} \]

Hyfeast returns zero for \(\epsilon_c > \epsilon_{cu}\) and does not append a tail branch.

ParabolaCEnv does not use Ec or Eci. The curve is a section-design parabola-rectangle relation, and the peak stress is \(\alpha f_{ck}\).

For DB input, the item strength is used as fck and alpha controls the design reduction. The DB item supplies the following section-design shape parameters, with fck in MPa:

KDS-2026:

\[ n= \begin{cases} 2.0 & (f_{ck} \le 40) \\ 1.2 + 1.5\left((100-f_{ck})/60\right)^4 & (40 < f_{ck} \le 90) \end{cases} \] \[ \varepsilon_{co}= \begin{cases} 0.002 & (f_{ck} \le 40) \\ 0.002 + 0.0001(f_{ck}-40)/10 & (40 < f_{ck} \le 90) \end{cases} \] \[ \varepsilon_{cu}= \begin{cases} 0.0033 & (f_{ck} \le 40) \\ 0.0033 - 0.0001(f_{ck}-40)/10 & (40 < f_{ck} \le 90) \end{cases} \]

EC2-2004:

\[ n= \begin{cases} 2.0 & (f_{ck} \le 50) \\ 1.4 + 23.4\left((90-f_{ck})/100\right)^4 & (50 < f_{ck} \le 90) \end{cases} \] \[ \varepsilon_{co}= \begin{cases} 0.002 & (f_{ck} \le 50) \\ \left(2.0 + 0.085(f_{ck}-50)^{0.53}\right)/1000 & (50 < f_{ck} \le 90) \end{cases} \] \[ \varepsilon_{cu}= \begin{cases} 0.0035 & (f_{ck} \le 50) \\ \left(2.6 + 35\left((90-f_{ck})/100\right)^4\right)/1000 & (50 < f_{ck} \le 90) \end{cases} \]

For KDS strength-design section checks, use \(\alpha=0.85\). For KDS limit-state design, use \(\alpha=0.85\phi_c\); \(\phi_c=0.65\) for ultimate load combinations and \(\phi_c=1.0\) for extreme-event, service, or fatigue load combinations. For EC2, use \(\alpha=\alpha_{cc}/\gamma_C\); \(\alpha_{cc}\) is a national parameter, typically between 0.8 and 1.0, and \(\gamma_C\) is 1.5 for persistent/transient situations or 1.2 for accidental situations.

Fig. 8.2-2. ParabolaCEnv function

docs.title: 8.1.6 *Function, Type=HognestadCEnv
docs.text:
Define the compressive envelope of concrete based on Hognestad's curve.

*Function, Type=HognestadCEnv, Name=name
  fco, Ec, ecu[, EciCurve]

*Function, Type=HognestadCEnv, Name=name
  KDS-2026-C<fck>|ACI318-2025-C<fck>|EC2-2004-C<fck>[, EciCurve][, ToDirectForm]

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• fco: compressive strength (required)
  • Ec: secant modulus to 0.4*fco (required)
  • ecu: ultimate strain (required for direct numeric input; DB input uses 0.003 for ACI and the standard ecu for KDS/EC2)
  • EciCurve: Optional curve-shape flag. If omitted, the curve is linear from the origin to 0.4*fco with slope Ec; if specified, the original Hognestad parabola is used from the origin.
  • KDS-2026-C<fck>, ACI318-2025-C<fck>, or EC2-2004-C<fck>: Concrete DB item. It can be used instead of the numeric dataline when keyword UnitSystem is omitted and a global UnitSystem is defined. ACI fills direct numeric fco and ecu with f'c and 0.003. KDS/EC2 fill fco and ecu with DB-derived fcm and the standard ecu. All standards use the DB-derived secant modulus for Ec.
  • ToDirectForm: Optional output option for DB item datalines. It must be the last token. When specified, saved/formatted output writes the resolved numeric dataline in the current global UnitSystem. If that unit system is the same as the global UnitSystem, no local UnitSystem is printed on the keyword line. If omitted, the DB item dataline is preserved.

Hognestad's compressive envelope of concrete is given as
