\[ f_c= \begin{cases} f_{co}\left[2\dfrac{\epsilon_c}{\epsilon_{co}}-\left(\dfrac{\epsilon_c}{\epsilon_{co}}\right)^2\right] & (\epsilon_c\le\epsilon_{co}) \\ f_{co}-0.15 f_{co}\dfrac{\epsilon_c-\epsilon_{co}}{\epsilon_{20}-\epsilon_{co}} & (\epsilon_{co}<\epsilon_c\le\epsilon_{20}) \\ 0.85 f_{co} & (\epsilon_{20}<\epsilon_c\le\epsilon_{cu}) \end{cases} \]

For the entered secant modulus Ec, Hyfeast derives the internal initial tangent and peak strain as

\[ E_{ci}=5(1-\sqrt{0.6})E_c,\qquad \epsilon_{co}=2f_{co}/E_{ci} \]

Hyfeast uses the internal value epsilon20=0.003; direct numeric input and DB output do not include epsilon20. By default, the curve segment from the origin to 0.4*fco is replaced by a straight line with slope Ec. When EciCurve is specified, the original parabolic curve is used from the origin.

Fig. 8.2-3. Hognestad concrete compressive envelope

docs.title: 8.1.7 *Function, Type=EC2CEnv
docs.text:
Defines an EC2-family concrete compressive envelope.

*Function, Type=EC2CEnv, UnitSystem=unitSystem, Name=name
 fcm, Ec, eco, ecu[, EciCurve]

*Function, Type=EC2CEnv, Name=name
 KDS-2026-C<fck>|EC2-2004-C<fck>[, EciCurve][, ToDirectForm]

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• fcm: compressive strength (required)
  • Ec: secant modulus to 0.4*fcm (required)
  • eco: strain at peak concrete strength (required)
  • ecu: ultimate strain (required)
  • EciCurve: Optional curve-shape flag. If omitted, the curve is linear from the origin to 0.4*fcm with slope Ec; if specified, the EC2-family curve is used from the origin.
  • KDS-2026-C<fck> or EC2-2004-C<fck>: Concrete DB item accepted by EC2CEnv. It can be used instead of the numeric dataline when keyword UnitSystem is omitted and a global UnitSystem is defined. <fck> is the compressive strength in MPa. The DB item supplies fcm, Ec, and the nonlinear-analysis eco and ecu coefficients.
  • ToDirectForm: Optional output option for DB item datalines. It must be the last token. When specified, saved/formatted output writes the resolved numeric dataline in the current global UnitSystem. If that unit system is the same as the global UnitSystem, no local UnitSystem is printed on the keyword line. If omitted, the DB item dataline is preserved.

The EC2-family curve is

\[ f_c=f_{cm}\frac{k\eta-\eta^2}{1+(k-2)\eta}, \qquad \eta=\frac{\epsilon_c}{\epsilon_{co}}, \qquad 0\le\epsilon_c\le\epsilon_{cu} \]

Hyfeast returns zero beyond ecu.

For the entered secant modulus Ec, Hyfeast first computes the strain at the 0.4-strength point:

\[ \epsilon_{0.4}=\frac{0.4 f_{cm}}{E_c}, \qquad x_{0.4}=\frac{\epsilon_{0.4}}{\epsilon_{co}} \]

The internal initial tangent is then selected so that the EC2-family curve passes through \((\epsilon_{0.4},0.4f_{cm})\):

\[ k=\frac{0.4-0.8x_{0.4}+x_{0.4}^2}{0.6x_{0.4}}, \qquad E_{ci}=k\frac{f_{cm}}{\epsilon_{co}} \]

Here \(k=E_{ci}\epsilon_{co}/f_{cm}\). When EciCurve is omitted, \(\epsilon_{0.4}\) is the end of the initial straight segment with slope Ec; when EciCurve is specified, the curve uses the derived \(E_{ci}\) from the origin.

Fig. 8.2-4. EC2-family concrete compressive envelope

docs.title: 8.1.8 *Function, Type=MPPCEnv
docs.text:
Define the compressive envelope of concrete based on the Mander, Priestley, and Park model.

*Function, Type=MPPCEnv, Name=name
  fco, Ec, eco, ecu, fcc, esp[, EciCurve]

*Function, Type=MPPCEnv, Name=name
  KDS-2026-C<fck>|ACI318-2025-C<fck>|EC2-2004-C<fck>[, EciCurve][, ToDirectForm]

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• fco: unconfined compressive strength (required)
  • Ec: unconfined secant modulus to 0.4*fco (required)
  • eco: strain at peak strength of unconfined concrete (optional, default 0.002)
  • ecu: ultimate strain (optional, default 2*eco)
  • fcc: confined compressive strength. (optional, default fco)
  • esp: spalling strain (optional, default ecu). A straight spalling branch from ecu to esp is used only when esp is greater than ecu; Hyfeast returns zero beyond esp.
  • EciCurve: Optional curve-shape flag. If omitted, the curve is linear from the origin to 0.4*fco or 0.4*fcc with the derived secant slope; if specified, the Mander-Priestley-Park curve is used from the origin.
  • KDS-2026-C<fck>, ACI318-2025-C<fck>, or EC2-2004-C<fck>: Concrete DB item. It can be used instead of the numeric dataline when keyword UnitSystem is omitted and a global UnitSystem is defined. DB input assumes unconfined concrete. ACI fills fco=f'c, eco=0.002, and ecu=0.003; KDS/EC2 fill fco=fcm, eco=standard value, and ecu=standard value. All standards use the DB-derived secant modulus for Ec, set fcc=fco, and set esp=ecu.
  • ToDirectForm: Optional output option for DB item datalines. It must be the last token. When specified, saved/formatted output writes the resolved numeric dataline in the current global UnitSystem. If that unit system is the same as the global UnitSystem, no local UnitSystem is printed on the keyword line. If omitted, the DB item dataline is preserved.

The Mander-Priestley-Park model can define both the confined and unconfined concrete model.

For the unconfined input values, Hyfeast interprets Ec as the secant modulus to 0.4*fco:

\[ E_{sec,0}=\frac{f_{co}}{\epsilon_{co}}, \qquad \epsilon_{0.4,0}=\frac{0.4 f_{co}}{E_c}, \qquad x_{0.4,0}=\frac{\epsilon_{0.4,0}}{\epsilon_{co}} =0.4\frac{E_{sec,0}}{E_c} \]

The Mander-Priestley-Park stress ratio is

\[ \frac{f_c}{f_{cc}}= \frac{x r}{r-1+x^r}, \qquad r=\frac{E_{ci}}{E_{ci}-E_{sec}} \]

Hyfeast solves the unconfined equation below for \(r_0\), then derives the internal initial tangent:

\[ 0.4=\frac{x_{0.4,0} r_0}{r_0-1+x_{0.4,0}^{r_0}}, \qquad E_{ci}=\frac{r_0}{r_0-1}E_{sec,0} \]

The direct input must satisfy \(E_c \ge E_{sec,0}\). If fcc differs from fco, the same \(E_{ci}\) is used for the confined curve. Hyfeast computes

\[ \epsilon_{cc}=\epsilon_{co}\left(1+5\left(\frac{f_{cc}}{f_{co}}-1\right)\right), \qquad E_{sec,c}=\frac{f_{cc}}{\epsilon_{cc}}, \qquad r_c=\frac{E_{ci}}{E_{ci}-E_{sec,c}} \]

and solves \(0.4=x_{0.4,c}r_c/(r_c-1+x_{0.4,c}^{r_c})\). The transition strain used by the default linearized branch is then

\[ \epsilon_{0.4,c}=x_{0.4,c}\epsilon_{cc}, \qquad E_{c,\mathrm{linear}}=\frac{0.4f_{cc}}{\epsilon_{0.4,c}} \]

When EciCurve is omitted, the curve is linear from the origin to this current 0.4-strength point. When EciCurve is specified, the Mander-Priestley-Park curve uses the derived \(E_{ci}\) from the origin.

Fig. 8.2-5. Mander-Priestley-Park concrete compressive envelope

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
*Function, Type=MPPCEnv, Name=MPPCEnvTest1
 25., 23500.   #   fco, Ec, eco, ecu, fcc, esp

*Function, Type=MPPCEnv, Name=MPPCEnvTest2
 25., 23500., 0.002, 0.004, 40., 0.006, EciCurve    #   fco, Ec, eco, ecu, fcc, esp

docs.title: 8.1.9 *Function, Type=MPPCIE
docs.text:
Define the inelastic strain of concrete based on the Mander, Priestley, and Park model.

*Function, Type=MPPCIE, Name=cover
  compressiveEnv, epeak

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• compressiveEnv: Compressive envelope function
  • epeak: strain at peak concrete strength (optional, default 0.002). If the given compressiveEnv is a type of MPPCEnv, Hognestad, and CEBFIB, epeak is neglected (automatically computed).

MPPCIE is a dimensionless strain function that computes inelastic strain from the referenced compressive envelope. Therefore UnitSystem is not allowed on the keyword line and is treated as an input error when specified.

Although this function defines the inelastic strain by the Mander-Priestley-Park model, it can be used with the arbitrary compressive envelope function

docs.title: 8.1.10 *Function, Type=MaekawaTEnv
docs.text:
Maekawa concrete tensile envelope

*Function, Type=MaekawaTEnv, UnitSystem=unitSystem, Name=coverTension
  Ec, ft[, c]

*Function, Type=MaekawaTEnv, Name=coverTension
  KDS-2026-C<fck>|ACI318-2025-C<fck>|EC2-2004-C<fck>[, c][, ToDirectForm]

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• Ec: secant elastic modulus (required for direct numeric input)
  • ft: tensile strength (required for direct numeric input)
  • c: parameter for Maekawa model (optional, default 0.4)
  • KDS-2026-C<fck>, ACI318-2025-C<fck>, or EC2-2004-C<fck>: Concrete DB item. It fills direct numeric Ec with the DB-derived secant modulus when keyword UnitSystem is omitted and a global UnitSystem is defined. It fills ft with \(7.5\sqrt{f'_c}\) for ACI items and \(f_{ctm}\) for KDS/EC2 items.
  • ToDirectForm: Optional output option for DB item datalines. It must be the last token. When specified, saved/formatted output writes the resolved numeric dataline in the current global UnitSystem. If that unit system is the same as the global UnitSystem, no local UnitSystem is printed on the keyword line. If omitted, the DB item dataline is preserved.

Maekawa et al. (2002) proposed the following tension softening curve for both normal concrete and reinforced concrete considering tensile hardening, using the same equation:

\[ \sigma = f_t \left(\frac{\epsilon_{tu}} {\epsilon_t} \right)^c \]

Here, \(c\) is the factor that determines the shape of the curve. For normal concrete, it should be determined by the following equation based on fracture energy and the characteristic length of the element:

\[ \int \sigma_t d \epsilon_t = \int f_t \left(\frac{\epsilon_{tu}} {\epsilon_t} \right)^c d \epsilon_t = \frac {G_F}{l_r} \]

In reinforced concrete, parameter analysis suggests a value of 0.4 for deformed bars and 0.2 for welded wire mesh. Figure 8.2-6 shows a representative result.

Fig. 8.2-6. Maekawa concrete tensile envelope

docs.title: 8.1.11 *Function, Type=ConcreteTime
docs.text:
Concrete time-dependent function set

*Function, Type=ConcreteTime, Name=name
 User, Aging=fcAge, ftAge, EcAge, Creep=creepDuration, creepLoadAge, Shrinkage=shrinkage

*Function, Type=ConcreteTime, Name=name
 EC2-2004-C<fck>, RH, h0, ts, cementClass

*Function, Type=ConcreteTime, Name=name
 KDS-2026-C<fck>, RH, h0, ts, cementType, curingType

*Function, Type=ConcreteTime, Name=name
 ACI209-1992-C<fc>, RH, V/S, ts, cementType, curingType

*Function, Type=ConcreteTime, Name=name
 ACI209-1992-C<fc>, RH, V/S, ts, cementType, curingType, creepUltimateScale, shrinkageUltimateScale

*Function, Type=ConcreteTime, Name=name
 ACI209-1992-C<fc>, RH, V/S, ts, cementType, curingType, moistCuringDuration, slump, fineAggregatePercent, cementContent, airContent

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• User: Uses existing functions as the user-defined time-dependent function set. The named-group form accepts one or more of Aging, Creep, and Shrinkage; omitted groups use neutral defaults.
  • Aging=fcAge, ftAge, EcAge: Function names for the compressive-strength, tensile-strength, and elastic-modulus age factors. The three functions must be specified together. They are evaluated with \(x=t\). If omitted, the three age factors are 1.
  • Creep=creepDuration, creepLoadAge: Function names for the creep duration factor and creep loading-age factor. creepDuration is evaluated with \(x=t-\tau\), and creepLoadAge is evaluated with \(x=\tau\). The two functions must be specified together. If omitted, the creep contribution is 0.
  • Shrinkage=shrinkage: Function name for the free shrinkage strain. It is evaluated with \(x=t\). For the User input function value, + means shrinkage and - means expansion; the sign is reversed when the value is used in the material. If omitted, the shrinkage contribution is 0.
  • EC2-2004-C<fck>: EC2-2004 concrete time-dependent function. <fck> is in MPa. cementClass is S, N, or R.
  • KDS-2026-C<fck>: KDS-2026 concrete time-dependent function. <fck> is in MPa. cementType is Type1, Type2, Type3, or Type5; curingType is Moist or Steam.
  • ACI209-1992-C<fc>: ACI 209R-92 concrete time-dependent function. <fc> is \(f'_c\) in psi. cementType is TypeI or TypeIII; curingType is Moist or Steam.
  • RH: Relative humidity in percent.
  • h0: EC2/KDS notional member size in mm.
  • V/S: ACI 209 volume-to-surface ratio in inch. It is used directly in the ACI 209 correction equations.
  • ts: Concrete age, in days, at the beginning of drying shrinkage.
  • creepUltimateScale, shrinkageUltimateScale: Optional ACI 209 additional scale factors. When these two tokens are omitted, both factors are 1.0.
  • moistCuringDuration, slump, fineAggregatePercent, cementContent, airContent: Detailed ACI 209 correction parameters. moistCuringDuration is in days, slump is in inch, fineAggregatePercent and airContent are in percent, and cementContent is in \(\mathrm{lb/yd^3}\). slump and cementContent use fixed units and are not converted from the global unit system.

ConcreteTime stores the six function series and evaluates EC2/KDS/ACI formulas according to the concrete DB common rules and standard-specific concrete DB descriptions above. It also provides an internal default first retardation time for material-side Kelvin-chain fitting. Built-in EC2/KDS ConcreteTime functions provide 1 day, while built-in ACI 209 and User ConcreteTime functions provide 5 days. If a different first retardation time is needed, specify lambda1 in the material LongTerm, Concrete dataline that uses this function.

In both standard EC2/KDS/ACI forms and the User form, the time variables \(t\), \(\tau\), \(t-\tau\), and \(t_s\) are evaluated in days, regardless of the time unit specified by *Environment, Type=UnitSystem. A Function referenced by the User form must not define keyword-line UnitSystem=.... This section lists only the input syntax and examples.

docs.title: 9. Surface
docs.text: The surface command is specified using *Surface which is an assembly of elements' faces. Surface is used to define load, constraint, etc. Each surface must have a unique name, and duplicate names are not allowed.

docs.title: Keyword line
docs.text: • Name=name: Name of surface

docs.title: First data line and subsequent data lines
docs.text:
• faceId: Number specifying the face of the element (optional, default 1). Defined based on the element type, with an index starting from 1.
  • target: Target element number, elset, or element pattern (required). The element number pattern is in the form start:end:spacing, and spacing can be omitted if it is 1.
  • surface: Surface to be added (all faces that make up the surface will be added).

Defines a surface composed of the faces of elements. The element face is selected and specified as shown in the diagram below.

Fig. 9.2-1. Face of elements

Note

When composing a surface with shell elements, the surface is defined based on the nodes that define the shell. That is, even if the shell has thickness, the front and back faces exist in the same location except for their orientation. Since surfaces are the reference for applying loads and boundary conditions, extra caution is needed.

docs.title: 4.1 Overview
docs.text:
The elements are created using the *Element command. The number of nodes connected to each element is determined by the element type. Element properties include Section properties, which are commonly used across various elements, and Distribution properties, which are applied directly to individual elements. In addition, special elements such as Cable elements and EmbeddedLine elements have field values that can change depending on the analysis stage. The table below summarizes the corresponding Section properties, Distribution properties, and field values for each element type.

Element type Description Section Distribution State T3D2 2-node truss Beam (CS) BeamCS Cable Cable Beam CableLength B2D2H 2D Bernoulli beam Beam (R) BeamEndRelease B3D2H 3D Bernoulli beam Beam (CS) BeamCS, (R) BeamEndRelease B2D2MH 2D Timoshenko beam Beam (R) BeamEndRelease B3D2MH 3D Timoshenko beam Beam (CS) BeamCS, (R) BeamEndRelease Spring 2-node spring/damper MCK (SF) ScaleFactor, (CS) UCS EarthSpring 1-node spring/damper MCK (SF) ScaleFactor, (CS) UCS PointMass 1-node mass MCK (SF) ScaleFactor, (CS) UCS MovingSpring Moving spring MovingSpring (P) InitialPosition Speed EmbeddedLine Embedded Line (Rebar or Tendon) EmbeddedLine (L) Spline, (H) HostElset TendonForce, TendonForceHold S3F 3-node flat shell Shell S3 3-node shell Shell S4F 4-node flat shell Shell S4 4-node shell Shell CS6 6-node solid shell Shell CS8 8-node solid shell Shell CPS3 3-node triangular plane stress solid Solid CPS4 4-node rectangular plane stress solid Solid CPE3 3-node triangular plane strain solid Solid CPE4 4-node rectangular plane strain solid Solid CAX3 3-node triangular axisym. solid Solid CAX4 4-node rectangular axisym. solid Solid C3D4 4-node tetra solid Solid C3D6 6-node triangular solid Solid C3D8 8-node hexahedral solid Solid C3D8I 8-node hexahedral acoustic solid(Incompatible) Solid C2D4PMDL 4-node rectangular strain stress solid(PMDL) Solid CAX4PMDL 4-node rectangular axisym. solid(PMDL) Solid C3D8PMDL 8-node hexahedral solid(PMDL) Solid AC2D3 3-node triangular acoustic solid Solid AC2D4 4-node rectangular acoustic solid Solid AC3D4 4-node tetra acoustic solid Solid AC3D6 6-node triangular acoustic solid Solid AC3D8 8-node hexahedral acoustic solid Solid AC2D4PMDL 4-node rectangular acoustic solid(PMDL) Solid AC3D8PMDL 8-node hexahedral acoustic solid(PMDL) Solid SC2D3 3-node triangular seepage solid Solid SC2D4 4-node rectangular seepage solid Solid SC3D4 4-node tetra seepage solid Solid SC3D6 6-node triangular seepage solid Solid SC3D8 8-node hexahedral seepage solid Solid

docs.title: 4.10 MovingSpring
docs.text:
The MovingSpring element simulates a moving spring (a combination of spring and damper) rolling on a line or surface defined by beam elements.

Fig. 4.9-1. MovingSpring Element on a Line Composed of Beams

Fig. 4.9-2. MovingSpring Element on a 3D Surface

Fig. 4.9-3. MovingSpring Element on a 2D Surface

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• When performing dynamic analysis, a preliminary static analysis considering self-weight must be conducted first.
  • To activate the MovingSpring element, the speed must be defined using *State, Type=MovingSpringSpeed.
  • If damping is considered, the overall stiffness matrix will become an asymmetric matrix.

docs.title: 4.10.2 *Element, Type=MovingSpring
docs.text:
*Element, Type=MovingSpring, Elset=elset
 id, n1{, S=section, P=x,y}
 ...

docs.title: First data line and subsequent data lines
docs.text: • P=x,y: Initial position relative to the reference point. Defined in the ECS. When targeting beam elements, the y value is ignored.

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text:
• No. of nodes: 1
  • No. of integration points: 1
  • Fields: SF=[...], SE=[...], DF=[...], DE=[...] at the element center.
  • Compatible section: MovingSpring
  • Active DOFs: Can include Y and Z depending on the definition.

Refer to *Element, Type=Spring for explanations of SF, SE, DF, and DE.

docs.title: 4.10.3 *Section, Type=MovingSpring
docs.text:
Defines the properties for a MovingSpring.

*Section, Type=MovingSpring, Name=name
  surface, refx, refy, refz, g1x, g1y, g1z, xRigid, yRigid, zRigid
  Spring, oneDof, coef|material
  ...
  Damper, oneDof, coef|material
  ...
  UnitSystem, force-length-time

*Section, Type=MovingSpring, Name=name
  line, xRigid, yRigid, zRigid
  Spring, oneDof, coef|material
  ...
  Damper, oneDof, coef|material
  ...
  UnitSystem, force-length-time

docs.title: First data line for Line
docs.text:
• line: Target beam elset ... The beams should be connected.
  • xRigid, yRigid, zRigid: Position vector from the reference node (rigid arm vector). x1 is required, others are optional.

docs.title: First data line for Surface
docs.text:
• surface: Target surface (required).
  • refx, refy, refz: Reference point (optional; default: 0, 0, 0).
  • g1x, g1y, g1z: Direction of travel (1, 0, 0).
  • xRigid, yRigid, zRigid: Position vector from the reference node (rigid arm vector) (optional; default: 0, 0, 0).

docs.title: Second and subsequent data line if necessary
docs.text:
• Spring|Damper: Spring or damper
  • oneDof: Degree of freedom to which the spring/damper is applied; one of X, Y, Z, RX, RY, or RZ
  • coef: Spring or damping coefficient
  • material: Reference material model used instead of the spring or damping coefficient. Must support uniaxial material behavior
  • referenceUnitSysem: Reference unit system of the material model, used when a material is specified. Optional; defaults to the current unit system. Should be specified in the first data line starting with Spring or Damper

docs.title: Second and subsequent data line starting with Spring
docs.text:
• oneDof: Degree of freedom to which the spring is applied; one of Y and Z
  • coef: Spring coefficient
  • material: Reference material model used instead of the spring coefficient. Must support uniaxial material behavior

docs.title: Second and subsequent data line starting with Damper
docs.text:
• oneDof: Degree of freedom to which the dmaper is applied; one of Y and Z
  • coef: Damping coefficient
  • material: Reference material model used instead of the damping coefficient. Must support uniaxial material behavior

docs.title: Optional single UnitSystem data line after second data line
docs.text:
• force-length-time: The local unit system applied to this section. force must be one of N, kN, kgf, tonf, lbf, or kip; length must be one of m, cm, mm, km, in, ft, yd, or mi; and time must be one of s, min, hr, or day.

Spring, Damper, Mass, and UnitSystem may be defined in any order, and Spring and Damper may be used multiple times depending on the DOF to which they are applied.

Spring or damping coefficients are generally defined as numerical values. However, when nonlinear behavior is to be represented, they may be defined by referencing a material that supports a uniaxial material model. For example, if a uniaxial material model is assigned to a Spring in the X direction, the stress?뱒train relation of that material is interpreted as a generalized force?밺isplacement relation in the Y direction.

  • localUnitSystem is optional and is specified in the form of force-length-time, such as kN-mm-s. The force unit shall be one of N, kN, kgf, tonf, lbf, and kip; the length unit shall be one of m, cm, mm, km, in, ft, yd, and mi; and the time unit shall be one of s, min, hr, and day.
  • If localUnitSystem is specified and a global UnitSystem is available, the section input is interpreted through the local-to-global relationship.
  • If localUnitSystem is specified while no global UnitSystem is currently defined, it is preserved as local metadata and does not cause an input-time error.
  • If localUnitSystem is not specified, the input for this Section follows the global UnitSystem defined by *Environment, Type=UnitSystem when one exists.
  • localUnitSystem defines the unit system for coef or material used in this Section.
  • If localUnitSystem is identical to the global UnitSystem, the input values are used directly without any additional scaling. If the two unit systems are different, appropriate unit conversion is performed internally. For example, if the global UnitSystem is kN-m-s and the localUnitSystem is kN-mm-s, and a material model is used for a Spring in the X direction, the displacement is converted from the m basis to the mm basis before evaluating the material model, and the generalized force computed by the material model is then converted back to the global UnitSystem and used in the analysis.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
*SECTION, Type=MovingSpring, Name=MSx
 rail
 Spring, Y, 1595E3
 Damper, Y, 1000E3
*SECTION, Type=MovingSpring, Name=MS
 rail
 UnitSystem, kN-mm-s
 Spring, Y, 1595E3
 Damper, Y, 1000E3

docs.title: 4.11 Interface
docs.text:
Interface elements can be regarded as a type of distributed spring element that models the mechanical behavior between adjacent elements. The element I2D4 is applicable to two-dimensional problems. Since interface elements are defined based on their geometric characteristics, they are not separately classified into plane stress or plane strain types. IAX4 is used for axisymmetric conditions, while I3D6 and I3D8 are applicable in three-dimensional analyses.

Fig. 4.10-1. Interface element

docs.title: 4.11.5 *Section, Type=Interface
docs.text:
Define a section for interface element

*Section, Type=Interface, Name=name
 matA,matB,matN,thick,localUnitSystem

*Section, Type=Interface, Name=name
 cohesive_material,thick

docs.title: First data line  for uncoupled uniaxial materials
docs.text:
• matA, matB, matN: reference uniaxial material models (required). A, B, and N correspond two tangential directions and normal direction.
  • thick: Trasverse thickness. Optional. default 1. Used in 2D interface element
  • localUnitSystem: local UnitSystem with force-length form (optional).

docs.title: First data line for cohesive material
docs.text:
• cohesive_material: Cohesive material model (required)
  • thick: Trasverse thickness. Optional. default 1. Used in 2D interface element

If three materials are specified, independent traction?뱑elative displacement relations are applied in each direction. In this case, the referenced materials shall support uniaxial material models only. For example, if the stress?뱒train relation of a uniaxial material model is used for the constitutive relation in the A-direction, it shall be interpreted as a traction?뱑elative displacement relation. The optional localUnitSystem shall be specified in the form of force-length, such as kN-mm. The following rules shall apply.

  • localUnitSystem is optional and shall be specified in the form of force-length, such as kN-mm. The force unit shall be one of N, kN, kgf, tonf, lbf, or kip, and the length unit shall be one of m, cm, mm, km, in, ft, yd, or mi.
  • If localUnitSystem is specified and a global UnitSystem is available, the section input is interpreted through the local-to-global relationship.
  • If localUnitSystem is specified while no global UnitSystem is currently defined, it is preserved as local metadata and does not cause an input-time error.
  • If localUnitSystem is not specified, the unit system shall follow the global UnitSystem defined by *Environment, Type=UnitSystem when one exists.
  • localUnitSystem defines the unit system for matA, matB, matN, and thick.
  • If localUnitSystem is identical to the global UnitSystem, matA, matB, and matN are used with a one-to-one conversion. Otherwise, an appropriate unit conversion shall be performed. For example, if the global UnitSystem is kN-m and the localUnitSystem is kN-mm, the relative displacement is internally converted from m to mm (횞1000) before evaluating the material model, and the traction computed by the material model in kN/mm짼 is then converted back to the analysis unit system, kN/m짼, for use in the analysis.

docs.title: 4.12 EmbeddedLine
docs.text:
The EmbeddedLine element is used to model embedded tendons or reinforcing bars, and is defined through the EmbeddedLine element type and the EmbeddedLine section type. When defining an EmbeddedLine section, the element profile is specified by a spline geometry. For each element, a host element set must be assigned. The applicable host element families are as follows:

  • 2D Beam elements: B2D2H, B2D2MH
  • 3D Beam elements: B3D2H, B3D2MH
  • Shell elements: S3F, S4F, S3, S4
  • Solid-shell elements: CS6, CS8
  • 2D Solid elements: CPE4, CPS4, CAX4, CPS3, CPE3, CAX3
  • 3D Solid elements: C3D8, C3D8I, C3D6

The host element set assigned to an EmbeddedLine element must consist of elements from the same family. For tendon analysis, prestressing loads can be applied using the *State command.

▪ Note

  • The EmbeddedLine element does not compute a mass matrix (it contributes only to stiffness).
  • Reinforcement modeling can alternatively be performed using truss elements(T3D2) combined with Embedded constraints. In this case, only straight bars can be represented and prestressing cannot be applied.
  • The EmbeddedLine element uses a single node, but only as a reference point for the spline geometry. No degrees of freedom are defined at that node.

Fig. 4.11-1. EmbeddedLine element

docs.title: 4.12.1 *Element, Type=EmbeddedLine
docs.text:
Define EmbeddedLine element

*Element, Type=EmbeddedLine, Elset=elset
  id, n1, S=sec, L=spline, H=hostElset

docs.title: First data line and subsequent lines
docs.text:
• L=spline: Spline defining the profile
  • H=hostElset: Host elset

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text:
• No. of nodes: 1
  • Fields: ED=[ED.X ED.Y ED.Z] and uniaxial material field at Gauss point
  • Compatible section: EmbeddedLine
  • Active DOFs: None

▪ Notes

  • The n1 node is used only as a reference point for defining the geometry and does not contribute to the stiffness or mass matrix of the element.
  • The number of integration points depends on the integration scheme specified in the cross-section (Aligned or Unaligned).

docs.title: 4.12.2 *Section, Type=EmbeddedLine
docs.text:
Define the properties for EmbeddedLine element

*Section, Type=EmbeddedLine, Name=name
  material, area, { Aligned, ngauss | Unaligned, nsegment }
  mu, kappa

docs.title: Keyword line
docs.text: • Name=name: Section name. Section names must be unique.

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• material: material (required)
  • area: area (required)
  • Aigned, ngauss: The spline is divided according to the host element for integration, and the Legendre integration with ngauss points is applied to each segment. (optional, default: Aligned, 3)
  • Unaligned, nsegment: The spline is divided into nsegment parts, and the Trapezoidal rule is applied for integration. In this mode, the subdivision does not match the host element mesh. If nsegment is not specified, it is determined automatically as twice the number of elements that the spline passes through. (optional) Total number of integration points are nsegment + 1.

docs.title: Second data line (optional)
docs.text:
• mu, kappa: Curvature and wobble friction coefficients (optional, default 0., 0.).

The curvature friction coefficient has a unit of 1/rad, and the wobble friction coefficient has a unit of 1/length. Their typical ranges are 0.15–0.3 /rad and 0.00021–0.007 /m, respectively.

docs.title: 4.2 Beam
docs.text:
The beam element is a structural element that transmits axial force, bending, and torsion, with its dimension along the longitudinal axis (x-axis in the ECS) being larger compared to other directions. The element type, cross-section, and distribution are as follows:

■ Element Type

  • B2D2H: 2-dimensional 2-node, Bernoulli beam (Hermitian shape function used)
  • B2D2MH: 2-dimensional 2-node, Timoshenko beam (Modified Hermitian shape function used)
  • B3D2H: 3-dimensional 2-node, Bernoulli beam (Hermitian shape function used)
  • B3D2MH: 3-dimensional 2-node, Timoshenko beam (Modified Hermitian shape function used)

■ Element Cross-Section

  • Beam: Beam element cross-section. Composed of one or more Cells.

■ Element-Specific Properties (Distribution)

  • BeamCS: Defines the ECS for the 3D beam element.
  • BeamEndRelease: Applies hinge conditions (moment release) at the element ends. Combination of Rx1, Ry1, Rz1, Rx2, Ry2, and Rz2. For example, Rz1|Rz2.

The B2D2H and B3D2H elements, which ignore shear deformation, support nonlinear material models and can simulate variable cross-sections. On the other hand, the B2D2MH and B3D2MH elements, which consider shear deformation, are applicable only for elastic materials. Since variable cross-section formulation is theoretically not possible, when cross-sectional properties are given as a variable cross-section, an average value is applied within the element.

The ECS of a 2D beam element is defined as the x-axis (member axis) and the y-axis perpendicular to it, as shown in Figure 4.2-1 below.

Fig. 4.2-1. 2D Beam Element ECS

For 3D beam elements, while the x-axis can be defined as the member axis, the y and z axes are determined by the reference vector r and an additional section rotation angle θ. Figure 4.2-2 below shows an example where the ECS is set with a section rotation angle θ=0. The default value of the r vector is set to r = (0,0,1), as shown in Figure 4.2-3. Exceptionally, when the member axis is parallel to the global coordinate system's Z-axis, the value of r is set to (1,0,0). Parallelism is determined when the member axis is within a slope of 1:100 (approximately 0.573 degrees) relative to the Z-axis.

The ECS can be further defined using a rotated coordinate system based on the section rotation angle θ from the r vector. The default value of θ is 0.

Fig. 4.2-2. 3D Beam Element ECS

Fig. 4.2-3. Default Reference Vector

In Hyfeast, the reference axis of the beam element is defined based on the line segment connecting the nodes, and it does not need to coincide with the centroid. However, the formulation is performed at the centroid. In particular, section forces and deformations are calculated with reference to the centroid, so caution is required.

The cross-section of the beam element, referred to as the Beam cross-section, is defined as a set of Cells that represent a geometric shape to which the same material is applied. The figure below shows the available Cells.

Fig. 4.2-4. Cell in Beam Section (viewed from the local +z direction)

The following is a summary of items related to cells:

  1. If the cross-section consists of a single cell, it is a homogeneous beam cross-section. If it consists of two or more cells, it is a composite beam cross-section.
  2. When configuring a beam cross-section with two or more cells, there are restrictions depending on the type of cell used.
  3. Value, Rectangle, Circle, and H/T/C/L/2C/2L/HR[-YUp] cells only allow elastic material (IsoElasticity) and can only output stress (S), total strain (E), mechanical strain (EM), elastic strain (EE), and other elastic-material field values at a few predefined material points, as shown in Figure 4.2-5.
  4. Direct H/T/C/L/2C/2L/HR[-YUp] standard-shape cells compute section constants using two-dimensional finite element analysis. The internally generated mesh uses quadratic elements such as Q8 and T6 to represent fillets and other curved boundaries accurately.
  5. For standard-shape cells, a shape token with -YUp, such as H-YUp or Mesh,H-YUp, aligns the section height with the local y-direction. It can be understood as a 90-degree rotation of the corresponding base shape cell and is useful for two-dimensional beams (B2D2H, B2D2MH) where the user cannot define the beam local coordinate system.
  6. Point, Layer, and Mesh cells can be used with both elastic and inelastic materials.
  7. Point cells can output the field values of the used materials, such as stress (S) and strain (E, EM), at all material points that constitute the cell.
  8. Layer cells can output the field values of the used materials, such as stress (S) and strain (E, EM), at the top and bottom of each layer.
  9. Mesh cells predefine the material points that form the mesh using *CellMeshPoints, and these material points can be used to output field values, such as stress (S) and strain (E, EM), for the used materials.
  10. Value, Rectangle, Circle, and H/T/C/L/2C/2L/HR[-YUp] cells are allowed to exist independently or in combination with Point cells only. (e.g., Rectangle (OK), Rectangle+Point (OK), Rectangle+Rectangle (NG), Rectangle+Value (NG))
  11. Layer cells are allowed to be combined only with Layer and Point cells. (e.g., Layer (OK), Layer+Mesh (OK), Layer+Point (OK), Layer+Layer+Point (OK), Layer+Rectangle (NG))
  12. Mesh cells are allowed to be combined only with Mesh and Point cells. (e.g., Mesh (OK), Mesh+Mesh (OK), Mesh+Point (OK), Mesh+Mesh+Point (OK), Mesh+Rectangle (NG))
  13. Point cells should generally be combined with other types of cells, but they can also be used independently. (e.g., Value+Point (OK), Rectangle+Point (OK), Point (OK), Point+Point (OK))
  14. When a cross-section uses Point cells, the Point cells only contribute to bending and compression calculations but do not contribute to shear or torsion calculations. For example, when calculating section constants, EA and EI are calculated considering the contribution of the Point cells, but GJ and GAs are not considered. (EA, EIy, EIz, EIyz)
  15. Layer cells are only applicable to 2D beam elements (B2D2H, B2D2MH).

Fig. 4.2-5. Output points in elastic cell (viewed from the local +z direction)

docs.title: 4.2.1 *Element, Type=B2D2H
docs.text:
2D 2-Node Bernoulli Beam Element

*Element, Type=B2D2H, Elset=elset
 id, n1, n2, [, S=section, R=beamEndRelease]
 ...

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text:
• No. of nodes: 2
  • No. of gauss points: 4 (Gauss-Lobatto rule used)
  • Fields: BSF=[Nx Mz Vy], BSE=[Ex Kz Gxy], BST=[T0 Tz] at Gauss point about centroid. Uniaxial model response at each layer of Gauss point
  • Compatible section: Beam
  • Active DOFs: X,Y,RZ

The Bernoulli beam element assumes zero shear deformation, meaning that shear forces are not defined as state variables and must be calculated using equilibrium conditions. In this formulation, the cross-sectional shear deformation is always zero, and \(V_y=–dM_z/dx\) is used to calculate the shear force.

\(V_y\) is computed by first interpolating \(M_z(x)\) using a polynomial based on the moment response at the integration points, and then differentiating \(M_z(x)\) to obtain \(V_y\).

The beamEndRelease option allows combinations of Rx1, Ry1, Rx2, and Ry2 (Rx1 and Ry1 correspond to the two rotations at the start node, and Rx2 and Ry2 correspond to the two rotations at the end node). For example, Ry1|Ry2.

docs.title: 4.2.2 *Element, Type=B3D2H
docs.text:
3D 2-Node Bernoulli Beam Element

*Element, Type=B3D2H, Elset=elset
 id, n1, n2, [, S=section, CS=beamCS, R=beamEndRelease]
 ...

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text:
• No. of nodes: 2
  • No. of gauss points: 4 (Gauss-Lobatto rule used)
  • Fields: BSF=[Nx My Mz Vy Vz T], BSE=[Ex Ky Kz Gxy Gxz Hx], BST=[T0 Ty Tz] at Gauss point about centroid. Uniaxial model response at each layer of Gauss point
  • Compatible section: Beam
  • Active DOFs: X, Y, Z, RX, RY, RZ

If the Bernoulli beam element assumes zero shear deformation, shear forces are not defined as state variables and must be calculated using equilibrium conditions. In this formulation, cross-sectional shear deformations \(\gamma_y\) and \(\gamma_z\) are always zero, and shear forces are calculated as follows:

\(V_y = –dM_z/dx, \quad V_z = dM_y/dx\)

\(V_y\) is computed by first interpolating \(M_z(x)\) using a polynomial based on the moment response at the integration points, and then differentiating \(M_z(x)\) to obtain \(V_y\). \(Hx\) represents \(d\theta / dx\).

The beamEndRelease option allows combinations of Rx1, Ry1, Rz1, Rx2, Ry2, and Rz2 (Rx1, Ry1, and Rz1 correspond to the three rotations at the start node, and Rx2, Ry2, and Rz2 correspond to the three rotations at the end node). For example, Rz1|Rz2.

docs.title: 4.2.3 *Element, Type=B2D2MH
docs.text:
2D 2-Node Timoshenko Beam Element

*Element, Type=B2D2MH, Elset=elset
 id, n1, n2, [, S=section, R=beamEndRelease]
 ...

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text:
• No. of nodes: 2
  • No. of gauss points: 4 (Gauss-Lobatto rule used)
  • Fields: BSF=[Nx Mz Vy], BSE=[Ex Kz Gxy], BST=[T0 Tz] at Gauss point about centroid
  • Compatible section: Beam
  • Active DOFs: X, Y, RZ

The beamEndRelease option allows combinations of Rx1, Ry1, Rx2, and Ry2 (Rx1 and Ry1 correspond to the two rotations at the start node, and Rx2 and Ry2 correspond to the two rotations at the end node). For example, Ry1|Ry2.

docs.title: 4.2.4 *Element, Type=B3D2MH
docs.text:
3D 2-Node Timoshenko Beam Element

*Element, Type=B3D2MH, Elset=elset
 id, n1, n2, [, S=section, CS=beamCS, R=beamEndRelease]
 ...

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text:
• No. of nodes: 2
  • No. of gauss points: 4 (Gauss-Lobatto rule used)
  • Fields: BSF=[Nx My Mz Vy Vz T], BSE=[Ex Ky Kz Gxy Gxz Hx], BST=[T0 Ty Tz] at Gauss point about centroid
  • Compatible section: Beam
  • Active DOFs: X, Y, Z, RX, RY, RZ

Hx represents \(d\theta/dx\).

The beamEndRelease option allows combinations of Rx1, Ry1, Rz1, Rx2, Ry2, and Rz2 (Rx1, Ry1, and Rz1 correspond to the three rotations at the start node, and Rx2, Ry2, and Rz2 correspond to the three rotations at the end node). For example, Rz1|Rz2.

docs.title: 4.2.5 *Section, Type=Beam
docs.text:
Defines a beam section.

*Section, Type=Beam,  Name=name, Taper=Group|Element, Mass=Consistent|Lumped
*CellMeshPoint
 ...
*Cell, Type=Rectangle|Circle|H/T/C/L/2C/2L/HR[-YUp]|Mesh|Mesh,Rectangle|Mesh,Circle|Mesh,H/T/C/L/2C/2L/HR[-YUp]|Layer|Point, Mat=mat
 ...
*ShearTorsionMaterial
 ...

docs.title: Keyword line
docs.text:
• Name=name: Section name (required). Section names must be unique.
  • Taper=Group|Element: Variable cross-section beam designation. Group treats connected beam elements as a group and assigns a variable cross-section, and Element assigns a variable cross-section for individual elements. If not specified, it means a constant cross-section beam (Optional, default None).
  • Mass={Consistent|Lumped}: Consistent or Lumped, which means consistent mass or lumped mass, respectively. (Optional, default Consistent)

docs.title: Sub-keywords
docs.text:
• *CellMeshPoint: Specifies the coordinates of points used when defining *Cell, Type=Mesh.
  • *Cell, Type=type, Mat=mat: Defines a cell within the cross-section. mat indicates the material used.
    • Value: Specifies the cross-sectional constants as values; mat must be linearly elastic.
    • Rectangle: Rectangular cross-section; mat must be linearly elastic.
    • Circle: Circular or hollow circular cross-section; mat must be linearly elastic.
    • H/T/C/L/2C/2L/HR[-YUp]: Standard steel shape cell; mat must be linearly elastic. These direct shape cells are treated as ShapeSection.
    • Mesh: Arbitrary cross-section given as a mesh. Cross-sectional constants are calculated using 2D finite element analysis.
    • Mesh,Rectangle: Generates a rectangular material point mesh.
    • Mesh,Circle: Generates a circular or hollow circular material point mesh.
    • Mesh,H/T/C/L/2C/2L/HR[-YUp]: Generates a material point mesh from a standard steel shape. These generated mesh cells are treated as MeshedSection.
    • Layer: Arbitrary cross-section given as a layer (only applicable to 2D beam elements).
    • Point: Point-shaped cell. Used for rebar modeling, etc.
  • *ShearTorsionMaterial: Specifies reference materials for shear and torsion behavior using uniaxial material model.

When a beam section is written in direct mesh form, the *Cell, Type=Mesh data lines are not limited to linear cells. The same *CellMeshPoint table can be referenced by T3, Q4, T6, or Q8 cells.

docs.title: 4.2.6 *CellMeshPoint
docs.text:
Specifies the coordinates of points used when defining *Cell, Type=Mesh.

*CellMeshPoint
 pointId, y, z, {y, z}
 ...

docs.title: First data line and subsequent data lines
docs.text:
• pointId: Point ID
  • y, z, {y, z}: Point coordinates [L]. If two values are given, they define a constant cross-section; if four values are given, they define a tapered cross-section.

The point table is shared by every direct mesh cell of the section, regardless of whether the mesh cell uses 3, 4, 6, or 8 point IDs.

docs.title: 4.2.7 *Cell
docs.text:
Defines the geometry, materials, and related properties within a beam-element cross-section.

*Cell, Type=type, Mat=mat
  data line
  ...

docs.title: Keyword line
docs.text:
• Type=type: Type of the Cell
    • Value: Specifies cross-sectional constants as values
    • Rectangle: Rectangular cross-section
    • Circle: Circular or hollow circular cross-section
    • H/T/C/L/2C/2L/HR[-YUp]: Standard steel shape cell. Add -YUp to align the shape height with the local y-direction.
    • Mesh: Arbitrary cross-section given as a mesh. Cross-sectional constants are calculated using 2D finite element analysis.
    • Mesh,Rectangle: Generates a rectangular material point mesh.
    • Mesh,Circle: Generates a circular or hollow circular material point mesh.
    • Mesh,H/T/C/L/2C/2L/HR[-YUp]: Generates a material point mesh from a standard steel shape.
    • Layer: Layered cross-section that can be used only for 2D beams
    • Layer,Stack: Generates layers by subdividing stacked layer data.
    • Layer,Circle: Generates a circular or hollow circular layered section.
    • Point: Point-shaped cell. Used for rebar modeling, etc.
    • Point,Circle: Generates a circular point pattern.
  • Mat=mat: Material used in the Cell

docs.title: Data line forms
docs.text:
*Cell data lines are divided into direct input forms and section DB reference forms.

  • numeric/direct data line: Default form that directly lists the dimensions, mesh points, layer fields, or point fields for the selected Type=.
  • section DB reference data line: Catalog-reference form written as DB, item. In supported cells, this form replaces a numeric geometry data line.

In syntax blocks, {A} | {B} means choose one of the two data-line forms. Do not type the braces or the | character.

docs.title: Common data-line options
docs.text:
The following options are appended to data lines; they are not keyword-line options.

  • C=yc, zc: Specifies the centroid location of the cell for cell types other than direct Mesh, Layer, and Point.
  • ExtraArea=area or ExtraArea=area0, area1: Additional area [L^2] appended to a numeric/direct data line. It is used only for mass and self-weight, and does not affect structural section constants, stiffness, stress/strain recovery, or result output locations.
  • ToDirectForm: Expands a generated mesh cell to direct mesh data when the model is saved or formatted. It is used only on the first data line.

C is an abbreviation for cell centroid coordinate. yc and zc are the centroid coordinates of that cell measured in the section reference axes, which are defined from the beam reference line connecting the beam element nodes. yc and zc are not the centroid of the assembled Beam section unless the section has only that one cell. The assembled section centroid is reported separately as yc and zc in section-property output.

For direct Value, Rectangle, Circle, and H/T/C/L/2C/2L/HR[-YUp] cells, append ExtraArea to the corresponding geometry data line. For tapered sections, each start/end geometry data line may have its own value, and the value is interpolated along the member. For direct Mesh, Layer, and Point cells, specify ExtraArea only on the first cell data line. A single value is used for both ends; in a tapered section, ExtraArea=area0, area1 gives the start and end values. When ToDirectForm is also used, write ExtraArea=... before ToDirectForm, and keep ToDirectForm as the last token on the data line.

docs.title: Section DB reference data lines
docs.text:
A section DB reference is a data-line alternative, not a separate cell type or keyword option. The Type= keyword still selects the Hyfeast cell family, so the referenced DB item must match that family. Do not add a DB marker token.

The following rules apply to section DB references.

  • A global *Environment, Type=UnitSystem must already be defined.
  • Runtime section DB files are loaded from tools/db/sections/*.hfdb.json.
  • Each section DB file declares its source length unit; DB dimensions and DB-provided ExtraArea are converted to the current global UnitSystem.
  • C= remains user input in the current model units.
  • User-authored ExtraArea= is not allowed on DB reference data lines. Only DB-provided ExtraArea is applied automatically.
  • For tapered sections, the second data line may also be a DB reference and may name a different item for the end-section geometry.

The DB data-line forms below include additional fields that may appear on the first data line.

Supported cell DB data-line form Note Circle DB, item, C=yc, zc Input shortcut for catalog radii. C is optional and defaults to 0, 0; saved/formatted as numeric circle data. H/T/C/L/2C/2L/HR[-YUp] DB, item, C=yc, zc C is optional and defaults to 0, 0. Preserved as a standard-shape DB reference when saved/formatted. -YUp variants use the same item and only change the section orientation. Mesh,Circle DB, item, nS, C=yc, zc, ToDirectForm C, nS, and ToDirectForm are optional fields used only on the first line. C defaults to 0, 0. nS is the number of circular segments. Do not specify nS or ToDirectForm on the second line of a tapered section. Mesh,H/T/C/L/2C/2L/HR[-YUp] DB, item, C=yc, zc, ToDirectForm C defaults to 0, 0. ToDirectForm is an optional field used only on the first line. Do not specify it on the second line of a tapered section.

The current built-in section DBs are AISC16 and KSD3502-2022.

The supported section DB item prefixes are as follows.

DB item prefix Matching Type= Meaning and examples AISC16 W, M, S, HP H, Mesh,H Wide-flange, miscellaneous beam, standard beam, and bearing-pile shapes. Examples: W14X90, M12.5X12.4, S24X90, HP18X204 AISC16 WT, MT, ST T, Mesh,T Tee shapes split from W/M/S shapes. Examples: WT22X204, MT6.25X6.2, ST12X60.5 AISC16 C, MC C, 2C, Mesh,C, Mesh,2C Channel shapes. The Type= value selects a single or paired channel. Examples: C15X50, MC18X58 AISC16 L L, Mesh,L Single angle shapes. Example: L12X12X1-3/8 AISC16 2L 2L, Mesh,2L Paired angle shapes. Example: 2L12X12X1-3/8 AISC16 HSS Circle, HR, Mesh,HR Round HSS items use Circle; rectangular and square HSS items use HR or Mesh,HR. Examples: HSS28X1.000, HSS20X12X.500 AISC16 Pipe Circle Pipe items. Examples: Pipe8SCH40, Pipe26STD KSD3502-2022 H- H, Mesh,H H shapes. Hyfeast cell-type prefix plus actual dimensions and thickness. Example: H-198x99x4.5x7 KSD3502-2022 T- T, Mesh,T T shapes. Example: T-150x150x7x10 KSD3502-2022 C-, 2C- C, 2C, Mesh,C, Mesh,2C Channel and paired-channel shapes. The Type= value selects a single or paired channel. Examples: C-200x80x6.5x11.5, 2C-200x80x6.5x11.5 KSD3502-2022 L-, 2L- L, 2L, Mesh,L, Mesh,2L Angle and paired-angle shapes. Examples: L-100x75x7x7, 2L-100x75x7x7

AISC16 round HSS and PIPE items are hollow circular sections, so the normal command form is *Cell, Type=Circle. No standard-shape template mesh generation is needed just to use the catalog dimensions. Mesh,Circle remains available only when a user explicitly wants a generated circular material-point mesh. AISC16 rectangular and square HSS items use HR or Mesh,HR; the DB data line supplies H, B, t, r from the catalog item. For AISC16 HSS and PIPE items, the DB-provided ExtraArea is applied automatically for mass and self-weight.

Direct H/T/C/L/2C/2L/HR[-YUp] cells and generated Mesh,H/T/C/L/2C/2L/HR[-YUp] cells preserve standard-shape DB reference lines as DB, item when the model is saved or formatted. The exception is a generated standard-shape mesh cell whose first data line specifies ToDirectForm; in that case the DB reference is intentionally expanded and saved as generated *CellMeshPoint data plus a normal *Cell, Type=Mesh direct form. Circle and Mesh,Circle DB references are input shortcuts for catalog radii and are saved/formatted as numeric circle data, or as direct mesh data when ToDirectForm is used.

docs.title: 4.2.7.1 *Cell, Type=Value
docs.text:
Defines the shape and material within the cross-section of the beam element.

*Cell, Type=Value, Mat=mat
  A, Iy, Iz, Iyz, J, Asy, Asz, ys, zs, C=yc, zc, ExtraArea=area
  ...add the above line if tapered section

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• A: Area [L^2]
  • Iy: 2nd moment of inertia about y w.r.t centroid(optional, default 0.) [L^4]
  • Iz: 2nd moment of inertia about z w.r.t centroid(optional, default 0.) [L^4]
  • Iyz: Cross product w.r.t centroid(optional, default 0.) [L^4]
  • J: torsional constant w.r.t centroid(optional, default 0.) [L^4]
  • Asy,Asz: Shear area [L^2]. If 0, it means use A. (optional, default 0.)
  • ys,zs: Shear centers w.r.t centroid(optional, default 0.) [L].
  • C=yc,zc: Centroid coordinates of this value cell in the section reference axes (optional, default 0.) [L].
  • ExtraArea=area: Optional additional area used only for mass and self-weight [L^2].

docs.title: 2<sup>nd</sup> data line
docs.text:
• Repeat if tapered section

The material applied to *Cell, Type=Value must always be an elastic material defined as *Material, Type=IsoElasticity. *Cell, Type=Value is used either independently or in combination with *Cell, Type=Point. When combined with a Point cell, only the constants for bending are adjusted and used as the overall composite cross-sectional constants.

For variable cross-section beams, the cross-sectional constants are interpolated along the length as follows.

\[ \begin{aligned} &A(x) = A_0 + (A_1 - A_0) \frac{x}{L} \\ &J(x) = J_0 + (J_1 - J_0) \frac{x}{L} \\ &I_y(x) = \left[ I_{y0} ^{1/m_y} + (I_{y1} ^{1/m_y} - I_{y0} ^{1/m_y} ) \frac{x}{L} \right] ^{m_y} \\ &I_z(x) = \left[ I_{z0} ^{1/m_z} + (I_{z1} ^{1/m_z} - I_{z0} ^{1/m_z} ) \frac{x}{L} \right] ^{m_z} \\ &I_yz(x) = \left[ I_{yz0} ^{1/m_{yz}} + (I_{yz1} ^{1/m_{yz}} - I_{yz0} ^{1/m_{yz}} ) \frac{x}{L} \right] ^{m_{yz}} \\ \end{aligned} \]

Here, the interpolation orders for \(I_y\), \(I_z\), and \(I_{yz}\) are set as \(m_y=2, m_z=2, m_{yz}=1\). The remaining shapes are interpolated for the cross-sectional constants based on the given shapes.

docs.title: 4.2.7.2 *Cell, Type=Rectangle
docs.text:
Rectangular cross-section shape – Applicable to elastic materials only.

*Cell, Type=Rectangle, Mat=mat
 B, H, C=yc, zc, ExtraArea=area
 {B, H, C=yc, zc, ExtraArea=area}

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• B: Width in the local y-direction (required) [L].
  • H: Height in the local z-direction (required) [L].
  • yc,zc: Centroid coordinates of this rectangle cell in the section reference axes (optional, default 0,0) [L].
  • ExtraArea: Optional additional area used only for mass and self-weight [L^2].

docs.title: 2<sup>nd</sup> data line
docs.text:
• Repeat if tapered section

The material applied to *Cell, Type=Rectangle must always be an elastic material defined as *Material, Type=IsoElasticity. *Cell, Type=Rectangle is used either independently or in combination with *Cell, Type=Point. When combined with a Point cell, only the constants for bending are adjusted and used as the overall composite cross-sectional constants.

The cross-sectional constants for the centroid are calculated using the following equations.

\[ \begin{aligned} &A = bh, I_y = \frac{bh^3}{12}, I_z = \frac{hb^3}{12}, I_{yz} = 0, \\ &J = \beta bh^3, ~{\rm where,~} \beta \approx \frac{1}{3} - 0.21 \frac{b}{h} (1-\frac{b^4}{12h^4}) , ~~\textrm{*In torsion, h is long dim., and b is short} \\ &A_{sy} = A_{sz} = 5/6A, y_s = z_s = 0 \\ \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: 4.2.7.3 *Cell, Type=Circle
docs.text:
Circular or hollow circular cross-section shape – Applicable to elastic materials only.

*Cell, Type=Circle, Mat=mat
  {outerR, innerR, C=yc, zc, ExtraArea=area} | {DB, item, C=yc, zc}
  ...add one of the above data-line forms again if tapered section

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• outerR: outer radious (required) [L].
  • innerR: inner radius (optional, default 0,0) [L].
  • C=yc,zc: Centroid coordinates of this circle cell in the section reference axes (optional, default 0,0) [L].
  • DB,item: Section DB reference alternative to the numeric circle fields. Examples: AISC16, Pipe8SCH40, AISC16, HSS28X1.000.
  • ExtraArea=area: Optional additional area used only for mass and self-weight [L^2].

docs.title: 2<sup>nd</sup> data line
docs.text:
• Repeat either the numeric circle data line or the DB reference data line if tapered section. The second DB item may differ from the first item.

The material applied to *Cell, Type=Circle must always be an elastic material defined as *Material, Type=IsoElasticity. *Cell, Type=Circle is used either independently or in combination with *Cell, Type=Point. When combined with a Point cell, only the constants for bending are adjusted and used as the overall composite cross-sectional constants.

The cross-sectional constants are calculated using the following equations.

\[ \begin{aligned} &A = \pi (r_1^2-r_2^2), I_y = I_z = \frac{\pi (r_1^4 - r_2^4)}{4}, I_yz = 0,\\ &J = \frac{\pi (r_1^4 - r_2^4)}{2}, y_s = z_s = 0, \\ &A_{sy} = A_{sz} = k_s A, ~{\rm where,~} k_s = \frac{6(1+m^2)^2}{7(1+m^2)^2+20m^2}, m=\frac{r_2}{r_1} \\ \end{aligned} \]
  • yc and zc locate the circle-cell centroid in the section reference axes.
  • Note that typical value of solid circle, \(k_s = 0\), but Cowper(1966)’s formula in case of \(\nu = 0\) is used here.

docs.title: 4.2.7.4 *Cell, Type=H/T/C/L/2C/2L/HR[-YUp]
docs.text:
Creates a standard steel shape as a direct shape cell. These cell types are ShapeSection cells, like Rectangle and Circle. Elastic materials only.

*Cell, Type=H, Mat=mat
  {B1, H, tw, tf1, B2, tf2, r1, r2, r3, r4, C=yc, zc, ExtraArea=area} | {DB, item, C=yc, zc}
  ...add one of the above data-line forms again if tapered section

*Cell, Type=H-YUp, Mat=mat
  {B1, H, tw, tf1, B2, tf2, r1, r2, r3, r4, C=yc, zc, ExtraArea=area} | {DB, item, C=yc, zc}
  ...add one of the above data-line forms again if tapered section

*Cell, Type=T, Mat=mat
  {B1, H, tw, tf1, r1, r2, r3, C=yc, zc, ExtraArea=area} | {DB, item, C=yc, zc}
  ...add one of the above data-line forms again if tapered section

*Cell, Type=T-YUp, Mat=mat
  {B1, H, tw, tf1, r1, r2, r3, C=yc, zc, ExtraArea=area} | {DB, item, C=yc, zc}
  ...add one of the above data-line forms again if tapered section

*Cell, Type=C, Mat=mat
  {B1, H, tw, tf1, B2, tf2, r1, r2, r3, r4, C=yc, zc, ExtraArea=area} | {DB, item, C=yc, zc}
  ...add one of the above data-line forms again if tapered section

*Cell, Type=C-YUp, Mat=mat
  {B1, H, tw, tf1, B2, tf2, r1, r2, r3, r4, C=yc, zc, ExtraArea=area} | {DB, item, C=yc, zc}
  ...add one of the above data-line forms again if tapered section

*Cell, Type=L, Mat=mat
  {B1, H, tw, tf1, r1, r2, r3, C=yc, zc, ExtraArea=area} | {DB, item, C=yc, zc}
  ...add one of the above data-line forms again if tapered section

*Cell, Type=L-YUp, Mat=mat
  {B1, H, tw, tf1, r1, r2, r3, C=yc, zc, ExtraArea=area} | {DB, item, C=yc, zc}
  ...add one of the above data-line forms again if tapered section

*Cell, Type=2C, Mat=mat
  {B1, H, tw, tf1, B2, tf2, c, r1, r2, r3, r4, C=yc, zc, ExtraArea=area} | {DB, item, C=yc, zc}
  ...add one of the above data-line forms again if tapered section

*Cell, Type=2C-YUp, Mat=mat
  {B1, H, tw, tf1, B2, tf2, c, r1, r2, r3, r4, C=yc, zc, ExtraArea=area} | {DB, item, C=yc, zc}
  ...add one of the above data-line forms again if tapered section

*Cell, Type=2L, Mat=mat
  {B1, H, tw, tf1, c, r1, r2, r3, C=yc, zc, ExtraArea=area} | {DB, item, C=yc, zc}
  ...add one of the above data-line forms again if tapered section

*Cell, Type=2L-YUp, Mat=mat
  {B1, H, tw, tf1, c, r1, r2, r3, C=yc, zc, ExtraArea=area} | {DB, item, C=yc, zc}
  ...add one of the above data-line forms again if tapered section

*Cell, Type=HR, Mat=mat
  {H, B, t, r, C=yc, zc, ExtraArea=area} | {DB, item, C=yc, zc}
  ...add one of the above data-line forms again if tapered section

*Cell, Type=HR-YUp, Mat=mat
  {H, B, t, r, C=yc, zc, ExtraArea=area} | {DB, item, C=yc, zc}
  ...add one of the above data-line forms again if tapered section

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• B1: Top flange or leg width (required) [L].
  • H: Overall height (required) [L].
  • tw: Web or vertical leg thickness (required) [L].
  • tf1: Top flange or horizontal leg thickness (required) [L].
  • B2: Bottom flange width (optional, default B1) [L]. Used by H, C, and 2C.
  • tf2: Bottom flange thickness (optional, default tf1) [L]. Used by H, C, and 2C.
  • c: Gap between paired shapes for 2C and 2L (optional, default 0) [L].
  • r1,r2,r3,r4: Fillet/toe radii used by the standard-shape template mesh [L]. Their meanings depend on the shape as shown below.
  • B,t,r: HR hollow-rectangle fields. H and B are the outer height and width, t is the wall thickness, and r is the inner corner radius [L]. If r=0, both inner and outer corners are generated as sharp corners. If r>0, the generated outer corner radius is r + t.
  • C=yc,zc: Centroid coordinates of this standard-shape cell in the section reference axes (optional, default 0,0) [L].
  • DB,item: Section DB reference alternative to the numeric shape fields. The Type= value still selects the Hyfeast cell family, for example AISC16, W14X90 with Type=H, AISC16, C15X50 with Type=C or Type=2C, and KSD3502-2022, H-198x99x4.5x7 with Type=H.
  • ExtraArea=area: Optional additional area used only for mass and self-weight [L^2].

docs.title: 2<sup>nd</sup> data line
docs.text:
• Repeat either the numeric shape data line or the DB reference data line if tapered section. The second DB item may differ from the first item.

The following table summarizes the fillet/toe radius conditions.

Type r1 r2 r3 r4 H Top web-flange root Bottom web-flange root Top flange free toe Bottom flange free toe T Flange-web root Stem free toe Flange free toe Not used C Top web-flange root Bottom web-flange root Top flange free toe Bottom flange free toe L Inside leg root Horizontal-leg free toe Vertical-leg free toe Not used 2C r1 of each C shape r2 of each C shape r3 of each C shape r4 of each C shape 2L r1 of each L shape r2 of each L shape r3 of each L shape Not used

For HR, use the separate H, B, t, r data line instead of r1 through r4.

The data line is positional. To specify a later optional field, fill the preceding optional fields in the same shape-specific form with their default values or 0.

Reference: Thin-walled H-shape

For an H section without fillets, the following thin-walled approximation can be used.

\[ \begin{aligned} &A = h_c t_w + 2bt_f,\quad I_y=\frac{h_c^2}{12}(h_c t_w+6bt_f),\quad I_z = \frac{b^3t_f}{6},\quad I_{yz}=0 \\ &J \approx \frac{1}{3}(h_c t_w^3+2bt_f^3),\quad y_s=z_s=0 \\ &A_{sy}=k_{sy}A,\quad k_{sy}=\frac{5}{3}\frac{bt_f}{A} \\ &A_{sz}=k_{sz}A,\quad k_{sz}=\frac{h_ct_w}{A} \\ &\mathrm{where,}\quad h_c = h - t_f \end{aligned} \]

Hyfeast computes the section constants using two-dimensional finite elements. For example, with b=0.20, h=0.40, tw=0.008, and tf=0.013, the thin-walled formula differs from the finite-element result by about 1.3% in area, 1.6% in major-axis bending inertia, 2.4% in torsional constant, and 2.5% in one shear area.

docs.title: 4.2.7.5 *Cell, Type=Mesh
docs.text:
Cell with an area divided into a mesh.

*Cell, Type=Mesh, Mat=mat
  p1,p2,p3, ExtraArea=area|{area0, area1}
  p1,p2,p3,p4
  p1,p2,p3,p4,p5,p6
  p1,p2,p3,p4,p5,p6,p7,p8
  ...

docs.title: First data line and subsequent data lines
docs.text:
• p1, p2, p3: pointIds defined in *CellMeshPoint. It is used as a T3 cell for finite element analysis.
  • p1, p2, p3, p4: pointIds defined in *CellMeshPoint. It is used as a Q4 cell for finite element analysis.
  • p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6: pointIds defined in *CellMeshPoint. It is used as a T6 cell for finite element analysis.
  • p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6, p7, p8: pointIds defined in *CellMeshPoint. It is used as a Q8 cell for finite element analysis.
  • ExtraArea=area or ExtraArea=area0, area1: Optional additional area used only for mass and self-weight [L^2]. Specify it only on the first data line. Use one value for both ends, or use ExtraArea=area0, area1 in a tapered section.

For T6 and Q8 cells, write corner nodes first and midside nodes after them. T6 uses the triangle corner ordering followed by its three edge midside nodes. Q8 uses the quadrilateral corner ordering followed by its four edge midside nodes.

docs.title: 4.2.7.6 *Cell, Type=Layer
docs.text:
Divides the area into layers. Used for defining 2D beam cross-sections.

*Cell, Type=Layer, Mat=mat
 pointId, y, b, {y, b}, ExtraArea=area|{area0, area1}
 ...

docs.title: First data line and subsequent data lines
docs.text:
• pointId: point id (required)
  • y: y coordinate [L].
  • b: width [L].
  • ExtraArea=area or ExtraArea=area0, area1: Optional additional area used only for mass and self-weight [L^2]. Specify it only on the first data line. Use one value for both ends, or use ExtraArea=area0, area1 in a tapered section.

The y values must increase continuously. If y1 and y2 are given in two consecutive rows, they must satisfy y1 <= y2.

On the other hand, pointId is used to specify the position of the result and does not need to be in consecutive order.

docs.title: 4.2.7.7 *Cell, Type=Point
docs.text:
Defines an area as a set of points with an associated area.

*Cell, Type=Point, Mat=mat
 pointId, y, z, area, {y2, z2, area2}, ExtraArea=area|{area0, area1}
 ...

docs.title: First data line and subsequent data lines
docs.text:
• pointId: point id (required)
  • y,z: y,z coordinates (required) [L].
  • area: area (required) [L^2].
  • y2,z2: y,z coordinates for right end in taper section (required if taper) [L].
  • area2: area for right end in taper section (required if taper) [L^2].
  • ExtraArea=area or ExtraArea=area0, area1: Optional additional area used only for mass and self-weight [L^2]. Specify it only on the first data line. Use one value for both ends, or use ExtraArea=area0, area1 in a tapered section.

The pointId used when defining *Cell, Type=Point is used to specify the position of the result.

docs.title: 4.2.7.8 *Cell, Type=Mesh, Rectangle
docs.text:
Creates a rectangular mesh.

*Cell, Type=Mesh, Rectangle, Mat=mat
 B, H, nB, nH, C=yc, zc, ExtraArea=area, ToDirectForm
 B, H, C=yc, zc, ExtraArea=area

docs.title: First data line
docs.text:
• B: Width in the local y-direction (required) [L].
  • H: Height in the local z-direction (required) [L].
  • nB,nH: Number of mesh divisions in width and height when used in Beam section.
  • C=yc,zc: Centroid coordinates used when generating the rectangular mesh points in the section reference axes (optional, default 0,0) [L].
  • ExtraArea=area: Optional additional area used only for mass and self-weight [L^2].
  • ToDirectForm: If it exists, the cell command is converted to the normal *Cell, Type=Mesh.

docs.title: 2<sup>nd</sup> data line

docs.title: 4.2.8 *ShearTorsionMaterial
docs.text:
Specifies reference materials for shear and torsion behavior using uniaxial material model.

*ShearTorsionMaterial
  ShearX|ShearY|Torsion, material, localUnitSystem
  ...

docs.title: First data line and subsequent data lines if necessary
docs.text:
• ShearX|ShearY|Torsion: Specified type. ShearX and ShearY correspond to shear behavior in two orthogonal directions, while Torsion refers to torsional behavior.
  • material: Referenced material model. Only uniaxial material models are allowed. Interpreted as a scaled shear force–shear strain relationship for shear, or as a scaled torsional moment–rotation relationship for torsion. The actual shear force or torsional moment is computed by multiplying the scaled quantity by the corresponding section stiffness constants—GAsy, GAsz, or GJ—defined in the section.
  • locaUnitSystem: local UnitSystem with force-length form (optional).

Shear and torsional behavior in beam elements is linear by default. To enforce nonlinear behavior, a uniaxial material model can be referenced to define a scaled shear force–shear strain or scaled torsional moment–rotation relationship. The resulting actual shear force and torsional moment are obtained by multiplying the scaled response by the corresponding section constants (GAsy, GAsz, or GJ).

When applied to shear behavior, if the local unit system is the same as the current unit system specified by *Environment, Type=UnitSystem, the scaled shear force and stress are converted on a 1:1 basis without any physical reinterpretation. If the unit systems differ, appropriate internal scaling is applied automatically. Likewise, when applied to torsional behavior, the scaled torsional moment and stress, as well as rotation and strain, are converted with the unit system taken into account, again without implying any direct physical equivalence.

docs.title: 4.3 Truss
docs.text:
The truss element can be considered a beam element that transmits only axial forces. Only the 3D 2-node truss element, T3D2, is supported. The following is a comparison with beam elements:

  • The truss element transmits only axial forces and has only translational DOFs without rotational DOFs at the nodes.
  • Variable cross-sections can be specified, similar to beam elements.
  • The ECS can be defined and is used to determine the direction when applying loads, but it is not related to the stiffness matrix calculation within the element.
  • EndRelease and Offset are ignored.
  • Elemental loads in directions other than the axial direction are distributed to both end nodes according to the distance but do not cause deformation.
  • Unlike beam elements, it cannot be used as a host element for EmbeddedLine element.

Fig. 4.3-1. Truss element

docs.title: 4.4 Cable
docs.text:
The Elastic Catenary Cable element is based on the analytical solution derived from a state subjected to self-weight and can be used to model cables in long-span bridges. Similar to truss elements, it can only transmit axial forces, and while it considers geometric nonlinearity, the material model is assumed to be linearly elastic.

The cross-section of the Cable element is defined as a Beam cross-section. In the first analysis step where the element is used, the unstressed length must be defined using the *State, Type=CableLength command.

If the Cable element is positioned in equilibrium with the gravity direction, the solution will not converge. Additionally, if the unstressed length is too large or too small, the solution may not converge, so careful use is recommended.

Fig. 4.4-1. Cable element

Precautions when using Cable elements

  1. The cross-section of a cable element uses a beam section with elastic material properties. Variable cross-sections cannot be applied, and only the area value is used in the formulation.
  2. Self-weight must be applied using *Load, Type=Gravity.
  3. The initial value of the stress-free length must be specified at the time of element creation using *State, Type=CableLength.
  4. Currently, Cable elements do not support mass matrices and can only be used in static analysis.
  5. Cable elements are geometric nonlinear elements, and nonlinear analysis will be performed if included in the analysis.

docs.title: 4.5 Shell
docs.text:
A shell structure can be defined as a structure with a thin thickness relative to its span. From the perspective of stress conditions, the stress in the thickness direction is zero, and shell elements must be used for the modeling of shell structures. Shell finite elements are broadly categorized into conventional shell elements and continuum shell elements (see Figure 7.1). Generally, a conventional shell element refers to a shell element that is discretized based on a reference plane, which is usually set as the mid-surface. Nodes on the reference plane have three translational degrees of freedom and two or three rotational degrees of freedom. In contrast, continuum shell elements have translational degrees of freedom at the nodes, similar to conventional continuum elements, and can be modeled similarly to continuum elements, making them convenient to use in certain situations.

Fig. 4.5-1. Shell elements

Element Types

  • S3F: 3-node triangular flat shell
  • S4F: 4-node quadrilateral flat shell
  • S3: 3-node triangular general shell
  • S4: 4-node quadrilateral general shell
  • CS6: 6-node triangular continuum shell
  • CS8: 8-node quadrilateral continuum shell

Element Cross-Section

  • Shell: Defines a uniform cross-section.

Element-Specific Properties (Distribution)

  • NodalThickness: Specifies the thickness at each node for variable thickness elements.

Conventional shell elements are divided into flat shell elements (S3F, S4F) and general shell elements (S3, S4). Flat shells are assumed to be flat. Therefore, the thickness direction vector is constant, and the ECS of the element is defined. During the formulation process, the stress-strain relationship is used as the constitutive equation. General shell elements, on the other hand, can model curved surfaces by defining the thickness direction vector (director vector) at the nodes, and the stress-strain relationship is used as the constitutive equation. Since the formulation is based on the reduction of continuum elements to a reference plane, it is also called a degenerated shell. As general shell elements are curved, different local coordinate systems (LCS) are defined at the material points. When applied to flat conditions, the results are the same as those of flat shells.

All conventional shell elements apply the AS (Assumed Strain) method using the MITC technique to eliminate shear locking. For integration in the thickness direction, three methods—Lobatto, Legendre, and Newton-Cotes—are supported. By default, Lobatto uses 3 points for linear materials and 4 points for nonlinear materials; Legendre uses 2 points for linear materials and 3 points for nonlinear materials; and Newton-Cotes uses 3 points for linear materials and 5 points for nonlinear materials.

Fig. 4.5-2. Element Coordinate System for S4F and S3F

Fig. 4.5-3. Local Coordinate System for S4 and S3

Conventional shell elements are defined with 5 degrees of freedom per node. However, if adjacent elements have 3 rotational degrees of freedom, if boundary conditions or load conditions are applied to the rotational degrees of freedom, or if the normal vector of the node differs from that of the adjacent shell elements, it automatically changes to 6 degrees of freedom.

Fig. 4.5-4. Handling 5/6 DOF in S3, S4, S3F, and S4F

Solid shell elements are shell elements that can be modeled in the same manner as regular solid elements. They have 3 degrees of freedom per node. Various locking issues are eliminated by applying the AS (Assumed Strain) method as well as the EAS (Enhanced Assumed Strain) method. The material model uses a 3D material model. Therefore, an arbitrary or desired orthogonal coordinate system can be chosen as the local coordinate system. However, for consistency with general shell elements, the thickness direction is set as the z-direction of the local coordinate system. Integration in the thickness direction is the same as for general shell elements. Three methods—Lobatto, Legendre, and Newton-Cotes—are supported. By default, Lobatto uses 3 points for linear materials and 4 points for nonlinear materials; Legendre uses 2 points for linear materials and 3 points for nonlinear materials; and Newton-Cotes uses 3 points for linear materials and 5 points for nonlinear materials.

Fig. 4.5-5. Local Coordinate System for SC8 and SC6

Shell elements can output results at the 4 or 3 integration points within the plane, as shown in the figure. S3F and S4F provide section forces and strains at the mid-surface, while S3, S4, CS6, and CS8 output stresses and strains at the top and bottom integration points in the thickness direction. Section forces are calculated based on the mid-surface using integration.

Fig. 4.5-6. Integration Points for 4-node and 3-node Shell Elements

Fig. 4.5-7. Definition of Section Forces in Shell Elements
