docs.title: 5.1 Theory of Sectional Constant Calculation
docs.text:
The sectional constants calculated for a non-composite section are as follows:

  • Sectional area (\(A\)): sectional area
  • Second moment of area: \(I_{y}\), \(I_{z}\), \(I_{yz}\) [with respect to the centroid]
  • Shear center: \(y_{s}\), \(z_{s}\) [with respect to the centroid]
  • Shear area: \(A_{sy}\), \(A_{sz}\)
  • Torsional constant: \(J\)
  • Centroid (\(y_c\), \(z_c\)): centroid in the given coordinate system

As shown in Fig. 4, the centroid is based on a given origin, but other properties that require a reference point are calculated based on the centroid.

Fig. 4. Coordinate System for Sectional Constant Calculation

Sectional area, first moment of area, and second moment of area can be calculated using the following equations:

\[ A = \int_A dA, \quad Q_y = \int_A z \, dA, \quad Q_z = \int_A y \, dA, I_y = \int_A z^2 \, dA, \quad I_z = \int_A y^2 \, dA \tag{1} \]

The centroid and the second moment of area with respect to the centroid are calculated as follows:

\[ y_c = \frac{Q_z}{A}, \quad z_c = \frac{Q_y}{A} \tag{2} \]

For arbitrary cross-sections where discretization is provided, such as a layered model or finite element mesh, the above equations can be calculated through simple integration. Shear center, shear area, and torsional constant can be calculated by solving a 2D potential problem with boundary conditions. For this, finite element analysis is performed on a 2D finite element mesh. This program uses 3-node and 4-node elements.

If it is a composite section, it is calculated in the form of \(EA\), \(EI_y\), \(EI_z\), \(EI_{yz}\), \(GA_{sy}\), \(GA_{sz}\), \(GJ\), where the elastic modulus and shear modulus are multiplied.

docs.title: 5.2 Theory of Nonlinear Section Analysis
docs.text:
Nonlinear section analysis is based on Bernoulli beam theory, which assumes that planes perpendicular to the neutral axis remain plane and perpendicular after deformation. The coordinate system used is shown in Fig. 5, and it is assumed that axial strain/axial force is applied at the origin, and moment/curvature is applied around the z-axis.

Fig. 5. Coordinate System and Loading

The sectional forces \(\mathbf{D}\) and corresponding sectional deformations \(\mathbf{d}\) at any section of the beam can be defined as follows:

\[ \mathbf{D} = \begin{bmatrix} N \\ M_z \end{bmatrix}^T ; \quad \mathbf{d} = \begin{bmatrix} \epsilon_0 \\ \kappa_z \end{bmatrix}^T \tag{3} \]

Here, \(N\) and \(M_z\) are the axial force and bending moment, and \(\epsilon_0\) and \(\kappa_z\) are the corresponding axial strain and curvature at the reference axis, respectively. The stress \(\sigma(y)\) and strain \(\epsilon(y)\) at any location within the section at position y from the reference axis can be defined, and the stress-strain relationship is determined from an appropriate uniaxial material model:

\[ \sigma = \sigma(\epsilon) \tag{4} \]

The relationship between strain and sectional deformation (kinematic relation) is given by:

\[ \epsilon(y) = \epsilon_0 - y \kappa_z \tag{5} \]

The sectional force is then computed as the integral of stress:

\[ \begin{bmatrix} N \\ M_z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \int_A \sigma(y) \, dA \\ -\int_A \sigma(y) y \, dA \end{bmatrix}, \tag{6} \]

In section analysis, sectional forces are calculated from given sectional deformations using Eq. (6). Additionally, the tangent stiffness matrix from the linearized section force-sectional deformation relationship is required:

\[ \begin{bmatrix} dN \\ dM_z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial N}{\partial \epsilon_0} & \frac{\partial N}{\partial \kappa_z} \\ \frac{\partial M_z}{\partial \epsilon_0} & \frac{\partial M_z}{\partial \kappa_z} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} d\epsilon_0 \\ d\kappa_z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \int_A E(y) \, dA & -\int_A E(y) y \, dA \\ -\int_A E(y) y \, dA & \int_A E(y) y^2 \, dA \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} d\epsilon_0 \\ d\kappa_z \end{bmatrix}, \tag{7} \]

The calculation of Eq. (6) and Eq. (7) requires appropriate discretization and integration of the section. In this case, a discrete point model is applied where the area is concentrated at arbitrary points, or a layered section model can be used. The sectional forces and tangent stiffness matrix for the discretized section are as follows:

\[ \begin{bmatrix} N \\ M_z \end{bmatrix} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \begin{bmatrix} N_i \\ M_i \end{bmatrix} \tag{8} \] \[ \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial N}{\partial \epsilon_0} & \frac{\partial N}{\partial \kappa_z} \\ \frac{\partial M_z}{\partial \epsilon_0} & \frac{\partial M_z}{\partial \kappa_z} \end{bmatrix} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial N_i}{\partial \epsilon_0} & \frac{\partial N_i}{\partial \kappa_z} \\ \frac{\partial M_i}{\partial \epsilon_0} & \frac{\partial M_i}{\partial \kappa_z} \end{bmatrix} \tag{9} \]

Where \(n\) is the number of layers or points in the discrete model, and \(N_i\), etc., are as follows:

docs.title: Layered Model
docs.text: \[ N_i = \int_{y_1}^{y_2} \sigma(y) b(y) \, dy, \quad M_i = -\int_{y_1}^{y_2} \sigma(y) b(y) y \, dy \] \[ \frac{\partial N_i}{\partial \epsilon_0} = \int_{y_1}^{y_2} E(y) b(y) \, dy, \quad \frac{\partial N_i}{\partial \kappa_z} = \int_{y_1}^{y_2} E(y) b(y) y \, dy \] \[ \frac{\partial M_i}{\partial \epsilon_0} = -\int_{y_1}^{y_2} E(y) b(y) y \, dy, \quad \frac{\partial M_i}{\partial \kappa_z} = \int_{y_1}^{y_2} E(y) b(y) y^2 \, dy \tag{10} \]

docs.title: Discrete Point Model
docs.text:
\[ N_i = \sigma_i A_i, \quad M_i = -\sigma_i y_i A_i \] \[ \frac{\partial N_i}{\partial \epsilon_0} = E_i A_i, \quad \frac{\partial N_i}{\partial \kappa_z} = 0, \quad \frac{\partial M_i}{\partial \epsilon_0} = -y_i E_i A_i, \quad \frac{\partial M_i}{\partial \kappa_z} = y_i^2 E_i A_i \tag{11} \]

Fig. 6. Layered Section

When using the discrete point model, sectional forces and tangent stiffness matrices can be calculated without numerical integration for the given section deformation, but with the layered model, numerical integration is required in each layer. Assuming the stress and width vary linearly within each layer, the coordinates \(y\), stress \(\sigma\), and width \(b\) in each layer can be expressed as functions of \(\xi \in [-1, +1]\) as follows:

\[ y(\xi) = N_1(\xi) y_1 + N_2(\xi) y_2, \] \[ \sigma(\xi) = N_1(\xi) \sigma_1 + N_2(\xi) \sigma_2, \] \[ b(\xi) = N_1(\xi) b_1 + N_2(\xi) b_2 \tag{12} \]

Where

\[ N_1(\xi) = \frac{1 - \xi}{2}, \quad N_2(\xi) = \frac{1 + \xi}{2} \tag{13} \]

Thus, applying Gauss-Legendre integration, we have:

\[ N_i = \sum_{k=1}^{2} w_k \sigma(\xi_k) b(\xi_k) \left\| \frac{dy}{d\xi} \right\|, \quad M_i = -\sum_{k=1}^{2} w_k \sigma(\xi_k) b(\xi_k) y(\xi_k) \left\| \frac{dy}{d\xi} \right\| \] \[ \frac{\partial N_i}{\partial \epsilon_0} = \sum_{k=1}^{2} w_k E(\xi_k) b(\xi_k) \left\| \frac{dy}{d\xi} \right\| \] \[ \frac{\partial N_i}{\partial \kappa_z} = 0, \quad \frac{\partial M_i}{\partial \epsilon_0} = -\sum_{k=1}^{2} w_k E(\xi_k) b(\xi_k) y(\xi_k) \left\| \frac{dy}{d\xi} \right\| \] \[ \frac{\partial M_i}{\partial \kappa_z} = \sum_{k=1}^{2} w_k E(\xi_k) b(\xi_k) y^2(\xi_k) \left\| \frac{dy}{d\xi} \right\| \tag{14} \]

Here, \(\xi_1 = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \quad \xi_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \quad w_1 = w_2 = 1\), and the integration is accurate for polynomials up to third order. List 1 shows the section state determination algorithm. In the case of the discrete point model, stress and strain are calculated at the discrete points, while in the layered model, stress and strain are calculated at the top and bottom edges of each layer.

List. 1. Section State Determination Algorithm

The theory presented so far applies to layered sections and sections composed of discrete points. Sections with a 2D mesh can also be analyzed in the same way. Strain is calculated at the nodes of the mesh, and stress is calculated at those nodes. Numerical integration is then performed on each element to calculate the sectional forces.

Fig. 7. Meshed Section

Until now, the origin was used as the reference point for axial strain/axial force, and the z-axis was used for moment/curvature. These values can be changed. For layered sections, the reference point for axial strain/axial force can be changed, and for sections with a mesh, the axis of rotation can also be changed.

Fig. 8. Reference Point and Rotation Angle

docs.title: 5.3 Nonlinear Section Analysis Algorithm
docs.text:
hfSectAnalyzer allows analysis by applying axial force or axial strain, moment, or curvature. The sectional forces and deformations given in the analysis are evaluated incrementally, and Newton's method is applied to satisfy equilibrium conditions within each increment if necessary. For pretension, the corresponding prestrain is calculated and set, and the analysis is performed to satisfy equilibrium conditions. For post-tension, the analysis is performed to satisfy the given prestress conditions and equilibrium.

List. 2. Analysis Algorithm

Additionally, the above analyses can be applied consecutively, and pretension and post-tension can be applied as well. The results of section analysis are calculated based on the given coordinates, and the neutral axis is calculated as follows. The position of the neutral axis satisfies the following condition:

\[ e = \frac{\epsilon_c}{\kappa_z} \tag{15} \]

This result is not provided by the program, as it becomes meaningless to define the neutral axis using the above equation when only axial force exists or when axial force dominates the moment.

docs.title: 5.4 Material Model
docs.text: The supported uniaxial stress-strain models are IsoElasticity for linear elastic materials, von Mises for plasticity, USteel for uniaxial steel, and UGeneric for uniaxial generic material, which is usally used for concrete. IsoElasticity can be used for modeling linear elastic materials. For steel, both vonMises and USteel can be used: USteel is applied for bilinear stress-strain relationships, and vonMises is applied for more complex relationships like multi-linear.

docs.title: 5.4.1 Modeling Rebars and Tendons with USteel
docs.text:
For rebars and tendons, the Menegotto-Pinto-based model (USteel) is provided.

Fig. 9. USteel Model (Menegotto-Pinto Model)

docs.title: 5.4.2 Modeling Concrete with UGeneric
docs.text:
Concrete is modeled as shown in Fig. 6. The tension and compression envelopes, as well as degradation under stress reversal, can be controlled through input.

Fig. 10. UGeneric Model

docs.title: 2.1 Overview
docs.text: hf2DStudio is the GUI workspace for drawing arbitrary cross sections, assigning materials and rebars, computing section constants, and running nonlinear section analysis.

docs.title: 2.1.1 Two tabs
docs.text:
The central area has two kinds of tabs.

  • Section: build geometry, define material/rebar, generate mesh, compute section constants. Entered with a new model or an unlocked model.
  • Analysis: review section-analysis results (chart, contour). Entered after run-analysis.

The Section tab carries two section views, left and right. Taper sections may have different geometry on each side; non-taper sections show the same geometry in both views.

docs.title: 2.1.2 Main screen areas
docs.text:
• Section View (left/right): section geometry, mesh, point/curve/face/rebar display. Both views are shown side by side.
  • Analysis View: analysis result chart and contour. Used in the Analysis tab only.
  • Model Tree (left): tree of section components (points, curves, faces, rebars, materials, sections, analyses).
  • Command dock (right): Function/Material/Section/Analysis editor widgets.
  • Output Window (bottom): messages, analysis log, failure causes.
  • Top menus: File / Display / Geometry / Definition / Operation / View / Help.
  • Toolbars: File / Display / Geometry / Operation (each toggleable).

Each area is detailed in the following GUI Guide pages.

  • Window and File — File menu and toolbar (New, Open, Import (DXF), Save, Save As, Open Folder, Option, Undo/Redo, Close)
  • View and Display — View menu (dock/toolbar visibility); Display menu (zoom, axes, grid, geometry/point/node/seed/label toggles, color, quad mesh hints)
  • Geometry — ortho/snap, drawing (point/line/arc/bezier/spline), shape generators, modify, select, merge/detach points, seed, make face, make rebar, edit/clear quad mesh corner hints, renumber
  • Definition — Environment (unit system), Function/Material/Section/Analysis editors, Section Wizard (template-mesh)
  • Operation and Analysis — Make Linear/Quadratic Mesh, Delete Mesh, Compute Section Constants, Move/Rotate, Run Analysis, Unlock model

docs.title: 2.1.3 Relationship to Remote Control
docs.text:
GUI actions and Remote Control commands are 1:1.

  • For the same action, GUI Apply and Remote Control record the same canonical tail into history and *.ipc.txt.
  • The Remote Control manual defines validation rules, failure codes, and JSON response structures per command.
  • Each GUI Guide page cross-links to the matching Remote Control section per action.

For an automation primer, see Remote Control Basics. For the command reference, see hf2DStudio Remote Control Overview.

docs.title: 2.1.4 When hfSectAnalyzer fits better
docs.text:
The following are better handled in hfSectAnalyzer than in the GUI.

  • Section definitions managed as text files directly.
  • Repeatable batch section analyses.
  • Precise control of the section command syntax.

docs.title: 2.2 Window and File
docs.text:
The hf2DStudio File menu and File toolbar create section models, open and save them, import DXF geometry, edit options, and close the program.

For automation of the same actions, see Remote Control Window and File.

docs.title: 2.2.1 Menu layout
docs.text:
• New: start a new empty section model
  • Open: open an existing .hf2d file
  • Import: import a DXF drawing as the current section's Geometry
  • Save: save to the current file
  • Save As: save to a different path
  • Open Folder in File Explorer: open the directory of the current file in the OS file explorer
  • Option: open the settings dialog
  • Recent Files: list of recently opened files (up to 5)
  • Undo / Redo: step backward/forward through the model-history stack
  • Close: quit the program

The File toolbar exposes New, Open, Import, Save, Option, Undo, and Redo.

docs.title: 2.2.2 New
docs.text:
Start with an empty section model.

If unsaved changes exist, the same save-confirmation flow as GUI File > New runs.

  • Yes: save the current section first. If there is no save path yet, the Save As dialog opens.
  • No: discard unsaved changes and create a new empty section.
  • Cancel: keep the current section open and abort the action.

Remote Control can skip this confirmation with --discard-unsaved.

If the current Untitled model only contains the startup UnitSystem choice, hf2DStudio discards it without asking.

Same action via Remote Control: new.

docs.title: 2.2.3 Open
docs.text:
Open the specified .hf2d section file.

  • If unsaved changes exist and the current file already has a path, hf2DStudio auto-saves first.
  • If unsaved changes exist and the current file has no path, Open fails because there is no place to auto-save, except for an Untitled model whose only user change is the startup UnitSystem choice.

Same action via Remote Control: open.

docs.title: 2.2.4 Import (DXF Geometry)
docs.text:
Import supported DXF entities into the active section's Geometry.

  • Supported entities: LINE, LWPOLYLINE, POLYLINE, ARC, CIRCLE, ELLIPSE, SPLINE. Uses the same reader path as the hfStudio DXF importer and converts the resulting Construction Guide primitives into Line, Arc, Bezier, and Spline curves.
  • DXF z coordinates are dropped; only (x, y) becomes the hf2DStudio Geometry coordinate.
  • DXF unit scaling is applied only when both the DXF $INSUNITS and the active section/global unit are valid; otherwise coordinates are taken without scaling.
  • Import fails if the active section already has a mesh. Remove the mesh first via Operation > Delete Mesh.

Same action via Remote Control: import-dxf-geometry.

docs.title: 2.2.5 Save / Save As
docs.text:
• Save: save to the current file path. If there is no path, the Save As dialog opens automatically.
  • Save As: pick a new path; that path is used and becomes the current file path.

Remote Control collapses both into one command — save.

docs.title: 2.2.6 Open Folder in File Explorer
docs.text: Open the directory of the current file in the OS file explorer. Useful for checking the result .xlsx file or other side outputs.

docs.title: 2.2.7 Option
docs.text: Open the settings dialog. Individual options are documented inside the dialog.

docs.title: 2.2.8 Recent Files
docs.text: Up to five recently opened files appear in the menu and can be opened directly. They follow the same unsaved-change handling as Open.

docs.title: 2.2.9 Undo / Redo
docs.text:
Apply the in-memory model-history stack of the session.

  • Disabled when no previous/next snapshot is available.
  • Triggered from the menu or toolbar buttons.
  • Rebuilds state from the stack rather than re-parsing input text, so it works across Geometry, Definition, and Operation actions.

docs.title: 2.2.10 Close
docs.text:
Quit the program.

  • If unsaved changes exist and the current file has a path, hf2DStudio auto-saves first.
  • If unsaved changes exist and the file has no path, Close fails, except for an Untitled model whose only user change is the startup UnitSystem choice.
  • Remote Control can quit immediately without auto-save using --discard-unsaved — quit.

docs.title: 2.2.11 See also
docs.text:
• Remote Control Window and File
  • Geometry — what to do after a DXF import
  • Operation and Analysis — Delete Mesh

docs.title: 2.3 View and Display
docs.text:
This page covers tidying the screen, fitting the camera, and toggling geometry/mesh/label display.

For automation, see Remote Control View. (Ortho mode and snap toggles live in the GUI Geometry menu but RC bundles them into the View command set — they are documented in the Geometry page.)

docs.title: 2.3.1 View menu — dock and toolbar visibility
docs.text:
The top-level View menu toggles dock widget and toolbar visibility. It is not a camera control.

Dock widgets:

  • Output Window
  • Model Tree
  • Command (Function/Material/Section/Analysis editors)
  • Remote Control Batch

Toolbars:

  • File
  • Display
  • Geometry
  • Operation

Each toolbar's right-click popup exposes the same toggles.

docs.title: 2.3.2 Section view and Analysis view
docs.text:
The central area has two kinds of views.

  • Section view (left): Section tab, left side. RC --view left.
  • Section view (right): Section tab, right side. RC --view right.
  • Analysis view: Analysis tab. RC --view analysis.

Most RC view commands accept --view <active|left|right|analysis>, defaulting to active (whichever view currently has focus).

docs.title: 2.3.3 Display menu — Zoom and camera
docs.text:
• Zoom fit: fit current view to its content. RC: fit.
  • Box zoom: zoom to a mouse-drawn rectangle (toggle). interactive only.
  • Rotate axes: open the axis-rotation dialog. RC: rotate-axes <angle-deg>.

Zoom fit accepts --view to fit only one section view or only the analysis view.

docs.title: 2.3.4 Display menu — Axes / Grid display modes
docs.text: Each item applies to both left and right section views (or to the analysis view in the Analysis tab).

docs.title: 2.3.4.1 Axes submenu
docs.text:
• None: hide axes
  • Point: show only the origin point
  • Line: show full axis lines

Automation: display-axis <on|off> — RC supports only on/off.

docs.title: 2.3.4.2 Grid submenu
docs.text:
• None: hide the grid
  • Point: show only grid intersection points
  • Line: show grid lines

Automation: display-grid <on|off>.

docs.title: 2.3.4.3 Grid Spacing (toolbar)
docs.text:
Set the grid spacing directly with the toolbar spin box.

  • In the Section tab, applies to both left and right section views.
  • In the Analysis tab, applies to the analysis view.

Automation: grid-spacing get|set <value>.

docs.title: 2.3.5 Display menu — display toggles
docs.text:
Most are also exposed on the toolbar with matching icons.

  • Display Geometry: show section geometry (independent from mesh). RC: display-geometry <on|off> — not for analysis view.
  • Display Point: show geometry points. GUI toggle.
  • Display Node: show mesh nodes. GUI toggle.
  • Display Seed: show curve seeds. GUI toggle.
  • Display Point Label: show point id labels. GUI toggle.
  • Display Curve Label: show curve id labels. GUI toggle.
  • Display Face Label: show face id labels. GUI toggle.
  • Display Rebar Label: show rebar id labels. GUI toggle.
  • Color by Face/Rebar: use a distinct color per face/rebar (off: color by material). GUI toggle.
  • Display Quad Mesh Corner Hints: show quad-mesh corner hints. GUI toggle.

Display Geometry off does not affect mesh display; it only hides the geometry layer.

docs.title: 2.3.6 Targeting another view
docs.text: Adding --view <left|right|analysis> to a Remote Control command applies the change to a specific view without changing active view. In the GUI, the equivalent flow is to activate the target tab/view first.

docs.title: 2.3.7 See also
docs.text:
• Remote Control View
  • Geometry — ortho mode, snap toggles

docs.title: 2.4 Geometry
docs.text:
The hf2DStudio Geometry menu and Geometry toolbar draw section outlines, edit points, build faces and rebars, and adjust mesh seeds.

For automation, see Remote Control Geometry. The ortho and snap toggles live in the RC View command set.

docs.title: 2.4.1 Editable preconditions
docs.text: Geometry create/edit commands require an editable geometry section. If a mesh already exists, remove it first via Operation > Delete Mesh.

docs.title: 2.4.2 Drawing aids
docs.text:
• Ortho mode (F3) — constrain mouse drawing to axis-aligned segments. RC: ortho-mode <on|off>.
  • Snap to geometry (F4) — snap to existing geometry. RC: snap-to-geometry <on|off>.
  • Snap to grid (F5) — snap to the grid. RC: snap-to-grid <on|off>.

The two snaps are independent and can be on at the same time. When both are on, geometry snap takes precedence over grid snap.

docs.title: 2.4.3 Point and line drawing
docs.text:
In the GUI, toggle the drawing mode on the toolbar/menu and then click coordinates. In Remote Control, pass coordinates as arguments directly.

  • Drawing Points: RC: draw-point <yp,zp>
  • Drawing Lines: RC: draw-lines <yp,zp|P<id>> <yp,zp|P<id>> ...
  • Drawing Arc: start/middle/end. RC: draw-arc <p1> <p2> <p3>.
  • Drawing Bezier2: quadratic. RC: draw-bezier2 <p1> <p2> <p3>.
  • Drawing Bezier3: cubic. RC: draw-bezier3 <p1> <p2> <p3> <p4>.
  • Drawing RBezier2: rational quadratic. RC: draw-rbezier2 <p1> <p2> <p3> --weights <w1>.
  • Drawing RBezier3: rational cubic. RC: draw-rbezier3 <p1> <p2> <p3> <p4> --weights <w1,w2>.
  • Drawing Spline: repeat the first point at the end to close. RC: draw-spline <p1> <p2> <p3> [...].

Coordinates use the yp,zp form. Quote tokens with negative coordinates (e.g., "-25,10").

docs.title: 2.4.4 Shape generators
docs.text:
• Generate Circle: closed circle of four rational quadratic bezier segments. RC: generate-circle <radius> <yp> <zp>.
  • Generate Circular Points: only points on the circle. RC: generate-circular-points <radius> <yp> <zp> <start-angle-deg> <count>.

docs.title: 2.4.5 Point editing
docs.text:
• Pencil (Modify): drag points with the mouse (toggle). RC: move-point <id> <yp,zp> [--merge <on|off>].
  • Merge Coincident Points: merge selected points sharing the same coordinate into one topology point. RC: merge-selected-points.
  • Detach Selected Points: split a point shared by multiple curves (blocked when face/rebar still references it). RC: detach-selected-points.

move-point --merge on explicitly connects the moved point to the existing topology at the destination. --merge off (default) only moves the coordinate.

docs.title: 2.4.6 Selection
docs.text:
• Select All: all-kinds selection mode (toggle). In RC, use select <kind> ... --mode replace per kind.
  • Select Point: point selection mode (toggle). RC: select point <id,...>.
  • Select Wire: curve selection mode (toggle). RC: select curve <id,...>.

RC select takes the kind (point|curve|face|rebar) and ids directly, with --mode <replace|add|remove|toggle> for combination.

Bulk delete of the current selection: delete-selection. Faces and rebars are deleted immediately; referenced curves/points stay selected.

Direct id-based delete (without selecting first):

  • delete-point <id,...> — points unreferenced by curves/rebars only; blocked ids reported as blockedIds
  • delete-curve <id,...> — curves unreferenced by faces only
  • delete-face <id,...>
  • delete-rebar <id,...>

docs.title: 2.4.7 Mesh seeds
docs.text:
• Edit seed: set the seed of selected curves manually. RC: set-seed --curve-ids <id,...> --seed <integer>.
  • Auto seed: compute rough seeds from the curves' max-H values, then apply conservative TFI interval correction where possible. RC: auto-seed --curve-ids <id,...>.

auto-seed produces the same result as the GUI Auto Seed button.

docs.title: 2.4.8 Face and rebar
docs.text:
• Make Face: resolve closed regions from selected curves and create faces. RC: make-face --material <name> --curve-ids <id,...>.
  • Make Rebar: place rebars at selected points. RC: make-rebar --material <name> --point-ids <id,...> --diameter <value>.

make-face creates one face directly when the requested curves form an exact face; otherwise it resolves bounded cells and creates a face per cell. Faces that already exist for the resolved curve set are skipped.

docs.title: 2.4.9 Quad Mesh Corner Hints
docs.text:
Hint how the quad mesh recognizes face corners.

  • Quad Mesh Corner Hints (Edit) — open the hint editor dialog
  • Pick Quad Mesh Corner Hints: pick hint points with the mouse
  • Clear Quad Mesh Corner Hints: clear all hints from the selected face

There is no separate RC command for the hints themselves. Mesh generation in Operation > Make Linear/Quadratic Mesh uses the hints automatically. When hints exist, both auto-seed interval correction and mesh generation use them before automatic corner inference.

docs.title: 2.4.10 Renumber (geometric entities)
docs.text:
Reassign sequential ids starting from 1 to the active section's points/curves/faces/rebars. External references to old ids become invalid; subsequent steps must look up the new ids.

Automation: renumber.

docs.title: 2.4.11 See also
docs.text:
• Remote Control Geometry
  • Remote Control View — ortho/snap
  • Definition — material definitions used by make-face/make-rebar
  • Operation and Analysis — mesh generation, renumber

docs.title: 2.5 Definition
docs.text:
The hf2DStudio Definition menu opens the environment (unit system), function, material, section, and section-analysis editors, plus the Section Wizard.

For automation, see Remote Control Definition.

docs.title: 2.5.1 Menu layout
docs.text:
• Environment: unit system editor (Command dock). RC: environment-unit-system get|set <text>.
  • Edit function: Function editor (Command dock). RC: function <type> <name> ....
  • Edit material: Material editor (Command dock). RC: material <type> <name> ....
  • Edit section: Section editor (Command dock). RC: section <name> ....
  • Edit section analysis: Analysis editor (Command dock). RC: analysis <name> --section <name> ....
  • Section Wizard: standard-section generator dialog (H/T/C/L/2C/2L/HR). RC: template-mesh <H|T|C|2C|L|2L|HR> <name> ....

GUI Apply records the same canonical Remote Control tail into history and *.ipc.txt.

docs.title: 2.5.2 Common content rules
docs.text:
Definition commands that edit block text (function, material, section, analysis) all use the same body syntax as GUI Apply.

  • Remote Control accepts either --content <text> or --content-file <file>.
  • Inside --content, line breaks are written \n. \\n is preserved as a literal.
  • Empty bodies are rejected.
  • On success, the section model is updated immediately and marked modified.

docs.title: 2.5.3 Environment (Unit System)
docs.text:
• force-length-time-temp 4-field token: N-m-s-K, kN-cm-s-K, N-mm-s-Celsius, ... Sets the section unit system.
  • none: clears the section unit system.

Automation: environment-unit-system get / set <token|none>. Apply in the Command dock's Environment editor produces the same result.

docs.title: 2.5.4 Function
docs.text:
Creates or updates one *Function, TYPE=<type>, Name=<name> definition.

Concrete-DB envelope inputs use the same command form, but the allowed standards depend on the function type. For example, a MaekawaTEnv body can be KDS-2026-C30, ACI318-2025-C4000, EC2-2004-C30, or those forms with a trailing , ToDirectForm. ParabolaCEnv is section-analysis input, accepts only the KDS/EC2 family, and may include alpha before ToDirectForm. For HognestadCEnv, EC2CEnv, and MPPCEnv, put EciCurve before ToDirectForm when the original initial curve is required. DB function bodies do not include a local UnitSystem=... keyword.

ConcreteTime is available in the Function editor. Its Builder provides a Direct mode for the User named-group form and a Standard mode for EC2-2004-C..., KDS-2026-C..., and ACI209-1992-C... datalines. The user-defined form only references existing functions. Standard datalines require the section global UnitSystem to be defined first, and Type=ConcreteTime does not use a local UnitSystem=... keyword.

Automation: function <type> <name> --content ....

docs.title: 2.5.5 Material
docs.text:
Creates or updates one *Material, TYPE=<type>, Name=<name> definition.

Extra options:

  • --neg-stop-strain <value>, --pos-stop-strain <value>: override stop strain after the material body is applied.
  • --signal <text> or --signal-file <file>: append a section-signal definition to the same material (mutually exclusive).

Automation: material <type> <name> --content ... [--signal ...].

docs.title: 2.5.6 Section
docs.text:
Creates or updates one *Section, Name=<name> definition.

Extra options:

  • --taper <on|off>: section taper attribute. Omit to keep the current state.
  • Switching to --taper on lets subsequent geometry manage left/right sides independently.

Automation: section <name> --content ... [--taper <on|off>].

docs.title: 2.5.7 Analysis
docs.text:
Creates or updates one *Analysis, Name=<name> definition. --section <name> is required.

Extra options:

  • --right <on|off>: in a taper section, use the right-side geometry as the analysis target (default off).
  • --ref <angle,yp,zp>: rotation angle (deg) and origin of the analysis reference coordinate system.
  • --output <Preselect|All>: result-item scope (default Preselect).

Automation: analysis <name> --section <name> --content ....

docs.title: 2.5.8 Section Wizard (Template Mesh)
docs.text:
Generate a mesh-only standard section (H, T, C, 2C, L, 2L, HR) from dimension inputs.

  • Does not create section geometry. Removes any existing geometry of the same name.
  • <H|T|C|2C|L|2L>: --B1, --tw, --tf1 required. --B2 defaults to --B1; --tf2 defaults to --tf1.
  • HR: --B (outer width), --t (wall thickness), --r (inner corner radius) required.
  • The generated mesh uses Q8 quad cells, T6 quarter-fillet cells, and HR annular-corner Q8 cells where applicable.
  • Section constants are computed immediately after mesh generation.

Automation: template-mesh <type> <name> --material <name> --H <value> ....

docs.title: 2.5.9 See also
docs.text:
• Remote Control Definition
  • Geometry — materials are referenced by make-face/make-rebar
  • Operation and Analysis — running the analysis

docs.title: 2.6 Operation and Analysis
docs.text:
The hf2DStudio Operation menu and Operation toolbar create/delete the mesh, compute section constants, transform the section (move/rotate), and run the analysis.

For automation, see Remote Control Operation and Analysis.

docs.title: 2.6.1 Menu layout
docs.text:
• Make Linear Mesh: generate a T3/Q4 mesh
  • Make Quadratic Mesh: generate a T6/Q8 mesh
  • Delete Mesh: remove the current mesh
  • Compute/Cancel Section constants: compute or invalidate section constants
  • Move section: translate the section by an anchor or explicit offset
  • Rotate section: rotate the section by an angle
  • Start Analysis: start the section analysis

docs.title: 2.6.2 Make Mesh
docs.text:
• Make Linear Mesh: T3/Q4 cells. RC: make-mesh build.
  • Make Quadratic Mesh: T6/Q8 cells. RC: same as above.
  • Delete Mesh: remove the mesh. RC: make-mesh delete.

Automation behavior:

  • Remote Control make-mesh build generates the mesh and computes section constants in the same step (centroid, shear-center, and other derived constants are ready right after).
  • Remote Control has no separate linear/quadratic option; it uses whichever mesh-order state the current hf2DStudio session is holding. Switch the order in the GUI first, then call make-mesh.
  • If a mesh already exists, build returns success without changing it. To rebuild at a different order, run delete first.
  • Mesh generation uses the currently stored curve seeds and Quad Mesh Corner Hints. make-mesh build does not rerun auto-seed interval correction or mutate seeds.

docs.title: 2.6.3 Compute Section Constants
docs.text:
Compute or invalidate section constants for the existing mesh.

Automation: compute-section-constants compute|invalidate|toggle.

make-mesh build already computes section constants by default; compute-section-constants is normally used to recompute or invalidate without touching the mesh.

docs.title: 2.6.4 Move Section
docs.text:
Translate the active section by an anchor rule or by an explicit offset.

  • top-left ~ bottom-right: move the corresponding 9-direction point of the axis-aligned bounding box to the origin
  • centroid: move the centroid (from current section constants) to the origin
  • shear-center: move the shear center to the origin
  • offset: translate by --offset <yp,zp> (does not change the reference point)

Automation: move <anchor> [--offset <yp,zp>]. --offset is required for the offset anchor and rejected for any other anchor.

docs.title: 2.6.5 Rotate Section
docs.text:
Rotate the active section by a given angle.

  • The rotation center is the current origin (yp=0, zp=0).
  • Positive angles rotate from the +y axis toward the +z axis.
  • Chain move centroid (or similar) afterwards to realign the reference point.

Automation: rotate <angle-deg>.

docs.title: 2.6.6 Renumber
docs.text: Documented in the Geometry page (the GUI menu places it under Geometry while the RC command lives in the Operation group).

docs.title: 2.6.7 Run Analysis
docs.text:
GUI Operation > Start Analysis starts the section analysis.

  • Requires a saved current file path.
  • If unsaved changes exist, the file is auto-saved before the analysis starts.
  • No additional CLI options. The analyzer launch path is the same as the GUI action.
  • Fails if an analysis is already running.
  • Removes the existing .xlsx result for the current section file just before starting a new run.

Automation: run-analysis.

docs.title: 2.6.8 Unlock Model
docs.text:
Available only when analysis results are loaded. Removes all results and returns the model to the editable state.

  • Removes the current .xlsx result file if present.
  • Clears any in-memory results.
  • Fails if an analysis is currently running.

Automation: unlock-model. GUI Apply records the same canonical tail into history.

docs.title: 2.6.9 Export commands (Remote Control only)
docs.text:
These commands have no dedicated GUI menu entry and are invoked through Remote Control. Each copies the result text to the clipboard and also returns it as the result JSON payload.

  • export-section — *Section, TYPE=Beam input text. Preserves current mesh order (T3/Q4 or T6/Q8).
  • export-guide-geometry — *Construction, TYPE=Guide text. Z=0 plane; --ref-cs to set the reference CS.
  • export-curve-mesh — 1D curve mesh input text. Accepts --node-id-offset, --element-id-offset.
  • export-domain-mesh — 2D domain mesh input text. CPS3/CPS4 for linear, CPS6/CPS8 for quadratic.

When the section model defines a global *Environment, TYPE=UnitSystem, every export prepends that UnitSystem block to the output.

docs.title: 2.6.10 See also
docs.text:
• Remote Control Operation and Analysis
  • Geometry — geometry construction and mesh seeds
  • Definition — analysis definition
  • Quad Mesh Generation — quad-mesh algorithm details

docs.title: 1 Hyfeast Tutorial Series
docs.text:
This section is a step-by-step tutorial set for new Hyfeast users.

This page now also serves as the old Tutorial 00 - Overview landing page.

The tutorials follow two tracks.

  • Modeling and analysis basics: 01 to 03
  • hfStudio remote control and automation: 04 to 08

If you are new to the tools, start here and then follow them in order.

docs.title: 1.1 Goal
docs.text:
This tutorial series is designed to introduce the full Hyfeast workflow.

After reading this page, you should be able to answer:

  • where the model is defined
  • how the analysis is executed
  • where the results are reviewed
  • when remote control becomes useful

docs.title: 1.2 Overall workflow
docs.text:
The standard Hyfeast flow is:

  1. Define the model
  2. write the .inp file directly, or
  3. create nodes, elements, materials, sections, and steps in the GUI
  4. Run the analysis
  5. use hfAnalyzer or run-analysis in hfStudio
  6. Review the results
  7. inspect step, frame, contour, vector, and history in hfStudio
  8. Automate repeated work
  9. use remote control and scripts when the same review sequence must be repeated

docs.title: 1.3 What this series covers
docs.text:
• When to use Beam, Shell, and Solid elements
  • How to build a simple cantilever model
  • The basic hfAnalyzer run workflow
  • How to inspect results in hfStudio
  • How to automate selection, display, postprocessing, and scripts with remote control

docs.title: 1.4 Which element family should you use
1.4.1 Beam
docs.text:
• good when the member is slender
  • good when section properties can be defined separately
  • good for quick global-behavior checks

docs.title: 1.4.2 Shell
docs.text:
• good for thin plates and walls
  • good when membrane and plate behavior must be reviewed together

docs.title: 1.4.3 Solid
docs.text:
• good when you want more direct stress distribution
  • good when you want to keep the 3D geometry without section assumptions

docs.title: 1.5 When Remote Control Helps
docs.text:
Remote control is especially useful when:

  • you want to compare the same model in multiple windows
  • you want to reproduce the same review scene every time
  • you want to save a review procedure as a script
  • you want to generate images or scenes repeatedly in batch mode

docs.title: 1.6 Tutorial list
docs.text:
1. Tutorial 01 - Beam Cantilever
  2. Uses a minimal beam cantilever to teach the basic modeling and analysis flow.
  3. Tutorial 02 - Solid Cantilever
  4. Solves the same problem with solid elements and compares it with the beam model.
  5. Tutorial 03 - Beam vs Solid
  6. Summarizes the criteria for choosing between beam and solid models.
  7. Tutorial 04 - hfStudio Basics
  8. Explains the basic hfStudio remote-control workflow and the view model.
  9. Tutorial 05 - Selection and Visibility
  10. Shows how to use selection and visibility safely and predictably.
  11. Tutorial 06 - Postprocessing with Remote Control
  12. Walks through step, frame, scalar, vector, and contour control over remote control.
  13. Tutorial 07 - Scripts and Automation
  14. Explains automation with script, script-save, and target set.
  15. Tutorial 08 - Portal Frame
  16. A full beam-frame example that covers modeling, analysis, and review.

docs.title: 1.7 Recommended companion documents
docs.text:
• Remote Control Overview
  • hfStudio Remote Control Overview
  • hfStudio Remote Control Preprocessing
  • hfStudio Remote Control Postprocessing
  • Command Manual Overview

docs.title: 1.8 Suggested reading path
docs.text:
• To learn modeling itself: this page -> 01 -> 02 -> 03
  • To learn remote-control automation: this page -> 04 -> 05 -> 06 -> 07
  • To see a practical review workflow: continue through 08

docs.title: 1.9 Recommended tools
docs.text:
• hfAnalyzer
  • hfStudio
  • sample files under Example/Tutorials
  • a command-line shell such as PowerShell or CMD

docs.title: 2.1 Goal
docs.text:
Use a realistic cantilever beam example to learn:

  • node and beam-element layout
  • material and section definition
  • distributed load and support definition
  • analysis execution
  • basic result review

docs.title: 2.2 Why start with a beam model
docs.text:
A beam model is ideal for getting started because it describes the same structural behavior with the smallest modeling cost.

  • small model size
  • fast results
  • clear interpretation of boundary conditions and loads

docs.title: 2.3 Tutorial case
docs.text:
This tutorial uses a linear-elastic reinforced-concrete cantilever that can represent a balcony beam or a short slab-supporting bracket.

  • span: 2.4 m
  • section: 300 x 600 mm rectangular beam
  • support: one fully fixed end at the wall face
  • load: 18 kN/m downward line load, representing tributary slab dead plus service load
  • mesh: 8 beam elements with type B3D2H

This is still simple enough for a first tutorial, but it is more realistic than a pure textbook point-load example.

docs.title: 2.4 Working input file
docs.text:
Repository file: Example/Tutorials/tutorial-beam-cantilever.inp

*Material, Type=IsoElasticity, Name=Concrete
 30e9, 0.2, 0, 2500   # E, nu, alpha, density

*Section, Type=Beam, Name=RC300x600
*Cell, Type=Rectangle, Mat=Concrete
 0.30, 0.60, 0, 0

*Node, NSet=AllNodes
 1, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0
 2, 0.3, 0.0, 0.0
 3, 0.6, 0.0, 0.0
 4, 0.9, 0.0, 0.0
 5, 1.2, 0.0, 0.0
 6, 1.5, 0.0, 0.0
 7, 1.8, 0.0, 0.0
 8, 2.1, 0.0, 0.0
 9, 2.4, 0.0, 0.0

*Element, Type=B3D2H, ELSet=Cantilever
 1, 1, 2, S=RC300x600
 2, 2, 3, S=RC300x600
 3, 3, 4, S=RC300x600
 4, 4, 5, S=RC300x600
 5, 5, 6, S=RC300x600
 6, 6, 7, S=RC300x600
 7, 7, 8, S=RC300x600
 8, 8, 9, S=RC300x600

*NSet, Name=Tip
 9

*Constraint, Type=Support, Name=FixedEnd
 1, X|Y|Z|RX|RY|RZ

*Load, Type=LineDistributed, Name=DeckLoad
 Cantilever, GCS, 0, 0, -18000, 0, 0, 0

*Step, Type=Static, Name=Service
 Uniform, 0.1, 1
*Activate, Type=Element
 Cantilever
*Activate, Type=Constraint
 FixedEnd
*Activate, Type=Load
 DeckLoad
*Output
 D, FN, BSF
*Print, File=tutorial-beam-cantilever.prn
 D@Tip, FN@1, BSF@Cantilever

docs.title: 2.5 Modeling sequence
docs.text:
1. create the nodes
  2. Node
  3. create the beam elements
  4. Beam Elements
  5. define the material
  6. Material
  7. define the section
  8. Modeling Convenience
  9. define constraints and loads
  10. Constraint
  11. Load
  12. define the analysis step
  13. Step

docs.title: 2.6 Run the analysis
docs.text:
You can save the .inp file and run hfAnalyzer, or import the same file into hfStudio.

Remote Control example:

hfStudio --remote import D:\Work\tutorial-beam-cantilever.inp --type Hyfeast
hfStudio --remote save D:\Work\tutorial-beam-cantilever.hdb
hfStudio --remote run-analysis

docs.title: 2.7 Review the results
docs.text:
Check these first:

  • whether the tip displacement points downward
  • whether the fixed-end reaction balances the total distributed load
  • whether the bending and shear-force output match the expected cantilever behavior

Postprocessing example:

hfStudio --remote post-step Service
hfStudio --remote post-frame 1
hfStudio --remote post-plot deformed on
hfStudio --remote post-scale deformed value 20

The following image shows the solved tutorial model with deformed shape display in hfStudio.

docs.title: 2.8 Main takeaway
docs.text:
• Beam models are fast and simple, but they do not directly show through-section stress distribution.
  • If the goal is global behavior review, beam modeling is usually very efficient.
  • For this tutorial case, the beam model is a good first pass before building a full 3D solid model.

docs.title: 2.9 Next step
docs.text:
• To solve the same problem with solids, continue with Tutorial 02 - Solid Cantilever
  • To compare beam and solid choices, continue with Tutorial 03 - Beam vs Solid

docs.title: 3.1 Goal
docs.text:
Solve the same cantilever problem from Tutorial 01, but with solid elements.

The purpose is:

  • to understand why solid models require more input than beam models
  • to experience the result-review advantages of a solid model

docs.title: 3.2 When a solid model is more appropriate
docs.text:
Use solids when:

  • you want direct stress distribution through the section
  • you need to inspect local stress concentration
  • the geometry is too complex for simple section assumptions

docs.title: 3.3 Tutorial case
docs.text:
This tutorial uses the same reinforced-concrete cantilever from Tutorial 01, but models the full 3D block.

  • geometry: 2.4 m x 0.30 m x 0.60 m
  • element type: C3D8
  • mesh: 8 x 2 x 4
  • support: full fixity on the x=0 face
  • load: 60 kPa downward pressure on the top face

Because the beam width is 0.30 m, the 60 kPa top pressure corresponds to the same 18 kN/m line load used in the beam tutorial. That makes the two tutorial models directly comparable.

docs.title: 3.4 Working input file
docs.text:
Repository file: Example/Tutorials/tutorial-solid-cantilever.inp

*Material, Type=IsoElasticity, Name=Concrete
 30e9, 0.2, 0, 2500   # E, nu, alpha, density

*Section, Type=Solid, Name=ConcreteSolid
 Concrete, 1

*Model, Type=Block3D
 Cantilever, Auto, Auto, C3D8, ConcreteSolid
 0.0, 2.4, 8
 0.0, 0.30, 2
 0.0, 0.60, 4

*Constraint, Type=Support, Name=FixedEnd
 Cantilever-NX, X|Y|Z

*Load, Type=SurfaceDistributed, Name=DeckPressure
 Cantilever-PZ, Pressure, 60000

*Step, Type=Static, Name=Service
 Uniform, 0.1, 1
*Activate, Type=Element
 Cantilever
*Activate, Type=Constraint
 FixedEnd
*Activate, Type=Load
 DeckPressure
*Output
 D, S
*Print, File=tutorial-solid-cantilever.prn
 D@Cantilever

docs.title: 3.5 Modeling sequence
docs.text:
1. define the material and solid section
  2. Material
  3. Solid Elements
  4. generate the 3D block mesh
  5. Model
  6. define the fixed-end support on the left face
  7. define the top-face pressure load
  8. define the static service step and run the solver

docs.title: 3.6 What changes relative to the beam model
docs.text:
• the number of nodes and elements grows quickly
  • both modeling time and analysis time increase
  • in return, stress contours are much more direct

docs.title: 3.7 Run the analysis
docs.text:
Remote Control example:

hfStudio --remote import D:\Work\tutorial-solid-cantilever.inp --type Hyfeast
hfStudio --remote save D:\Work\tutorial-solid-cantilever.hdb
hfStudio --remote run-analysis

docs.title: 3.8 What to review
docs.text:
• whether the free-end displacement is in the same range as the beam model
  • how the stress distribution appears near the fixed end
  • how sensitive the result is to mesh refinement

Postprocessing example:

hfStudio --remote post-step Service
hfStudio --remote post-frame 1
hfStudio --remote post-plot contour on
hfStudio --remote post-plot deformed on
hfStudio --remote post-scalar S.Mises
hfStudio --remote post-display scalarbar on

The following image shows the same cantilever in hfStudio with deformed shape and von Mises stress contour.

docs.title: 3.9 Practical takeaway
docs.text:
• If you only need global behavior, beam modeling is faster.
  • If detailed stress review matters, solid modeling is more persuasive.
  • A common workflow is beam first, solid later for local detail.

docs.title: 3.10 Next step
docs.text: • Continue with Tutorial 03 - Beam vs Solid for a direct comparison guide.

docs.title: 4.1 Goal
docs.text: Summarize the criteria for choosing between a beam model and a solid model for the same structural problem.

docs.title: 4.2.1 When beam is the better choice
docs.text:
• the structure is slender
  • section properties can be defined separately
  • the main goal is global displacement, reaction, or member-force review
  • fast iteration matters

docs.title: 4.2.2 When solid is the better choice
docs.text:
• the 3D geometry cannot be represented well by simple section assumptions
  • local stress concentration matters
  • the internal stress distribution must be reviewed directly
  • connection or boundary geometry strongly affects the result

docs.title: 4.3.1 Beam
docs.text:
• faster to model
  • faster to solve
  • simpler to interpret

docs.title: 4.3.2 Solid
docs.text:
• heavier to model
  • more sensitive to mesh quality
  • larger solve time and larger result files

docs.title: 4.4 Recommended strategy
docs.text:
In practice, this order works well:

  1. check the global behavior with a beam model
  2. validate boundary conditions and loads
  3. build a local solid detail model only where needed

docs.title: 4.5 What to compare in hfStudio
docs.text:
When comparing beam and solid results:

  • align the same step and frame
  • use the same camera view
  • start with deformed shape and reactions before detailed contour review
  • create two render views if needed and inspect both models side by side

Example:

hfStudio --remote view add render
hfStudio --remote view list
hfStudio --remote --view-id r0 camera view +z
hfStudio --remote --view-id r1 camera view +z

docs.title: 4.6 Conclusion
docs.text:
• Beam is strong for quick decisions and global behavior review.
  • Solid is strong for detailed stress and local effects.
  • They are not competing tools so much as complementary stages of review.

docs.title: 4.7 Next step
docs.text: • To move into remote-control-based view control, continue with Tutorial 04 - hfStudio Basics

docs.title: 5.1 Goal
docs.text:
This tutorial covers the core concepts you need before using hfStudio remote control in practice.

It focuses on the current implementation of:

  • remote target selection
  • currentView and activeRenderView
  • viewId-based view control
  • display/camera commands and --view-id

docs.title: 5.2 Set the remote target first
docs.text:
If only one instance is running, you can send commands without --target.

If you repeatedly work with one instance among several, set the default target first.

hfStudio --remote list
hfStudio --remote target set 8f6d1c2b
hfStudio --remote status
hfStudio --remote focus

Key rules:

  • --target <id> is a one-shot override
  • target set <id> stores the local default target
  • target clear removes the stored default target

docs.title: 5.3 Open and save files
docs.text:
hfStudio --remote open D:\Work\frame.hdb
hfStudio --remote save
hfStudio --remote write-scene D:\Work\frame.png

A useful starter flow is:

  1. open
  2. camera fit
  3. representation both
  4. write-scene

The following program shot shows the tutorial frame.inp model after import, camera fit, representation both, and display-control grid off.

docs.title: 5.4 Views now use --id
docs.text:
view commands now work with viewId, not the old position-based index.

hfStudio --remote view list
hfStudio --remote view add render
hfStudio --remote view activate --id r1
hfStudio --remote view close --id c0

Typical viewId patterns:

  • render view: r0, r1
  • node table: n0
  • element table: e0
  • chart: c0

docs.title: 5.5 currentView and activeRenderView can differ
docs.text:
The selected central view is the currentView.

The default target for display, camera, and visibility commands is the activeRenderView.

For example:

  • the current central tab may be a chart
  • but the active render target may still be r1

That is why view list must be read with both concepts in mind.

docs.title: 5.6 Display and camera commands target activeRenderView by default
docs.text:
hfStudio --remote representation both
hfStudio --remote transparency on
hfStudio --remote display-control grid off
hfStudio --remote camera fit

These commands apply to the current activeRenderView unless you override the target.

docs.title: 5.7 Use --view-id to target another render view directly
docs.text:
You do not have to change the active render view just to adjust another one.

hfStudio --remote --view-id r0 camera view +z
hfStudio --remote --view-id r1 camera view +z
hfStudio --remote --view-id r1 display-control grid off
hfStudio --remote --view-id r1 visibility element all on

Benefits:

  • no change to currentView
  • no temporary active-view switch
  • easier side-by-side comparison across render views

docs.title: 5.8 Recommended startup checklist
docs.text:
When you open a new model, this sequence is stable:

  1. status
  2. view list
  3. camera fit
  4. representation both
  5. if needed, display-control grid off
  6. save the scene with write-scene

docs.title: 6.1 Goal
docs.text:
This tutorial explains the two most repeated hfStudio tasks:

  • what to select
  • what to show or hide

In the current remote-control design, selection and visibility are closely related but not the same thing.

docs.title: 6.2 Selection defines the working set
docs.text:
Selection defines what later commands will act on.

Typical examples:

  • node-delete __selected__
  • element-divide parametric --source __selected__
  • nset PICKED --content "__selected__"

Basic syntax:

hfStudio --remote select <kind> <items|none> [--mode <current|union|intersection|xor|cur-diff-prev|prev-diff-cur>]

docs.title: 6.3 Common selection kinds
docs.text:
The most common kinds are:

  • node
  • element
  • surface
  • edge
  • constraint
  • load
  • sensor

Examples:

hfStudio --remote select node 1:20
hfStudio --remote select element 101:140 --mode union
hfStudio --remote select edge "17-42-23,31-32"
hfStudio --remote select surface "2@1:40"

Some examples keep quotes for readability. In PowerShell or cmd.exe, quotes only group one command-line argument, so tokens such as 1:20, 1496-1494,1817-1496, and 2@1:40 behave the same with or without quotes when they contain no spaces.

docs.title: 6.4 Reuse the current set with __selected__ { #reuse-the-current-set-with-selected }
docs.text:
When a later command should use the current selection, __selected__ is the key token.

hfStudio --remote select node 1:10
hfStudio --remote nset PICKED --content "__selected__"
hfStudio --remote node-delete __selected__

This pattern also fits well when the GUI creates the selection first and remote control consumes it next.

docs.title: 6.5 Visibility is render-view specific
docs.text:
Visibility does not modify the model itself. It only changes what is shown inside a given render view.

Basic syntax:

hfStudio --remote visibility <kind> <items|all> <on|off>
hfStudio --remote --view-id r1 visibility <kind> <items|all> <on|off>

Key rules:

  • the default target is activeRenderView
  • --view-id lets you target another render view directly
  • this is not a global all-view switch; it behaves like the ModelTree checkboxes

docs.title: 6.6 Common visibility kinds
docs.text:
Common kinds:

  • node
  • element
  • node-set
  • element-set
  • constraint
  • load
  • surface
  • construction
  • sensor

Examples:

hfStudio --remote visibility node 1:10 off
hfStudio --remote visibility element all on
hfStudio --remote visibility node-set TOP_NODES off
hfStudio --remote --view-id r1 visibility surface S1,S2 on

docs.title: 6.7 Recommended workflow
docs.text:
This sequence is reliable:

  1. build the working set with select
  2. clean up the scene with visibility if needed
  3. apply the editing command
  4. clear the selection afterwards with select none

Example:

hfStudio --remote select element 201:240
hfStudio --remote visibility element 201:240 off
hfStudio --remote select none

docs.title: 6.8 Important distinction
docs.text:
• Selection changes the current working set
  • Visibility changes the display state in the current render view

They often appear together, but they do not store the same thing.

docs.text:

docs.title: 7.1 Goal
docs.text:
This tutorial explains the basic remote-control workflow for hfStudio postprocessing.

It covers:

  • run-analysis
  • post-step
  • post-frame
  • post-plot
  • post-scalar
  • post-vector
  • post-contour
  • post-display

docs.title: 7.2 You must be in postprocessing mode first
docs.text:
Post commands only work when results are available.

The simplest flow is:

hfStudio --remote open D:\Work\frame.hdb
hfStudio --remote run-analysis

If the model already contains results, you can use post commands right after open.

docs.title: 7.3 Pick the step and frame first
docs.text:
hfStudio --remote post-step STEP1
hfStudio --remote post-frame 3

The recommended order is always:

  1. post-step
  2. post-frame
  3. choose plot and scalar/vector options

docs.title: 7.4 Decide which plot you want
docs.text:
hfStudio --remote post-plot contour on
hfStudio --remote post-plot deformed on
hfStudio --remote post-plot vector off

Common plot toggles:

  • contour
  • deformed
  • vector
  • diagram
  • sensor

docs.title: 7.5 Choose scalar and vector fields
docs.text:
hfStudio --remote post-scalar S.Mises
hfStudio --remote post-vector D

Typical use:

  • use post-scalar for stress contour review
  • use post-vector for displacement or direction review

docs.title: 7.6 Refine the contour appearance
docs.text:
hfStudio --remote post-contour auto-range off
hfStudio --remote post-contour range 0 250
hfStudio --remote post-contour bands 12
hfStudio --remote post-display scalarbar on

If needed, switch to custom mode and set explicit levels.

docs.title: 7.7 Commands fail in the wrong mode
docs.text:
If you send post-* commands while still in preprocessing mode, the response is INVALID_STATE.

That means:

  • run the analysis first, or
  • open a file that already contains results

docs.title: 7.8 You can compare with multiple render views
docs.text:
Postprocessing can also be reviewed across multiple render views.

hfStudio --remote view add render
hfStudio --remote --view-id r0 camera view +z
hfStudio --remote --view-id r1 camera view +z

The post commands themselves still follow the active-render flow by default, so set up the comparison layout first.

docs.title: 7.9 Recommended review sequence
docs.text:
hfStudio --remote post-step STEP1
hfStudio --remote post-frame 1
hfStudio --remote post-plot contour on
hfStudio --remote post-scalar S.Mises
hfStudio --remote post-display scalarbar on
hfStudio --remote post-plot deformed on
hfStudio --remote post-scale deformed value 10

docs.text:
• hfStudio Remote Control Postprocessing
  • hfStudio Remote Control Recipes

docs.text: • To save repeated review work as scripts, continue with Tutorial 07 - Scripts and Automation

docs.title: 8.1 Goal
docs.text:
This tutorial explains how to save repeated work into files and replay it later.

Main topics:

  • script
  • script-save
  • target set
  • fail-fast behavior

docs.title: 8.2 Group repeated work into scripts
docs.text:
If the same review sequence must be repeated, store it in a file.

Execution:

hfStudio --remote script D:\Work\review.ipc.txt

docs.title: 8.3 Use target set for the default instance
docs.text:
If you do not want to repeat --target <id> every time, set the default target first.

hfStudio --remote list
hfStudio --remote target set 8f6d1c2b
hfStudio --remote script D:\Work\review.ipc.txt

Important:

  • target set is not a command inside the script file
  • it is configured outside the script, at the CLI level

docs.title: 8.4 A script file contains command tails only
docs.text:
Inside the script file, do not repeat hfStudio --remote.

Example review.ipc.txt:

open D:\Work\frame.hdb
camera fit
representation both
display-control grid off
write-scene D:\Work\frame.png

docs.title: 8.5 script-save records the current workflow
docs.text:
hfStudio --remote script-save D:\Work\last-session.ipc.txt

This stores the canonical command tails from the current session into a *.ipc.txt file.

The saved file can later be replayed with script.

docs.title: 8.6 Remember that scripts are fail-fast
docs.text:
Scripts run in fail-fast mode by default.

That means:

  • if any command in the file fails
  • execution stops at that point

For that reason, a good script usually:

  • stabilizes the target model and view state near the top
  • places exports and screenshots near the end

docs.title: 8.7 Think about --view-id per command
docs.text:
Some script lines may need to target a specific render view.

When that happens, first confirm in the Remote Control manual whether that command supports --view-id.

For early scripts, it is usually best to keep things simple and stay on the default activeRenderView.

docs.title: 8.8 Recommended workflow
docs.text:
1. perform the task once in the GUI or CLI
  2. save the sequence with script-save
  3. review the saved *.ipc.txt and remove unnecessary lines
  4. rerun it later with script

docs.title: 8.9 Related documents
docs.text:
• Remote Control Overview
  • hfStudio Remote Control Recipes

docs.title: 9.1 Goal
docs.text:
This tutorial combines the full workflow around a beam-based portal-frame example:

  • model review
  • analysis run
  • render-view layout
  • result review
  • optional script capture

docs.title: 9.2 Why use a portal frame
docs.text:
A portal frame is a good example because the strengths of a beam model are easy to see.

  • member forces and deformed shape are easy to read
  • full-frame behavior can be compared quickly
  • the roles of beams and columns are visually clear

docs.title: 9.3 Recommended sequence
docs.text:
1. open the model
  2. clean up the base scene
  3. run the analysis
  4. set the result step and frame
  5. inspect contour and deformed shape
  6. split the render views if comparison is needed

docs.title: 9.4 Example flow
docs.text:
hfStudio --remote open D:\Work\portal_frame.hdb
hfStudio --remote camera fit
hfStudio --remote representation both
hfStudio --remote display-control grid off
hfStudio --remote run-analysis
hfStudio --remote post-step STEP1
hfStudio --remote post-frame 1
hfStudio --remote post-plot deformed on
hfStudio --remote post-plot contour on
hfStudio --remote post-scalar S.Mises
hfStudio --remote post-display scalarbar on

docs.title: 9.5 Compare two views
docs.text:
For example:

  • r0: overall deformed shape
  • r1: stress contour

can be assigned separate roles.

hfStudio --remote view add render
hfStudio --remote --view-id r0 camera view +z
hfStudio --remote --view-id r1 camera view +z
hfStudio --remote --view-id r1 display-control grid off

docs.title: 9.6 What to review
docs.text:
• story drift or overall frame sway
  • stress concentration near beam-column connections
  • differences between load-case steps
  • response changes frame by frame

docs.title: 9.7 Save the workflow as a script
docs.text:
If the scene setup works well, save it.

hfStudio --remote script-save D:\Work\portal-review.ipc.txt

Then replay it later with:

hfStudio --remote script D:\Work\portal-review.ipc.txt

docs.title: 9.8 Summary
docs.text: The portal-frame example is a good practice case for showing how beam analysis, result review, and remote-control automation connect together.
